title: Family Reunion
story: Three years after my daughter vanished, I saw her in a wedding video from a mountain village. She wore a red bridal gown and kept shaking her head at the camera. I brought the police to that house. The girl who opened the door was her. The moment she saw me, her first words were: “I don’t know this man.” Why?
answer: The daughter had been abducted and sold into the mountains, where she bore a child. The family hired a photographer from the city to stage a belated wedding, hoping the video would dress a purchased marriage up as a happy occasion. She shook her head at the camera in the hope that, once the video circulated, someone would notice her plight. By the time her father arrived with the police, the buyer had already carried the baby into the backyard and was holding scissors to the child’s throat, forcing her to swear she had stayed of her own free will. She denied her father at the doorway while her eyes kept drifting toward the backyard. Her father thought she had forgotten him; in truth she was trading her own captivity for her child’s life.
hints: In those three years she had gained a family member she could never have carried away alone.
The head-shaking in the video and the denial at the door answered two different threats.
The buyer was holding her child; the denial was forced on her, to make the rescuers leave.

title: Encore
story: The theater caught fire, and the audience took it for part of the show, laughing and applauding. The actors screamed for their lives, and the applause only grew louder. The one who made no sound was the clown who played a mute. He drew a blade across his own face — and the front row finally began to run. Why?
answer: The production sold itself on hyper-real disaster scenes, and its publicity even warned the audience that actors might appear as trapped victims crying for help. When the fire broke out backstage for real, the crowd took the flames and the screams for theater — the more desperate the actors became, the more delighted they were. The mute clown came through the actors’ passage to the front of the house, saw that people still would not leave, and took off his mask. He slit his own face open with a blade from his makeup kit, let the blood drip down right before the first row, then pulled aside the cloth curtain blocking the exit. Only when the audience saw a performer wrecking his own makeup, ripping down the scenery, and the smoke-filled passage behind it did they understand that no one was ever going to call a halt to this fire.
hints: The show already featured lifelike cries for help and disaster scenes.
The real pleas for help were taken for part of the performance.
The clown broke the audience’s misreading by ruining his makeup and uncovering the real fire behind the scenery.

title: Outside the Window
story: The power went out at the mountain inn, and someone outside the window kept a flashlight fixed on me. Terrified, I shrank under the quilt. The innkeeper came and drew the curtains tight for me, saying it was the local children. The next day, when the rescue team stranded on the mountain reached the inn, the first thing they did was throw the innkeeper to the ground. Why?
answer: She was the survivor of a crash in the mountains, carried off by the innkeeper; her leg was hurt, and she believed he was nursing her. He had taken her phone and told her the mountain roads were cut off and the hills outside were full of men roaming the slopes to rob stranded travelers. In fact the crash survivors had been searched for all along; the innkeeper was hiding her, planning to sell her on, and he himself had cut the inn’s power. The flashlight at the window that night belonged to the searchers. They had spotted the figure upstairs and were signaling her to answer. The innkeeper covered the window just in time and lied that no one was upstairs. Blocked by the ruined road, the rescue team stayed the night on the mountain; at first light they found her bloodstained coat dumped in the ditch behind the inn, turned back, searched the place, and freed her.
hints: The innkeeper’s explanation for the people outside was not to be trusted.
She had been hurt before she ever checked in, and someone had been searching for her all along.
The flashlight was the search party; the innkeeper was hiding her and keeping her from answering.

title: Fingernails on the Wall
story: When I was locked in the cellar, the walls were already covered with scratch marks. Every time someone was taken out, one more appeared behind the door. On the day my turn came, the woman who had never once spoken lunged at me and clawed my hand open. In the confusion, she pressed a fingernail into my palm. Why?
answer: A gang of kidnappers was moving its victims out in batches, and the woman had been using the scratches to tally how many were taken. Her husband was held in the room next door; once, while a guard looked away, he rolled a thin plastic strip engraved with the gang’s address through the crack in the door to her, and was killed for it soon after. She cut the strip down to the size of a fingernail and hid it beneath a loose false nail. Knowing that as a witness she would most likely never leave alive, she picked a deliberate fight with the girl about to be moved out and pressed the false nail, address and all, into her hand. The claw wounds let the girl keep her hand curled as if in pain, hiding what she held. When the transport van stopped, the girl dropped the plastic strip to a scrap collector at the roadside.
hints: The woman wanted one thing carried out of the cellar.
The fingernail she gave could be peeled off.
Beneath the false nail lay the gang’s address, and the fight was cover for passing on the cry for help.

title: Stand-In
story: For the last scene of the film, the director found me a stand-in who looked just like me. I lay down in the coffin and watched her walk to the cliff in my place. She turned her head and smiled at me. The director called “Action” — and the coffin lid closed at that very moment. Why?
answer: She had come into an inheritance, and her husband, on the pretext of investing in a movie, had arranged for her to star in a thriller shot in a remote mountain district. He brought in his mistress, who resembled her, planning to film the mistress in a long shot walking to the cliff’s edge, then push his wife over and stage it as a filming accident. The coffin scene and the cliff scene were described to her as one continuous shot, so she climbed into the coffin. The director and the whole crew were accomplices the husband had hired; the call of “Action” was in fact the signal to seal the coffin and carry her to the clifftop. The stand-in she watched walking away in her own clothes was there to leave pictures of “the wife herself” at the edge — footage to match the body that would appear at the bottom of the cliff.
hints: The location and the crew had all been arranged by her husband.
The stand-in had to be filmed as her, while the real her had to disappear from the camera.
The husband meant to shoot the stand-in’s distant figure first, then push his wife off the cliff and fake a filming accident.

title: The Wake
story: Past midnight at the wake, cries for help came from inside the coffin. I scrambled to flee, but my grandfather took up a pair of pliers and drew out the coffin nails one by one. The lid opened, and the person inside climbed out alive. Only then did I see that my grandfather was wearing the burial clothes that had been laid out for him. Why?
answer: In the wars of the old days, the villagers used a funeral to hide a wounded man the soldiers were hunting, planning to carry him through the blockade in the coffin the next day. Grandfather was the carpenter in on the escape, and had long since left breathing holes in the lid. Too many mourners kept watch, so the wounded man had held his silence until deep in the night, when the pain forced him to call out. Grandfather had known all along who was inside; he pulled the nails to let the man out, breathe, and change his dressings. With the searching troops about to enter the village, grandfather decided the wounded man would dress in his clothes and pass as a mourning relative, while he himself put on the burial clothes, lay down in the coffin, and played the dead man for the inspection. The grandson had known only that the family was holding a funeral; not until he saw the burial clothes and the two trading outfits did he understand this was an arrangement for carrying a living man out.
hints: The person in the coffin had been alive the whole time, and grandfather knew who he was.
This funeral was meant to carry a hunted man through the blockade.
Grandfather would wear the burial clothes and play the corpse, letting the wounded man walk out as a mourner.

title: Ten Minutes Behind
story: The mirror in my grandmother’s house ran ten minutes slow. As a child, I would pull faces at it, then sit down and wait for it to copy me. After she died, I went back to sort out her things and fixed my hair in front of the mirror first. Ten minutes later, as I turned to leave, it suddenly seized the me that was still standing before it. How is this possible?
answer: The mirror kept a living image of whoever had stood before it ten minutes earlier, and the thing inside could seize that image before it faded and drag the person it belonged to into the glass. Grandmother had kept a seal pressed against the back of the frame, and while she lived the lag was only a harmless oddity. After her death, a relative sorting out her things tore the seal away by mistake. The granddaughter had stood before the mirror, then turned to go, believing she was safely out of its reach; her image from ten minutes before had only just appeared. The hand in the mirror closed on that image, and the real woman was dragged back before the glass.
hints: The past inside the mirror was still connected to the living person outside it.
While grandmother lived, something on the frame had been holding it in check.
Once the seal was torn away, the thing in the mirror could seize the living through their ten-minute-old image.

title: The Mender
story: The old craftsman said that anything broken, brought into his shop, would be restored to the shape it wore the day before by the next morning. I took him my smashed wedding photograph. The next day, the husband in the photo came back. I was overjoyed — until he looked down at his own hands, and then at the drawer where I had hidden the knife. Why?
answer: The shop’s mending restored a photograph, and the person inside it, to the state of twenty-four hours before it was brought in — body and memory alike fixed at that moment. The craftsman wrote this price on the back of the receipt. The wife had killed her husband the night before, and in the struggle the wedding photograph had been smashed. Wanting the room set back to rights, she had looked only at the price and never read the receipt. Twenty-four hours back, the husband was still alive — and had already happened to see her hide the knife in the drawer. When the photograph was restored, he woke in the house too; he looked down at the cut left on his hand from chopping vegetables the day before, and followed his memory to the drawer. The photograph she had wanted mended brought back the very man she had just killed.
hints: The mending of a photograph reaches the person inside it.
Body and memory both return to twenty-four hours before it was brought in.
She had killed her husband the night before; the restored husband still remembered where she hid the knife.

title: Finish It Before Bed
story: At a secondhand book stall I bought a horror novel whose heroine bore my name. When I read of her hearing a knock at her door in the middle of the night, there came a knock at mine. I threw the book into the stove. The last page curled in the fire, and only one line could still be read: “She thought the story was over.” How is this possible?
answer: The stall owner had written his own ordeal into a book that passes its misfortune on. Any reader who reads her own name in it becomes the story’s heroine, and everything not yet read plays out in the real world in the order written; only by finishing the book does the reader reach the way out — changing the heroine’s name back to that of the book’s previous holder. To free himself, the owner had sold it to her for almost nothing. By the time she read of the knocking, the curse had already passed to her, and burning the book destroyed nothing but the way out. The last line she saw stood at the end of the story proper; tucked after it had been the page for changing the name, left there by the owner. The thing outside the door went on knocking.
hints: The stall owner knew exactly what the book would do.
By the time she read her own name, the book’s ordeal had already become hers.
The way out was hidden at the back of the book; the fire destroyed the cure, and the curse already transferred went on.

title: The Sea Behind the Door
story: My daughter drew a door on her bedroom wall and said that Mommy came home through it every day. I thought she missed her mother too much, so I drew a lock on that door. That night, knocking came from inside the wall. The next morning, her bed was soaked with seawater. How is this possible?
answer: The daughter could paint doors that truly opened onto the land of the dead, and a door connected to one particular dead person only when she wrote that name upon it. Her mother had drowned in the sea; every night the girl let her step briefly into the bedroom and sent her back before dawn. Seawater could pour through whenever the door opened, so she opened it only a crack. The father knew nothing of his wife’s name written on the inside of the doorframe, nor that a lock drawn upon the door would lock it from the side of the living. That night the mother, coming to her door, was shut outside it. Once her father was asleep, the daughter rubbed the lock out and pushed the door open in her haste, and the sea poured into the room. The water on the bed held the damp print of an embrace; the mother had gone back.
hints: The mother died in the sea, and the door the girl drew really did open.
A drawn lock works too — and when the door opens, the water outside can come through.
The father had locked the returning mother outside; the girl erased the lock and opened the door, and the sea broke in with her.

title: The Awning
story: A rainstorm had washed out the road, and we took shelter for the night in a mountain temple. Past midnight the abbot knocked at every door, asking the guests to come stand for a while under the awning in the courtyard. When he came to the last guest, the man suddenly sank to his knees. The abbot looked down at the man’s feet, and told the monks behind him: “Found him.” Why?
answer: The temple had taken in a girl who had been kidnapped; her kidnappers had tracked her there and mingled with the travelers sheltering from the rain. The girl was hiding on top of the awning, the iron chain still on her ankle, a stretch of it showing through a gap in the boards. When the abbot found her at midnight, he learned from her that she had bitten through her kidnapper’s trouser cuff and left blood on the upper of his right shoe. He gathered everyone under the awning so that he could study each man’s shoes and trousers in the lamplight without alarming the kidnapper still in the guest rooms. The last man saw the chain he had let fall dangling above his head, knew the girl was right there above him, and saw the monks already closing in around him — so he dropped to his knees and begged.
hints: The temple was sheltering someone who needed protecting.
What the abbot studied was the guests’ shoes and trousers.
The kidnapper’s shoes and trousers still carried the marks of the girl’s fight, and her ankle chain hung down from the top of the awning.

title: The Borrowed Umbrella
story: At the train station, my mother lent her umbrella to a woman. The woman took it, looked at me, said thank you, and ran. As my mother hurried after her, I saw the umbrella fully open for the first time: its underside was covered with photographs of the same child. Why?
answer: The boy had been abducted and forced to call the woman who took him “Mama.” At the station she had picked out a traveler carrying a small child, and the loan of the umbrella was her pretext for striking up conversation, so she could follow the woman and steer her somewhere secluded. Days earlier, while the woman was out, the boy had torn his own missing-child flyers from the street and pasted them inside the umbrella. On rainy days she carried it folded, and had noticed nothing. The traveler opened it, matched the photographs to the boy she had just looked at, and ran straight to the officer on duty with her child in her arms. The abductor chased after her, meaning to snatch the umbrella back and destroy the evidence. The boy had finally found someone willing to really look at the umbrella.
hints: The woman the boy called mother had brought him to the station for another purpose.
The photographs were pasted there by the boy himself, plain to whoever opened the umbrella.
Inside the umbrella were his missing-child flyers, and the woman who received it ran for the police.

title: The Seventh Step
story: Every night when Father came home, the seventh stair creaked once. Mother said I could come out of the cupboard only when I heard it. That day Father was away on business — and I heard the creak all the same. I had just touched the cupboard door when Mother, outside, began to weep and beg me not to come out. Why?
answer: Father was a forest ranger, and the boss of a poaching ring had been threatening Mother for a long time. She hid the child away and only let him out to move about when her husband was home. The boss knew the family’s rhythm; he broke in while Father was away, demanding the evidence of poaching that Father had gathered. Mother lied that the boy had been sent elsewhere. Searching the house, he stepped on the seventh stair, and the child in the cupboard mistook it for Father coming home. Mother heard the cupboard door stir; terrified that the boss would find the boy and take a second hostage, she could only scream and plead to hold him back. The footstep that had always meant safety belonged, this time, to the man hunting them.
hints: Mother hid the child to keep him away from a living man.
The creak proved only that someone had stepped on that stair.
While Father was away, the man threatening Mother broke in, and the child mistook his step for Father’s.

title: Night Shift
story: When the power failed at the funeral home, a woman came running out of the morgue. She seized me and begged me not to call security. I took her for frightened out of her mind, and pressed the buzzer anyway. The guard pushed through the door — and called out a name she had not gone by for ten years. Why?
answer: The woman had changed her name to escape the husband who used to beat her, and had lately been working as a cleaner at the funeral home. Her husband, asking after her everywhere, had altered his face and taken the job of night guard, waiting for a chance to take her away when the building was empty. The blackout was his doing. She had gone into the morgue to check the emergency lights and, through the glass of the door, saw the guard lifting his head to search for her; she knew the old scar, and the ring he never took off, and fled to the attendant newly on duty. The attendant thought her half-mad with the dark and the dead, and rang for a guard to help. The old name the man blurted at the door told the attendant why she had begged him not to ring; he locked the inner door and called the police.
hints: The woman who came running out worked there.
She had changed her name to escape someone who knew her old identity.
The night guard was the abusive husband who had tracked her down, and the blackout was his; the bell called him straight to her.

title: Fourth Place
story: On the island, the race gave its prizes to the top three alone. On the last lap I saw my father standing just past the finish line, and I deliberately fell. As the third-place runner passed me he even turned back to laugh. Before the awards, Father dragged me aboard a boat without letting me so much as put on my shoes. Why?
answer: The island’s warlord had lured a crowd of young men there with talk of recruiting athletes, and the race was his way of picking out the three strongest bodies, to be sold to an underground fighting ring. The rest would be sent away, so that the recruiting front could go on working. Father, who had once run boats for the warlord, learned by chance that his son was on the island and raced to save him. He could not warn the boy in front of the guards, so from beyond the finish line he kept flashing the “fall down and play dead” signal from the chasing game of the boy’s childhood — a sign only the two of them knew. The son understood and dropped himself to fourth. Using the boat that carried away the rejected runners, Father got him off the island. Third place stayed behind the iron gate at the back of the podium.
hints: The prize for winning was nothing the runners imagined.
Father was making a sign only his son could read.
The top three were to be kept and sold; he fell to fourth on purpose and bought himself the chance to leave.

title: Letters Home
story: After my brother was trapped in the mine, a letter home would come out through the food slot every few days. The first six all said he was safe. The seventh held nothing but a blank sheet of paper. Mother felt the corner of the page, then suddenly ordered the pumps stopped. Down in the mine, the owner kept pressing: “Hurry it up — everyone’s waiting!” Why?
answer: After the collapse, the mine’s owner had locked the men who knew the truth of the accident in an abandoned gallery and forced them to write letters home, to keep up the appearance of a rescue in progress. The drain pipes, meant for pumping water out, in fact ran into the small hollow where the men were sheltering; once switched on, they would pour the pooled surface water in on them. My brother had discovered that the sheets were drawn one by one from beneath carbon paper: the earlier letters had been dictated by the owner, and he had never found a way to send a warning. The seventh time, he deliberately handed out the bottom sheet, the one with no ink on it. Into its corner he had pressed, with his fingernail, the danger mark he and his mother had agreed on when he was small, and on the sheet above he had borne down hard as he wrote “the water comes in from above,” letting the words sink into the blank page below. Mother tilted the paper to the light, saw the pressed lines, and stopped the pumps just in time.
hints: The owner controlled what the letters said, and the food slot, and the pipes.
The blank sheet carried words pressed into it.
Under the name of drainage the owner meant to flood the hollow where the men hid, and my brother sent his warning out in the dents.

title: The Ferry Crossing
story: By night, the ferryman would take only one living passenger across the river. Father carried me up the boat on his back, and the ferryman shook his head. He set me down and walked alone into the reeds. When he came back, the ferryman took his coin and even helped me hold Father steady. Why?
answer: The crossing joined the bank of the living to the bank of the dead, and a single boat might carry only one living soul; the dead could ride as bodies. The child had caught a ghost-illness whose only cure lay across the river, and could no longer sit upright alone. Father knew the ferryman told the living by their heartbeat, and knew the boat would never leave the shore with two live passengers. He walked into the reeds and took the deadly poison he had long carried with him — the dead of this crossing can still move until sunrise. The father who came back had no heartbeat, and could carry the child aboard. The ferryman steadied the body as it stiffened, and ferried the child to the cure.
hints: The river joins the world of the living to the world of the dead.
When Father came out of the reeds, he was no longer one of the living.
He had made himself one of the dead who can move before sunrise, leaving the boat’s single place for the living to his child.

title: Don’t Turn On the Light
story: I fled into the house, and the thing chasing me stopped outside the door. My little brother said, don’t be afraid, it’s safe in here. He reached for the light switch — and I lunged at him and bit his hand. In the dark, my own voice came from beyond the door: “Turn on the light. I’m so cold.” Why?
answer: A thing had come to the town that walks about draped in people’s shadows. Touch a person’s shadow where it falls on the ground, and it can crawl up the shadow into the body and strip out the skin and the voice. The elder sister had been chased down the street and had fled into the unlit house; with no light, her shadow vanished, and the thing could not come near. It had already heard her voice, and stood at the door mimicking her, baiting her brother to turn on the light. For if the light came on, the sister standing by the door would throw her shadow out through the crack of the door — straight into its reach. She knew to whom that voice outside belonged, and she fought with everything she had to keep her brother’s hand from the switch.
hints: It must touch a person’s shadow before it can do them any further harm.
The house was safe because there was no light in it.
Light would have pushed the sister’s shadow out through the crack of the door, giving her pursuer a path to her.

title: Snow for the Whole Village
story: The village had not seen snow for thirty years, yet the family portrait hanging in the ancestral hall was always white with it. Every day the clan elder wiped the snow from the photograph and warned us never to touch the frame. Yesterday he died. This morning, a trail of wet footprints lay before every house in the village. How is this possible?
answer: Thirty years before, to seize the camera brought by a family of outsiders, the clan elder had left that family trapped on the snowy mountain, waited until they froze to death, and taken their photograph. The camera binds the dead it captures into their final scene, and the weather in the picture keeps replaying itself; once the snow buries the edge of the image, the dead can climb out of the frame along it. Every day the elder wiped away the snow that truly grew on the photograph’s surface, keeping the prison sealed. The villagers had taken that family for the elder’s own kin, never knowing that the “family portrait” in the ancestral hall held a household of murdered souls. After he died there was no one left to wipe the snow; the dead stepped over the frame and went from house to house, seeking out everyone who had shared in the killing.
hints: The snow inside the photograph piles up for real.
Wiping it away every day held a boundary shut.
The elder had trapped the murdered family in the photograph; once the snow rose past the frame, they walked out.

title: Your Turn to Sleep
story: My brother had not slept for seven days. He tied me to a chair and begged me: tonight, whatever happens, do not fall asleep. I promised. At dawn he opened his eyes, saw me, and held me and wept for a long time. On the chair behind his bed, hair had grown thick and full. Why?
answer: The brothers had moved into a cursed house where an empty chair had been left behind. If, in the night, the thing in the house finds every living soul asleep, it grows a whole body out of the chair and eats one of them; while anyone is awake, it can do no more than slowly put out hair. The elder brother had been trapped alone in the house for seven days, the door locked from outside by the landlord, food passed in through a small hatch. When the landlord tricked the younger brother, who had come looking for him, inside as well, the elder brother could at last sleep in shifts. Afraid his brother would give out and drop asleep on the floor, he tied him to the chair facing the empty one, so that he would keep his eyes on the thing as it grew and let fear hold him up. The younger brother never once closed his eyes that night. When the elder woke and saw that the hair had not yet formed a body, only then did he dare believe they had both lived to the dawn.
hints: The elder brother needed sleep, and he needed someone awake in the house at all times.
Something was growing out of the other chair, the one his brother faced.
As long as someone was awake and watching it, it could not grow the body it needed to eat them.

title: The Song Next Door
story: In the prison, someone sang every morning. The jailers said it was the released ones saying farewell to us all. I kept longing for the day I would hear my own voice. On my day, the song rose from the cell next door — and the jailer brought a strip of black cloth for my eyes. Why?
answer: The prisoners were held in a secret prison cut off from the world. On arrival, each man was made to record a song; the authorities said it would be played on the day of his release, to remind everyone that keeping the rules meant a way out. In truth the songs were played to drown the sounds of execution, and to make the rest believe that the men taken away had gone free. The song the narrator waited for was the one recorded on his own first day. Only when he saw the black cloth and heard the jailer tell him to hand over his last effects did he understand that the men who sang every morning had never once left the prison.
hints: The songs had all been recorded when the prisoners arrived.
Nothing was ever heard again from the ones said to be released.
The singing covered the executions, and kept the prisoners believing in the promise of release.

title: The Red Cloth
story: On the eve of the wedding, my grandmother cut a length from the hem of my bridal gown. I ran crying to my mother, and the moment she saw the dress she began to weep too. Before daybreak she sent me out through the window. When I came home again, that strip of red cloth was hanging in the mourning hall. Why?
answer: In the old days, a rich family in the village had bought a bride for their dead son — a ghost marriage, where a living girl is wed to the dead — and the matchmaker had kept all of it from the girl, telling her the marriage would pay for her mother’s medical treatment. Grandmother had sewn such bridal gowns in her youth, and she saw at once that beneath the bright red overskirt lay a white lining marked with the dead man’s birth and death dates. Watched by the family members who were selling the girl, she could not run away with her granddaughter alone, so she cut the overskirt short in front of everyone and, under cover of the girl’s sobbing, sent her running to her mother to look at the dress. The mother saw the death date laid bare, and knew that someone meant to send her living daughter down to be buried with the dead; that same night she smuggled her away. Grandmother was beaten to death in the family’s revenge. The mother hung the red cloth grandmother had left in the mourning hall, and hid the white lining away, waiting for her daughter to come back with people from beyond the mountains to bear witness.
hints: The groom had been dead all along, and the girl was never told.
Cutting the dress laid bare writing hidden in the lining.
Grandmother knew it for a ghost-marriage gown; she warned the mother by ruining it, saved her granddaughter, and paid with her life.

title: Lost and Found
story: After the ship went down, I went to claim the luggage the salvagers had raised. The clerk handed me my father’s suitcase, and I told him he was mistaken. I knew that suitcase, and I knew the things inside it. Father would never have taken that prosthetic leg with him. Why?
answer: Before setting sail, Father had locked away in the old house the prosthetic leg the daughter’s dead brother had left, saying he never wanted to see it again. He was taking his daughter on the voyage to be rid, along the way, of the evidence of the brother he had killed years before; packed in the suitcase with the leg were the clothes the brother had been wearing when he vanished, and a bloodstained knife. The sinking had dredged the suitcase up with the ordinary lost luggage. The daughter had always thought Father kept the leg out of sentiment; only when she saw the clothes, the knife, and the old things packed together did she understand that Father had spent years hiding what became of her brother. Father was there at the claims desk; afraid of putting him on his guard, she first denied that the suitcase was her family’s, then quietly turned to the staff for help.
hints: She denied the suitcase in front of her father for a reason.
It was packed with old things that belonged to a missing member of the family.
Father had meant to drop the evidence of her brother’s murder into the sea; the wreck raised it up in front of everyone.

title: The Door Chain
story: Someone knocked in the middle of the night, and Father spoke to him through the door chain. The man outside never lifted his head, yet Father suddenly shouted for me to run. By the time I got down the stairs, Father was climbing out of the back window too. He was clutching a bunch of keys in his hand — and the door of our house had already been opened. How is this possible?
answer: Father, who had once done the lock work for this old building, had found signs that someone had been through the house that night. He changed the lock first of all, kept the new keys clutched in his hand, and was about to call the police. The knock in the night came from a robber who had followed them home. The man outside bent over his bag on purpose, drawing Father to the door, while a second accomplice, already hidden inside, heard the talking and reached from behind Father to slip the chain off its track. In the reflection on the door’s glass, Father saw that hand. He sent the child down the back stairs at once and climbed out the back window himself; the door was then opened by the accomplice within. The keys had never left Father’s hand, and he understood at last that the real danger had entered the house before he ever changed the lock.
hints: Father had changed the lock that same night, and the keys never left his hand.
The glass in the door showed him the small patch of hallway behind his back.
The robber’s accomplice was already hidden inside, unhooking the chain from within.

title: Praying for Rain
story: The village had been dry for three years, and we sent the last child into the temple of the mountain god. The next day, the rain came at last. The grown-ups knelt in the mud and knocked their foreheads to the ground; I raised an umbrella instead and went from house to house telling everyone to run. Where the rain fell into the bowls, it cried like an infant. What was happening?
answer: The mountain god had agreed to give back what the villagers had offered it; it had never once promised rain. Through those three years the clan chief had named each vanished child the price of asking for rain, and child after child had gone up the mountain. The last time, the narrator stole close enough to hear the god’s actual words inside the temple, and understood that the villagers had read them wrong. The mountain god was giving back the children it had swallowed, changed into rain: each vessel the falling water filled would gather itself into a child who still remembered being offered up. The clan chief meant to knock every vessel over before that could happen. The narrator held an umbrella over the bowl at one doorstep — the bowl that held the narrator’s own little sister — and hurried the villagers away with their children, out of the path of the chief, who was coming up the slope with a blade.
hints: The god’s answer was a return of the offerings, which the villagers took for a promise of rain.
When the rain fills a vessel to the brim, it gathers back into the person who was sacrificed.
The children were coming back; the true danger to them was the clan chief, afraid of his crime coming to light.

title: The Second Vow
story: We were married in a mountain valley, where the wedding vows must be spoken twice. I had finished the first vow when the bride clamped her hand over my mouth. The second vow was finished for me, from the other side of the mountain. She let go of me, walked toward that voice, and never once looked back. Why?
answer: Something in the valley can mimic a human voice it has heard once. If the bride hears the same voice speak the wedding vows twice in a row, she will take the source of the second voice as her husband and follow it forever. To keep the village safe, the villagers dressed this soul-snatching rule up as a wedding custom and invited outside couples into the valley to hold their ceremony. After the first vow, the bride saw a figure identical to the groom standing beneath the far cliff wall; remembering an old woman's warning from the road, she hastily covered the groom's mouth. But the thing had already learned his voice, and it spoke the second vow for him. From then on the bride acknowledged only the voice from beyond the mountain, leaving the real groom standing in place.
hints: Something in the valley can mimic a human voice it has just heard.
The second vow decides whom the bride will recognize as her husband.
The villagers lure couples into the valley with the wedding custom, letting a thing that imitates the groom take the bride away.

title: The Cell Door
story: The cell door has no lock, and the guard died long ago. I have lived here for forty years, and every day I watched my wife standing outside the door. She grew older day by day. Today she finally stopped coming — and for the first time, I heard someone outside the door calling me Papa. Who was calling me?
answer: With a forbidden art he had pulled his dying wife back from death as she was about to give birth; the price was a cell that only his own child could lead him out of. The wife lost the child in childbirth and, believing her husband could never be freed, came to visit every day. Forty years later she died, and in the underworld she found their child, who had died before growing up. The child had stayed the age he was at death and could not recognize his father on his own, so the mother finally led him to the cell door and taught him to say 'Papa.' The door's binding had never required the child to be alive. The father stepped out at last — and could only close his hands around two small, icy ones.
hints: The price of his imprisonment was bound up with bringing his wife back to life.
The only person who can lead him out is the child who never got to grow up.
After her death, the wife found the child who died young and brought the one who could break the binding to the cell door.

title: The One Who Came Back
story: Two lines of footprints crossed the snow, mine and my brother's. At the village gate he suddenly told me to close my eyes, and carried me on his back into the ancestral hall. At dawn I went out and found the shoes he had left behind. Outside the hall door there was a new line of bare footprints, leading all the way to my brother's grave. What had happened?
answer: The brother had died on the snow mountain a year before. This time it was the younger brother who got lost on the mountain and lay close to death; the elder brother's ghost followed the trail the boy stamped into the snow, took on the appearance of a living man for a while, and carried his frozen, half-conscious brother back to the village on his back. The ancestral hall can preserve a living person's life, but it strips a ghost of its borrowed form. The brother told the boy to keep his eyes closed because he did not want him to watch his body come apart. Waking in the hall, the younger brother at last remembered that his brother had been buried long ago. The ghost left the shoes he had worn in life, walked barefoot back to his grave, and left one last trail in the snow.
hints: The younger brother was freezing and barely conscious on the mountain; his brother had died long before.
Entering the ancestral hall returns a ghost to what it truly is.
The brother came back to save him, carried him to safety, left his shoes behind, and returned to his own grave.

title: The Audition
story: A film crew came to town hiring professional mourners. I could cry the most convincingly, and I was the one rejected. The bus home had barely pulled away when the director chased it down and brought me back alone. He said that after seeing me, his leading lady had finally agreed to speak. When I stepped into the room, she was huddled in the corner, calling me Mama. Why did she call me Mama?
answer: The 'film crew' was a broker arranging a ghost marriage for a rich household — a wedding for the dead. They hired mourning actors so the ceremony would look like an ordinary funeral on camera and hush the village gossip. The 'leading lady' they were holding was the mother's daughter, missing for years. The mother had traced a suspicious casting notice to this village and applied under a false name. After recognizing her through a crack in the door, the daughter kept crying out; the director, afraid she would fall apart at the wedding, decided a hired mourner might soothe her and had the bus chased down. Stepping into the room, the mother saw the chain on her daughter's feet, and across from her the memorial portrait of the groom. The safety call she had arranged before setting out was never made — and the police waiting outside the village moved in, as agreed.
hints: The mother took the job while searching for her missing daughter.
The 'film crew' is arranging hired relatives for a ghost marriage.
The daughter recognized the mother who had come for her in disguise; the brokers, thinking a hired mourner could calm her, delivered the mother right to her.

title: The Last Group Photo
story: After the avalanche, the rescue team found our group photo buried at the camp. Six people were in the photograph; only five of us were rescued. When the team leader asked about the sixth, not one of us would speak. In the end he peeled the photograph apart — and there was one more person on the back. What were we hiding?
answer: The expedition had set out with seven. When the blizzard trapped them, the leader left a badly wounded climber behind in a crevasse, took his food, and told the others he was already dead. Another climber learned the truth and prepared to go for help alone; before leaving, he glued two photographs face to face, with the abandoned man's photo hidden on the back and his location written beside it, and buried them beneath the rescue marker next to the tent so the leader would not find them. He died on his way back to the crevasse. The five survivors knew what the leader had done and, fearing the blame, hid the true number together. The rescue leader, feeling the photograph's odd thickness, peeled it open — and found the seventh man, still waiting in the crevasse.
hints: The party that set out was larger than the front of the photo showed.
Someone wanted to leave a clue but feared the leader would find it.
Two photographs were glued together; hidden inside was the location of the deliberately abandoned seventh man.

title: Two Coughs
story: At the funeral, my daughter suddenly coughed twice toward the coffin. I rushed to cover her mouth. From inside the coffin came two coughs in answer. My husband, seated in the front row, stood up and shut the doors of the mourning hall. Why did he shut them?
answer: The wife had discovered that her husband murdered his business partner. With her younger brother, who worked at the funeral home, she used the partner's funeral as cover to hide the witness her husband was holding captive inside a second coffin that was due to be shipped out. The daughter had once agreed with the witness on two coughs as an all-clear signal; seeing a familiar shoe showing through the lid that had never been properly closed, she could not help sending the greeting. The witness, thinking his rescuers had come, answered her. The husband knew the voice at once — the man he was hunting for was hidden in that coffin — and he sealed the mourning hall's exit. The wife had covered the girl's mouth to keep her from giving them away; she was a step too late.
hints: One of the coffins in the mourning hall holds a living man.
The two coughs were an agreed signal.
The wife used the funeral to rescue the witness her husband had locked up; the child's early signal gave away his hiding place.

title: The Eighteenth Candle
story: Every year on my sister's birthday, Father lit only seventeen candles. My sister always sat quietly in her chair, and I blew them out for her. The year I turned eighteen, I secretly added one more candle. When Father saw it, he lifted my sister out of her chair for the very first time. Why?
answer: At seventeen, the sister had discovered a murder her father committed, and he had silenced her. He preserved her body into a crude specimen and kept it in an abandoned freezer room, bringing his young son in there each year for a birthday party and telling him his sister had a strange illness that left her unable to speak or move. As the boy grew, the smell, the stitching, and a face that never changed told him the truth. On his own eighteenth birthday, he added one more candle to his sister's cake on purpose, to see whether his father would still insist his sister remained seventeen. The father understood that his son had seen through everything, and gathered up the specimen, ready to move it. The son had already sent the freezer room's location to a friend, with one agreement: if no reply came back, call the police.
hints: The sister's face and age are stopped at seventeen.
The father invented the story of her illness.
What sits in the chair is the sister's remains; the extra candle told the father his son had seen through the lie.

title: Resurfaced
story: The diver surfaced from the sunken ship dragging a man behind him, and the man clung to him and would not let go. The crew on the boat cheered them both — until the diver took off his mask. I knew that face at once, and shouted for the rope to be cut. Why did I have it cut?
answer: They had been hunting the pirates who hijacked a pleasure boat; the narrator was a rescued passenger helping to identify faces. The real diver was ambushed beside the wreck by a pirate dressed in dive gear of his own and left injured and unconscious. The pirate lashed the diver's arms around his own chest and swam for the rescue boat, posing as the rescuing diver, so that everyone on deck took the scene for a drowning man clinging in terror to his savior. As the pirate pulled off his mask to climb the ladder, a passenger recognized the face — and a knife showed at his sleeve. What the narrator had cut was the thin cord binding the real diver's arms, so the rescuers could pull the hostage away from the pirate.
hints: The man in the diving gear was swapped underwater.
The arms wrapped around him were tied there.
The pirate wore the rescuer's gear, bound the real diver to himself, and boarded the boat posing as the savior.

title: The Man Outside the Photo
story: In the old house there hangs a wedding photograph with a strip cut away from the right side. Aunt said someone ill-omened once stood there. After my father died, I found that cut strip in the pocket he wore against his chest. The man who had been cut out looked exactly like my father. Who was he?
answer: The father had an elder twin brother, standing on the right in the wedding photo. The two had run a mine in partnership until they fell out over money. The father engineered a mine disaster that killed his brother, then spread the story that the elder brother had fled with the mine's funds, and the aunt, believing the lie, had hated her eldest brother ever since. The family cut the brother out of the wedding photograph and never mentioned him again. Yet the father kept the cut strip for decades, and before he died he wrote a letter confessing the truth about the mine disaster, hiding it with the photograph in the pocket over his heart. Only when the son drew out that strip of a face did he understand: the man whose face his father always claimed not to remember had been carried against his heart the whole time.
hints: The two men in the photograph are twins.
The family was always told that their uncle had run off with the money.
The father killed his brother in a staged mine disaster, cut him from the public photo, yet kept the strip hidden and left the truth in a last letter.

title: The Third Bell
story: In this town, the bell strikes only twice. When a third strike sounds, whoever stands outside your door must be let in. After Father died, Mother sat waiting by the door every night. Last night the third strike finally came — and she barred the door, held me tight, and said, 'This time, nobody answer.' Why?
answer: Whenever one of the town's dead is granted leave to come home, the bell strikes a third time. The returning spirit may enter only if someone inside answers through the door — and whoever answers is taken away in the dead one's place. At first the mother knew only that the bell could bring her husband home, and she kept watch by the door. Near midnight, searching her husband's effects, she had found an old soul-exchange deed: years before, to save himself, he had made the child's grandmother answer the door, trading her away to buy back his own life. Last night she heard her husband outside calling one name only — the child's — and understood he meant to borrow a life again. She barred the door, covered the child's mouth, and waited for the bell to pass.
hints: The third bell gives the dead one chance to come home — for a price.
Whoever answers the call at the door pays that price.
The father wanted the child to answer and trade the child's life for his return; the mother had just discovered the rule.

title: Calling Her Back
story: After my mother disappeared, I went to the well every day to call her name. On the first day, the well answered once. On the second day, it answered twice. On the seventh day, a great many voices rose out of it at once, all of them begging me to stop calling. That night, my mother stood dripping wet beside my bed. Why?
answer: Call a dead person's name at the old well for seven days running, and the well will send them back — but every call takes the shadow of one of the dead below and sews it into a body for the one returning. The mother had been murdered and thrown into the well; hers was the first voice that answered. As their shadows were stripped from them, the other dead below also heard the child's calling and hurried to stop him. On the seventh day the mother left the well in a body stitched together and came to the child's bedside. The face was still hers, but behind it crowded many shadows sewn into one, and from inside her body came the voices of those people, begging the child to send them back into the well.
hints: The well already held many dead.
The calling was stitching a body back together for the mother.
That body was pieced from other ghosts' shadows, and their cries for help came home with her.

title: Tomorrow's Obituary
story: A newspaper dated tomorrow was delivered to my door, and the obituary inside carried my own name. In the photograph, I was wearing a wedding dress. I canceled the wedding at once and burned the dress. At midnight, my fiancé carried in a new one, saying we still had a ceremony left unfinished. What ceremony?
answer: The fiancé had made a bargain with a ghost at the newspaper: the next day's paper, already printed with what will have happened, could be delivered to him early — but the paper records only the final outcome, and nothing a reader does can change it. He meant to offer his bride-to-be as a sacrifice in a ghost marriage to bring back his dead first wife. The bridal portrait in her obituary was the very notice he would place afterward. He left the paper at her door on purpose, so that fear would drive her to call off the wedding and stay home alone; once the public ceremony with its guests was canceled, he could take her away to the soul-exchange rite. The dress she burned was the one made for a living bride — the one he brought at midnight was the dress in the obituary photograph.
hints: The one who delivered the paper and the one who brought the new dress were following one plan.
Canceling the public wedding left her alone, without her guests.
The fiancé meant to trade a ghost marriage for his first wife's return; the dress in the obituary belonged to the midnight rite.

title: The Last Row
story: In this cinema, the last row is never sold. As the audience filed out, I saw my mother sitting there. I ran toward her — but the me on the screen got there first. She took that boy's hand and walked out through the far side of the screen. How is this possible?
answer: On a dead person's death anniversary, the cinema screens the day they most wished to live over again. The last row is kept for the dead; the people in the film are that day's memories, and the living can only watch. The mother had died in the accident the day her young son went missing, and to her last breath she wished she could take his hand and lead him home. Years later the son walked into the screening without knowing — and the film showing was that very day. As he ran toward his mother, the little boy on the screen, the him of that day, had just been found. The mother took that remembered child by the hand, led him out of the accident scene, and, her wish fulfilled at last, faded away together with the picture. The grown son reached only an empty seat; all that was left on it was her movie ticket.
hints: The film on the screen showed the day of the mother's deepest regret.
The boy in the film was him as a small child.
In that memory, the mother finally found her lost child; her wish complete, she left the cinema.

title: Growing Up for Her
story: My sister was sixteen when she died, and every year Mother added one more wrinkle to her memorial portrait. I told her that people don't age that quickly, and she told me to mind my own business. This year I turned thirty, and the hair in my sister's portrait had gone completely white. Mother looked at me and cried herself hoarse overnight. Why?
answer: The mother had borrowed her daughter's remaining years from the spirit in the portrait, and with them saved her young son, who should have died with his sister in the car crash. Under the bargain, every year the son lived cost the sister's ghost, dwelling in the portrait, three years of her remaining life, and the portrait aged with the loss. The mother added the strokes herself each year to hide the change from the boy. The sister had sixty years of life left — enough for her brother to live twenty more; he was saved at ten, and at thirty he spent the last of them. Seeing the portrait turn white-haired overnight, the mother knew the spirit was coming to take his life — and that at last there were no wrinkles left to add.
hints: The sister's portrait was bound to her brother's lifespan.
Every year the brother lived cost the sister three years of her remaining life.
His life was borrowed when he was ten; twenty years later, the sixty years his sister could lend was used up.

title: The Signpost
story: My sister died on the road that leads out of the mountains. The village said she had ignored all warnings and taken the wrong path. When I went to burn paper offerings for her, I saw that the signpost had been replanted, its arrow turned to point the opposite way. Later, every girl who escaped from those mountains raised a memorial stone for her. Why did they honor her?
answer: The mountain village had long held trafficked women captive. At the fork on the way out of the mountains, a signpost had been planted pointing the wrong way on purpose, so that anyone fleeing by its arrow walked straight into the abandoned mine the guards controlled. On her first escape, the elder sister discovered the trap, and because she knew the mine from the labor she had been forced to do there, she slipped out through a ventilation shaft. She returned to the fork and set the arrow right, to leave the true way out for those who came after — and the guards who caught up killed her there. What the younger sister saw was her sister's body by the replanted signpost. The villagers' claim that she took the wrong path covered up a killing; the girls who escaped later remembered the signpost that now pointed the true way, and that is why the stones were raised.
hints: The signpost once pointed, on purpose, down a road where fugitives would be caught.
After finding the trap, the sister turned back and changed the signpost's direction.
She left the true road out for the ones behind her, and was killed as she reset the sign.

title: The Observation Window
story: After the aquarium closed, a human face was pressed against the far side of the viewing window. I called to my coworker to look — instead he seized a rag and wiped the glass until it was spotless. The face was still there. And for the first time I noticed: it was turning its head to follow my coworker's hand. What was happening?
answer: A maintenance worker was trapped in the flooded service room beside the viewing pool, with only a pocket of air left at the top. He pressed himself to the glass to beg for help; his face could be seen at an angle through the public viewing window. The coworker had locked him in there earlier to cover up his smuggling of rare fish — the worker had caught him — and meant to deal with him after closing. The wiping was to block the new duty officer's line of sight, and with the rag he gestured threats, ordering the man in the water to back off. The trapped worker turned his head to follow the hand — and the motion exposed the bleeding wound at his temple. The duty officer recognized the face of a man he had worked beside that very day, pressed the alarm at once, and drained the service room from the control room.
hints: The face in the window was the aquarium's own maintenance worker, still alive.
The man wiping the glass knew why he was trapped there.
The wiping hid his plea for help; the gestures threatened him into backing away.

title: The Seventh Package
story: After my husband disappeared, six packages arrived in all. Each one I opened cost me another sleepless night. When the seventh package came, the police said it was safe to open. Inside I saw his watch — and I threw my arms around the courier instead. Why did I embrace the courier?
answer: Debt collectors had taken her husband. The first six packages held personal effects stripped from him, the last of them even stained with blood, pressing her to pay. The real husband escaped during a transfer; a courier hid him in the delivery truck and drove him to the police. So as not to alert the accomplices watching near the wife, the police had the courier deliver a package as usual, while the husband put on a work uniform and played the loader riding with the truck. Husband and wife had long ago agreed on a sign: if he was safe, he would lay his watch face-down in the box, so the photograph of the two of them on the caseback showed. When she saw the watch placed that way and looked up at the man keeping his head down with the delivery crew, she recognized her husband at last — beaten, his head shaved.
hints: The first six packages came from the kidnappers; the seventh came from somewhere else.
The way the watch lay in the box was the couple's agreed all-clear sign.
Her escaped husband had hidden among the couriers; the package is what let her recognize him.

title: The Last Bus
story: We stood in line in the underground shelter, drawing lots; whoever's number came up could board the last bus out. When my number was called, my mother snatched the lot from me and swallowed it. I hated her for it — until the sound of engines started up overhead. That bus never once drove away, yet the front of the line kept growing quieter. What was happening at the front of the line?
answer: During the war, the garrison, wanting rid of the civilians who consumed their supplies, lied about arranging buses to evacuate them. Those whose numbers came up were led into a sealed storeroom that opened onto the surface; the bus stood outside it with its engine running, to drown out the gunfire. The mother had once been called out to bag up the previous group's belongings, and on the floor she had found shell casings and blood; she understood that the lottery was choosing who would die — but the guards had warned her that one word would cost her whole family. So she swallowed her son's lot, lied that he had misheard his number, and kept him back in the line. The engines went on and on, and no one who went inside ever came out to board; only then did the son grasp why his mother would rather take a beating than let him go.
hints: The bus was there to cover a sound.
The mother had already seen what happened to the group before.
The lottery was choosing people for execution; the mother swallowed the lot to keep her son from being taken.

title: The Hatmaker
story: A hatmaker came to the little town, giving away a free hat to anyone who wanted one. He had barely finished measuring my head when he began pressing me about when my brother would be back. I told him my brother was dead. He put his measuring tape away, left town the next day, and never gave away a single hat. Why?
answer: The hatmaker had once been beaten half-dead by a man who made off with stolen money; all he could remember of him was a ring of surgical scars around his head. He traced the man to this town, posed as a hatmaker, and used the head measurements for a chance to part every man's hair and search. The younger brother looked like the wanted robber, but he had no such scar. Only through his questioning did the hatmaker learn that his real target, the elder brother, was already dead of illness. Once he knew where the grave was, he dug it open that same night and took the key to the hidden money, which the brother had sewn into a hat lining while he lived. The free hats were only a pretext; once the target was found, there was no reason to keep up the act.
hints: He came close to men's heads to search for one particular scar.
The two brothers looked alike.
The false hatmaker was hunting the man who took the stolen money; once he learned the elder brother was dead, he turned to the grave for the buried clue.

title: Don't Photograph the Face
story: For our group photo after we got out of the forest, the guide kept his face covered, saying that local people must not be photographed. I took it for a custom, so I photographed everyone's feet instead. When the prints came back, I took the photograph to the police that very night. The next day, the police began digging at the camp. Why did I go to the police?
answer: People had gone missing in that forest, and the narrator's older sister was one of them. He joined the hiking group hoping for news of her, carrying a photograph of the camp she had left behind. In it, the trek leader wore a special built-up boot on his left foot and walked with a slight limp from an old injury. This time the guide went by another name and hid his face from the camera — but on his feet was the same custom-made boot, down to the three white repair stitches on its side. So the narrator handed both photographs to the police, pointing out that the guide had also led the group past the camp where his sister was last seen. Following that lead, the police traced the guide's old identity, and in the search they uncovered the missing people's belongings and remains, buried under the camp.
hints: The one taking the picture was searching for a missing sister.
The guide had changed his name and his face, but he still wore one distinctive boot.
The photograph of the feet tied the guide to the leader from before the sister's disappearance, and the camp became the search site.

title: The Old Newspaper
story: Father kept the windows pasted over airtight, saying the plague outside had not yet passed. I grew up in the basement and turned twenty there, never once seeing the street. Yesterday, a hole broke open in the window. Outside, people were setting off fireworks — and hanging beneath the fireworks was a photograph of Father as a young man. Why was his photograph there?
answer: The father had once abducted a pregnant woman, and the child was born in that basement. After killing the mother, he raised the child as his own family and kept them from going out with the lie of a plague. Every year, on the city's day for the missing, volunteer search groups lay out case materials in the crowded squares. That day a festival was being held nearby, and under the fireworks the searchers had raised a projection screen showing a photograph of the suspect from those years, still young. Through the hole in the window the child saw Father's face and heard the crowd speaking the mother's name — and understood that the place they had lived in all along was a cell that had never once been unlocked.
hints: The life outside had long since given the plague the lie.
Father's photograph appeared at an event for missing persons.
The child was born into the scene of the abduction; the plague story kept them shut in the basement for years.

title: The Grip
story: The idol held out its hand and said that whoever grasped it would see their dead. When I took its hand, I did see my daughter. She stood behind the idol, shaking her head through her tears. I tried to let go — and found my fingers had already turned to stone. Why was she shaking her head?
answer: The idol endures on living bodies. Whoever grasps its hand first sees the dead person they long for, then turns to stone from the fingers inward; only when the whole body has become stone can the one trapped inside the idol go free. The daughter had come here herself, years before, searching for her mother, and had become the idol's last occupant. What the father saw was her soul, squeezed out of the stone body; she shook her head because she knew he was taking her place in the prison. The reunion the idol promised did come true — and the father became the next one to hold out a hand to passersby.
hints: The idol, too, was once a living person.
Every handshake changes who is imprisoned.
The daughter was the idol before him; as he saw her, he was turning to stone in her place.

title: The Toll
story: The old man on the bridge would take no money — only a secret I had never told a living soul. I told one, and he smiled and let me pass. At the middle of the bridge, the corpses in the river suddenly rolled over, every one of them watching me. Only then did I remember: the secret I had just spoken had never mentioned the river. Then how had they heard it?
answer: Beneath the bridge lie the dead of many murders that could never be pinned on a killer. The bridge keeper has the power to carry a sincerely spoken secret to every dead soul it concerns, all at once. The man had killed his victims and sunk them, one by one, in this river; to the old man he admitted only 'the missing people — I killed them all,' believing that leaving out the place would keep his dumping ground safe. He did not know what the toll was for. The dead bound to his confession heard the killer's own mouth confirm it, recognized him at last, and rose one after another to the surface. The old man had let him walk to the middle of the bridge on purpose, delivering him to the dead who had waited so long for a name.
hints: The dead below the bridge never knew who their killer was.
A spoken secret is heard by every ghost it touches.
He confessed to the killings; even without the place, the victims could know him by the secret.

title: It Got Smaller
story: I shut the monster from under my bed inside a shoebox. At first it was the size of a cat; now it was no bigger than a mouse. I told Mother happily that it was about to starve to death. She glanced into the box, then turned and nailed shut every window in the house. Why?
answer: Monsters of this kind molt their shells as they grow, and each shed shell keeps shrinking, so the thing in the box looks as if it is wasting away. The monster had already slipped out through the bottom before the child sealed it in, leaving behind a hollow husk that could still twitch. The mother had seen the same thing when she was a girl. Flipping the box over, she found the fresh split of the molt in its base and knew the escaped creature had grown big enough to swallow a person. Such monsters come to the windows at night, hunting the one who caged them, so the mother sealed the windows at once and moved the child into the windowless storeroom. Inside the box, the empty husk went on shrinking — while outside the window, the breathing grew heavier and heavier.
hints: What the shoebox holds no longer tells you the monster's true size.
The mother found the molt's opening in the bottom of the box.
It is the old shell that shrinks; the grown monster has escaped and is hunting the one who caged it.

title: The Safe
story: Before he died, Father left behind a safe and instructed me to open it only after ten years. In the ninth year, something inside began to knock, calling my childhood name and saying it was Mama. I misremembered the opening day. When I opened it, one day late, there was nothing inside but a memorial portrait of Father. Why did that one day matter?
answer: The safe seals a dead soul inside it for ten years. If it is opened even once within those ten years, the soul seizes the opener's body; if it is still unopened when the term runs out, the soul is locked forever into its own photograph. Before dying, the father placed his own memorial portrait inside, intending to take his son's body once the boy was grown, and he deliberately named a date one day short of the true deadline. The mother had been destroyed by the same trick years before. Inside the safe, his ghost put on her voice to hurry the son into opening it early. But the son was kept away for a day and passed the real deadline — and when he opened the safe, he saw only his father in the photograph, palms pressed flat against the picture, mouth torn wide open.
hints: The date Father gave concealed a design against his son.
What waits inside the safe mimics familiar voices, luring whoever is outside to open it early.
The father meant to rise again in his son's body; the son's one-day delay trapped him forever in his own portrait.

title: Under the Table
story: At a wedding banquet, the bride suddenly ducked under the table. When I leaned down to look, she was tying everyone's shoelaces together. The groom came over to fetch her; she lifted her head and said, 'Just you left.' The next second, the whole table went over.
answer: The bride had been lured to a remote villa by a fake-marriage gang; the relatives at the banquet were all accomplices planning to hold her and extort her family. Coming out of the bathroom, she overheard them splitting the money and found the doors locked, so she had no choice but to return to the table and play drunk. She slipped under the table, ostensibly to pick up a dropped earring, and hastily knotted together the shoelaces of the people sitting within reach, to slow any pursuit. The narrator was the photographer hired to shoot the banquet and knew nothing of this; the bride whispered to him to run for the kitchen's back door. As the groom approached, she overturned the table to create chaos and, while everyone tangled to their feet, escaped with the photographer. Her words 'just you left' were meant to hold the groom's attention for one more moment before she flipped the table.
hints: The relatives at the banquet were all acting, and the bride had only just discovered it.
The tied laces were meant to make them stumble when they stood up to give chase.
Faking drunkenness, she crawled under the table, created chaos, and fled together with the unwitting photographer.

title: The Last Bus
story: When the night bus reached the cemetery, a woman boarded and bought two tickets. I kept staring at the empty space behind her, then couldn't help moving forward a few rows. The driver shut the rear door, made a sudden U-turn, and drove the bus straight into the police station.
answer: The night driver had an arrangement with local residents for silently calling for help: boarding alone but buying two tickets meant someone was following you and you dared not say so out loud. After paying her respects at the cemetery that night, the woman discovered a knife-wielding man tailing her; she hurried to the stop and, as agreed, bought one ticket too many. The driver saw the man in his mirror walking along the side of the bus toward the rear door, immediately shut it, and drove to the nearest police station. The narrator thought she was buying a ticket for something invisible and moved forward a few rows; the driver knew the thing she truly wanted to shake off was the living man outside the bus.
hints: Buying two tickets was a signal agreed between the driver and regular passengers.
The real danger was still outside the bus.
The woman was being tailed by a man with a knife; the second ticket was her plea for the driver to take everyone to safety at a police post.

title: The Hemline
story: The tailor shortened my wedding dress and insisted on coming to watch me marry. As I walked into the church, she suddenly pointed at my feet and burst into tears. The groom turned and ran, and a strange man chased after him. Before I could understand what was happening, the tailor was kneeling on the ground, holding my feet.
answer: As a small child, the girl was abducted; fleeing, she was cut across the ankle by wire and left with a ring of scars. She was raised as an adopted daughter and never knew where she came from. The groom had taken part in the abduction and, in league with the adoptive family, planned to sell her off again under the cover of marriage. Her birth mother had searched for years; by chance she saw a familiar face at a dress fitting and, posing as a tailor, took on the job of altering the wedding dress. She saw the old scar on the ankle and recognized the groom as one of the abductors, and immediately contacted her husband and the police. On the wedding day she shortened the hem so that the birth father waiting at the door could see his daughter's scar too. The groom recognized the couple who had been hunting him for years and turned to flee; the father gave chase, and the mother at last held the daughter who had been missing all those years.
hints: The shortened hem was meant to reveal the old scar on her ankle.
The groom recognized a couple who had spent years tracing an old abduction case.
The woman altering the dress was her birth mother, who had searched for her for years; the scar let her parents reclaim their daughter at the wedding.

title: Empty Tins
story: Only one last crate of tins was left in the bunker. My brother poured all the meat out of them and told me to carry the empty tins and go first. I called him crazy, but he pressed his own tin into my arms as well. After walking a long way, I heard clanging begin behind me.
answer: A brother and sister were held in a bunker under enemy occupation; across the entrance hung an alarm made of empty tins. The brother found a side drainage channel, but its opening was so narrow that only his sister could squeeze through. He packed all the food from the last crate into her cloth bag, wrapped the empty tins in cloth and slipped them over the snapped iron bars to cover the jagged ends, and handed her a few more to drop along the way, marking each fork she passed. He stayed behind in the bunker, tore down the tin alarm at the entrance, and dragged it away down the opposite corridor, drawing the guards toward himself. The ringing grew farther and farther away, and his sister never heard him come after her.
hints: The empty tins had a specific use in the escape.
The way out was too narrow for the brother to fit through.
The brother handed his sister materials for protection and trail-marking, then used the clanging to draw the guards the other way.

title: The Violin Case
story: Before being led to the execution ground, my father asked to play the violin one last time. The jailer handed him the violin case; he took one look inside and said he would not play. After the gunshot, I opened that case and finally understood why my father had never cried out his innocence.
answer: My father had been forced to take the blame for a killing committed by a warlord. Before the arrest, he hid papers exposing the true culprit in a false lining of the violin case and entrusted his daughter to carry it out. His request to play was a way of confirming the papers were safely gone. In the case the jailer brought, the violin had been removed and replaced with the hairpin his daughter had worn that day; the jailer whispered in his ear that if he dared recant in public, his daughter would be the next to face the firing squad. The warlord had already intercepted the girl but had not yet found the papers she had passed on. Seeing the hairpin, the father went to his death in silence, and the daughter was released afterward, as promised. She retrieved the violin case and found, scratched beside the hairpin with a broken string, the words 'live on' — and knew he had understood the threat.
hints: The request to play was the father's way of confirming the whereabouts of a piece of evidence.
In the empty violin case lay his daughter's hairpin.
The hairpin meant the daughter had fallen into the warlord's hands; her father traded his silence for her life.

title: All the Lights On
story: My little brother was afraid of the dark, so I fitted his bedroom with twelve lamps. Every night he could sleep in peace. I thought I had finally taken good care of him. Then came the night of the blackout, and twelve little brothers knocked on my door together.
answer: My brother had brought back from an old temple a shadow-dwelling evil thing; it hid inside his shadow, and each time a separate light source cast it as a complete shadow, it memorized one more outline of a living person — when all the lights went out at once, every recorded shadow took form. When there was only the bedside lamp, my brother had heard something in the dark imitating him and was too frightened to sleep. His sister added more lamps, which pinned the shadows to the walls for a time, but let the thing stockpile twelve outlines. After the blackout, twelve false brothers walked out of the room and knocked; the real brother, wedged under the bed, never made a sound.
hints: Every lamp added also added a shadow to the room.
Those shadows would turn into things that could move once all the lights went out.
All twelve knockers were shadows imitating the brother; the real one was still hiding under the bed.

title: Nine Minutes
story: When the killer broke in, I dialed the phone that could take me back nine minutes. The room returned to how it had been, and I hurried to lock the door. Nine minutes later, sirens sounded outside — and the killer stepped out of the wardrobe. He said, 'This time, you locked the door yourself.'
answer: The old phone sends the caller's consciousness back into herself nine minutes earlier, and the world runs on from that moment. The killer knew what the phone could do and had slipped into the wardrobe more than twenty minutes before.
