answer: While the lamp was lit, time inside the lighthouse ran slow: one night within, ten years without. When the black tide came, someone had to stay under the light, or the fishing villages along the shore would be swallowed. At last the old man found a new keeper who would agree to stand only one night, stepped out of the lighthouse before the lamp was lit, and left ten years of savings behind as wages. He waited outside, night after night, until the appointed morning ten years later, when the tower door opened again. By the time the narrator walked out, the old man was already at the pier waiting for the boat, and the waiting room still held the missing-person notice the narrator’s family had posted ten years before. The old man’s money had bought the coast ten years of safety, and he had put off the moment of explaining that price until after the watch changed hands.
hints: Time passed differently inside the lighthouse and outside it.
His family had begun looking for him ten years ago.
One night in the tower was ten years outside; the wages were paid for the time the world went through.

title: Before the Verdict
story: The city’s judge had never once judged wrong. After every sentencing, he made the defendant say, in his own voice, “The verdict is just.” That day, the defendant clenched his teeth and refused to open his mouth. The judge said the words for him — and his own tongue dropped out. Why?
answer: The contract upon the judgment seat punished anyone who endorsed a wrong verdict aloud: whoever said “The verdict is just” staked his own tongue on it. For years the judge had forced defendants to endorse his sentences; whenever a tongue fell, he declared it a criminal struck down by God, and so kept his name as the judge who was never wrong. This defendant had been wrongly imprisoned, knew the contract’s wording from an old family legal code, and would rather take a beating than open his mouth. Wanting to end a trial that was drawing a bigger crowd of onlookers by the day, the judge pointed to his own verdict and said “The verdict is just,” believing that only defendants were bound. The contract bound everyone who gave the pledge before the bench. He had vouched for a wrongful conviction, and his tongue fell onto the verdict.
hints: The words of endorsement after sentencing carried a special weight.
The punishment fell on anyone who endorsed a wrong verdict, whatever his position.
The judge had always forced defendants to vouch for the verdict; this time he gave the pledge himself, and bore the price of the wrongful judgment.

title: Relabeled
story: The creature behind the glass had always mimicked the visitors, and the staff had long since grown used to it. The new director found the old label too hard to understand and replaced it with a single word: “Human.” When the doors opened the next day, the glass was packed with visitors, and the creature was standing at the ticket counter. Why?
answer: The display case was made under an old contract that bound species: the category written on the label decided what was shut inside. The old label described the creature’s features in detail, so even when it mimicked human movements it could not slip its binding. The new director took it for an exhibit that played at being human and changed the category, on his own authority, to “Human.” After opening, the first person to come near the case was drawn inside, and the visitors entering the hall were reclassified as exhibits one after another; the new label no longer restrained the creature at all. It had learned the staff’s movements, walked out through an open staff door to the ticket counter, and went on putting new visitors into the hall.
hints: The words on the label carried a real binding force.
The glass held whatever matched the category on the label.
With the category changed to Human, the visitors became the exhibits, and the creature lost the condition of its captivity.

title: The Return Ticket
story: Everyone crossing the river was given two tickets. The ferryman said to keep the second one for the journey home. I found my friend buried on the far shore and pressed my second ticket into his hand. After the boat set out on the return trip, soil began to grow out from under my feet. Why?
answer: The river let the living visit the dead: the outbound ticket allowed a living body to set foot on the dead men’s shore, while the return ticket preserved the holder’s place among the living. Once a ticket was handed to a dead person on that shore, the status passed over with it, and the original holder had to stay behind and become part of the graveyard. The ferryman printed the rules on the back of the ticket, but the narrator took it for an ordinary fare and assumed his friend could simply ride the boat with it. The moment he handed it over, warmth came back to his friend’s body, while the earth began to swallow him. His friend was still holding his hand as he boarded; only after the boat cast off did he see that the hand had become a root reaching out from a grave.
hints: The return ticket preserved a certain status belonging to its holder.
After his friend took the ticket, warmth returned to his body.
He had given his place among the living to his dead friend, and stayed on the shore of the dead, slowly dissolving into the graveyard.

title: A Little Colder
story: The freezer room held a man who would never die. Whenever the temperature rose, he would start pounding on the door. The boss said turning up the cold would settle it. That day I did as I was told, and of the hundred thermometers on the wall, only one was still falling. Why?
answer: The man in the freezer could share the cold he endured with anyone linked to his shadow, yet could never be frozen to death. The boss had ninety-nine people seized and pins engraved with their names driven into the man’s shadow, using the victims’ body heat to threaten him into working for him; the hundred thermometers tracked him and the ninety-nine. The pounding on the door was a plea for the boss to stop lowering the temperature. When the new attendant turned the cold up as instructed, the man finally tore loose from the restraints on his feet and pulled out every pin. From that moment the cold returned to him alone: the other ninety-nine bodies began to warm, and only the thermometer bearing his name kept falling. The attendant saw the pins on the floor and the names on the wall in the monitor feed, followed the lines that linked them to the room where the victims were held, then cut the freezer’s power and called the police.
hints: The hundred thermometers each recorded one person’s body temperature.
The man in the freezer could share his cold with the other ninety-nine.
He pulled out the pins that linked him to the others, took all the cold back onto himself, and the ninety-nine victims began to warm.

title: Test Bite
story: At the night market, an old man was selling a set of teeth, and he swore they could bite through anything. I bit through a length of iron wire, and paid. As I stepped away from the stall, my tongue found a loose tooth, and I pulled it out. Everyone on the whole street covered their mouths. Why?
answer: The old man was selling a set of proxy teeth. When the wearer bit down, the force was drawn from everyone in the night market who had pledged their teeth as collateral; pull out one of these teeth, and the tooth in the same position dropped from every pledger’s mouth. The price board by the stall said the teeth were shared and refundable, but the old man had deliberately buried the exact terms of the contract beneath his money box. The narrator believed he had bought an ordinary pair of magic dentures; once they were fitted, he bit through the iron wire and proved that the bite of many had gathered in his own mouth. When he pulled the tooth, every stallholder on the street who had pledged teeth suffered with it, and the true price of the goods came to light. The old man covered his own mouth as well, and never managed to call the buyer back.
hints: The strength of these teeth came from what many people had given up together.
They stayed linked to everyone on the street who had pledged a tooth.
He pulled out one of the shared teeth, and the tooth in that same spot fell from every pledger’s mouth at once.

title: Unanimous
story: In that town, every major decision required the consent of all residents. That day, I was the only living soul left in the square. I raised my hand, meaning to end the rule. Behind me, in the graveyard, a hand rose slowly too. Why?
answer: The town’s founding charter defined a resident as anyone entered on the register who had never formally moved away; death struck no name from the rolls. The dead could answer only when a vote was called, and could not otherwise act. After the plague, the narrator was the only one left alive. Wanting to abolish the rule of unanimous consent, he rang the bell that summoned every registered resident. He took the hand rising from the graveyard for a ghost trying to stop him, but in truth every one of the dead was willing to be released; their bodies lay layered upon one another in a common grave, and only the topmost hand could reach the surface. Working down the register, the narrator called each name in turn, heard the ayes come one after another from under the earth, and at last closed the vote. After the final answer, the bell split by itself.
hints: Residency was decided by the register, and death removed no name from it.
The dead had the right to answer a vote, and wanted the bond ended too.
Everyone below was raising a hand in assent; in the shared grave, only the topmost hand could break the ground.

title: The Arrow on the Wall
story: In the old castle we found a body with an arrow through its chest. Everyone rushed to search for the archer outside the window, but the restorer told us to look up at the wall. The hunter painted there still held his bow raised, its string snapped, and where an arrow had once been painted there was now a hole. Why?
answer: The castle’s owner had hidden a working bow inside a relief painting, the real arrow shaft merging into the painted background as one. His plan, on the day of the forgery sale, was to release the mechanism holding the bowstring with a concealed pull-cord, kill the buyer standing at the appointed spot, and pass the arrow off as a shot from beyond the window. The restorer had catalogued the frame beforehand and knew some of its ornaments were real objects; when the victim fell, he saw a fresh hole where the arrow had been, and the snapped string hanging down from the picture. The paint on the arrowhead matched the residue inside the painting. And the window the owner had opened to draw attention away let the light fall upon the pull-cord behind the canvas, not yet drawn back in.
hints: The painting carried ornaments that stood out from its surface — real objects.
The hunter’s bow, and the arrow everyone had seen at first, were genuine instruments.
The killer hid the bow in the relief painting, fired from inside the room, and turned every eye toward the window.

title: The Eighth Word
story: After the enemy took the radio station, they kept broadcasting the song we listened to every day. Halfway through, the commander ordered the whole unit to withdraw. I asked him what he had heard. He said: “They sang it right.” Why?
answer: For years, the singer at the underground station had sung the eighth word of the lyric as a different word — a slip at first, later fixed upon by the couriers as the sign that the station was still safe. The enemy seized the staff and, to lure the city’s resistance into gathering as planned, obtained an official recording of the same song and aired it on schedule. They held the program list, but knew nothing of the long-kept wrong word. The moment the commander heard the official lyric, he suspected the station had fallen, and pulled the unit out of the rallying point as prearranged. Scouts later watched enemy soldiers sweeping that very ground, and it was confirmed: the correctly sung song was the trap.
hints: The version they knew by heart carried one long-standing error.
That error had come to serve as the sign that the station was still safe.
The enemy played the official record, sang the signal word right, and gave away that the station had already fallen.

title: Snow in the Yard
story: White “snow” began to fall inside the prison. The prisoners dropped to their hands and knees to gather it up; only one man stamped the paper scraps frantically into the mud. When the guards seized him, he wept: “I already burned the letter — why is there still more?”
answer: A wartime informer had sold the underground network to the occupying army. Believing the letter the courier had passed him before execution to be the only evidence, he had burned it. The underground later retook the print works outside the city, copied the captured original of his betrayal into leaflets, and scattered them over the prison wall by kite, to warn the prisoners away from him. The informer saw his own signature, his payment, the list of his victims, and scrambled to destroy the scraps at his feet. A new guard on patrol picked up a leaflet at the same time, and heard him volunteer the detail of the burned letter; he had the man isolated for protection and reported it up the chain. The original left outside the walls finally laid the whole transaction bare.
hints: Every white scrap carried a printing of the same document.
The man stamping on the paper believed he had already destroyed the only evidence.
The network had recovered the original of the betrayal left with its recipient, and copied it into leaflets rained over the prison.

title: The Tangled Thread
story: When the sarcophagus was opened, the expedition leader stared at the red thread wound around the corpse’s wrist, then suddenly ordered everyone out of the burial chamber. The assistant said it was thread for protecting the artifacts — that he had tied it there himself. The leader asked: “When were you inside?”
answer: The chamber had never been officially opened, yet the assistant had long been slipping in through a robber’s tunnel, stealing the grave goods and setting modern replicas in their places. He had tied red thread around one fragile bracelet to hold it fast; while he moved things, the thread wound onto the corpse’s wrist, and he forgot to take it off. Under the leader’s eye he rushed to explain the red thread as ordinary working material, and so gave himself away as having entered the tomb early. The leader had already found fresh drill holes beside the stone door and, fearing the robbery had undermined the supports, moved the team back to safety before pressing him further. Later, in the private photographs the assistant had kept, the others saw the grave goods that had not yet been replaced.
hints: This was the team’s first official opening of the chamber.
The assistant’s claim to have tied thread inside meant he had gone in before.
He had left the red thread securing a replica when he looted the tomb; explaining it away betrayed what he had done.

title: Beneath the Curtain
story: Before the premiere, the star cut the costly stage curtain in half, and the theater’s owner was furious enough to call the police. She made him stand at center stage and slowly raise his head. The owner looked through the cut — then took up the scissors himself. Why?
answer: In rehearsal, the star had watched someone slip behind the curtain and remove the fittings that held a heavy set piece hanging, and soon after, she was warned to keep her mouth shut. Fearing the owner might be in it with them, she dared not expose it alone; she waited until the whole company was present, then cut the curtain open, so that the heights behind it could be seen by everyone at once. Standing center stage, the owner looked through the slit, saw the heavy flat already tilting on its empty mountings, and cleared the house at once. The remaining cloth still hid the maintenance ladder, so he cut away another length, letting the crew come close enough to shore the set up in safety. The two cuts served two ends: the first to make the danger public, the second to open the way for repairs.
hints: The curtain was hiding a danger above the stage.
The first cut let everyone see it; the second let the crew reach it.
Someone had sabotaged the fittings of a heavy set piece; the star cut the curtain in public to force the theater to deal with it at once.

title: After the Paper Came Down
story: In the interrogation room, the man played the video over and over, insisting the victim was still alive. In the footage, the man on screen held up that day’s newspaper and smiled at the camera. I froze the frame at the instant the paper came down. The man reached out to shut off the screen — and was held down. Why?
answer: The man had a fake newspaper printed in advance, dated that very day, forced the victim to record the short clip the day before, and used it to forge the time of his last appearance. Held high, the paper covered the doorway; in the instant it came down, the glass door mirrored the construction notice on the wall and a doorframe only half installed. The investigator had already obtained the building management’s original acceptance photographs, confirming that the door had been complete by the previous evening — the “same-day” footage contradicted itself in time. The man was the one who had delivered the fake newspaper, and the moment he grasped that the frame had betrayed the doorframe, he lunged for the screen. The inquiry later found the unused extras from the same print run, and the original video file, and the forgery stood proven.
hints: A newspaper’s date can be arranged by hand; the room’s construction kept records of its own.
When the paper came down, the glass reflected a doorframe not yet finished.
Acceptance photographs proved the frame was complete the day before; the footage was shot earlier, and the date on the paper was forged.

title: Five Stars
story: We came out of the horror escape room, and the blood-soaked actor chased us all the way to the front desk, begging us to give him a five-star review. Everyone in our group laughed; only one girl took out her phone and called the police. When the actor saw her dialing, the smile finally left his face, and he sat down on the floor and cried. Why?
answer: At the start, the actor had agreed with the group on a signal: five raised fingers meant pause — any player who was hurt, or truly frightened, could end the experience with it. Midway through, an escaped convict broke in through the back door, beat him down, hid in the staff area, and forced him to see the players off as usual. Not daring to call for help under the convict’s watching eye, the actor chased them to the front desk, where the public cameras covered the room, holding up five fingers again and again, dressed up as begging for a rating. The girl recognized their agreed pause signal, saw his wounds still seeping blood, and stepped outside the glass door to call the police. Only when he was sure she was through to them did the actor dare stop at the desk and wait for help.
hints: At the start, the actor had set a gesture for stopping the game.
The fingers he kept raising while asking for five stars were the pause signal.
Under the convict’s threat the actor kept performing — the plea for five stars was cover, a plea for the players to fetch help.

title: Knocking in the Leather Bag
story: The caravan bedded down at a relay station for the night, and I heard knocking from inside the bag of hides. The merchant said it was a monkey caught on the road. The night watchman, smiling, took a banana, crouched before the bag, and dangled it — then suddenly flung back the merchant’s blanket and threw his boots into the fire. Why?
answer: The merchant had kidnapped a boy and meant to carry him through the pass as cargo under cover of night. Hearing the word “monkey,” the watchman used the banana as a pretext to draw close, and through the gap at the bag’s mouth saw a human hand wearing the wooden tag of the local school. He recognized the missing student the whole station had been hunting that day; playing along with the merchant, he walked back toward the fire, and on the way to fetching a second banana threw the boots hidden under the blanket into the flames. The merchant lunged for them on instinct, and in that moment the watchman dragged the bag behind the counter where other men kept watch, calling the boy’s name aloud. Robbed of the chance to keep his hostage at arm’s length, the kidnapper was seized by the station hands who came running.
hints: Crouching by the bag, the watchman had seen the hand inside it.
He recognized the wooden tag the missing student wore.
The boots went into the fire to pull the kidnapper away, so the bag holding the boy could be dragged to safety first.

title: The Lamp in the Sky
story: Through the telescope of the abandoned observatory, a star was blinking in rhythm. The student with us said we had finally received a signal from the aliens. The teacher pressed the telescope downward — and went rigid: behind that long-sealed window, someone was holding a flashlight against an eye. Why?
answer: No one had noticed, coming in: the telescope had long since been turned toward the old watchroom on the cliff across the valley. Focusing on the bright point in the dark, the student had taken the flashlight behind the distant window for a star. The teacher, hearing the distress rhythm in its blinking and suspecting the light was near, dropped the magnification and lowered the tube a little — and only then did the window frame appear. The trapped man was the caretaker who had come out earlier to survey the old station; he had climbed in through a side hatch, and toppled cabinets had blocked his way back, leaving the sealed window as his only way to call for help. He held the flashlight to his eye to aim it at the one place that could still see him: the observatory.
hints: No one had checked that the telescope was pointing at the sky.
With the magnification dropped, a window frame appeared around the light.
The “starlight” was a distress signal — a flashlight in the hand of a man trapped in the old watchroom across the valley.

title: The Water Still Running
story: A man died at the mountain lodge, and the hot water in the bathroom ran all night. The owner said the guest had slipped while drunk. I turned off the tap — and heard water still running inside the next wall. When the police arrived, the first thing they did was tear that wall open. Why?
answer: The dead man had found the owner’s smuggled goods hidden in a cavity wall, and the owner had killed him for it. Dragging open the wall’s hidden door, he had cracked a concealed length of pipe, and the sound of water betrayed the hollow behind it. He turned on the hot water to stage a drunk’s fall in the shower and to bury the leak under the noise of the spray, buying time to move the goods before the body was found. The cleaner came on shift early, shut off the shower, heard water still running inside the wall, saw it welling from a corner tied to none of the bathroom’s pipes, and reported it along with the alarm. Beside the leak the police found bloodstains and the hidden door, and took out both the goods not yet moved and the photographs the dead man had hidden away.
hints: The two sounds of water came from two different places.
The owner needed the shower’s noise to cover the new leak inside the wall.
The pipe behind the hidden door, cracked while he killed the man and stashed the contraband, gave the game away — the leak led straight to the wall that held the evidence.

title: The Man-Made Dawn
story: In the ninth year after the sun went out, we finally built a new one. As it rose, the whole city cheered. Ten seconds later came the institute’s order: everyone lie down at once, close your eyes, play dead. The shadows in the square were already standing up. Why?
answer: The catastrophe nine years before had left a form of life dwelling in human shadows; the unbroken dark kept them from taking shape, while mankind credited its survival to the shelter city. The institute’s early small-scale lighting tests had raised only brief, blurred shadows, and the things inside them had never fully stood up. The new sun gave light as steady and as clear as the old sun’s, and every parasite took shape at once. They could claim a host only along the shadow of someone still moving; the moment a person lay flat and still, the shadow folded beneath the body, and the way in was closed, for a time. Testers at the institute had watched their motionless samples survive, and sent the order at once, shutting the sun down in the same breath. When the survivors opened their eyes again, a few upright figures still stood in the square.
hints: The nine years of dark had been keeping something from appearing.
The new sun made human shadows steady and sharp.
The parasites enter the body along a moving shadow; lying still blocks them for a time, until the light itself is switched off.

title: Storm Under Glass
story: At a flea market I bought a glass ornament with a little town inside it. Every time it was shaken, rain fell where we lived. Excited, I carried it to the weather station. The station chief saw the date on its base, clutched it to his chest, and ran for the incinerator room. Why?
answer: The ornament sealed a whole town inside; when it was shaken from outside, rain fell within — the world the townsfolk knew had never reached past the glass. What the narrator bought was a control duplicate kept circulating inside the town, one that could pass a motion on to the true ornament outside. The base carried the closing date of the outer exhibition, and on that date the master piece, town and all, would be collected and melted down. The station chief had read the records his predecessor left in the old files, and he knew that date, and the crest on the duplicate. Melt the control piece, and the master would come apart as well — and the town would be set loose into the outer world. He ran for the furnace room to end the imprisonment before the outside came to reclaim it.
hints: The town they lived in was itself sealed inside another, larger ornament.
The ornament inside the town was a control copy, able to act upon the master outside.
The date on the base was the deadline for reclamation; melting the copy first broke the master’s seal.

title: The Man Who Couldn’t Kneel
story: Every day, the kingdom’s subjects knelt before the royal statue. Only the old soldier never knelt, and the guards dared not lay a hand on him. When the new king was crowned, he had the old soldier put to death. At court the next morning, the whole hall stood — and not one of them could bend a leg. Why?
answer: The old king had ruled his kingdom by puppetry: the knee joints of every subject were tied to a single invisible line, and at his pull they all knelt. The old soldier had lost both legs in the war, and the craft found no knee in him to tie; so the old king hid the master line inside his prosthetic legs, named him Keeper of the Line, and ordered the guards to protect him. When the old king died, the new one knew only that the soldier defied the rite. He cared nothing for the exemption written into the ceremony, nor for the royal seal on the prosthetics, and had him executed and his legs burned. In the fire the master line drew tight and set, and the knees of every subject locked straight. While the old soldier stood alone, the kingdom could still kneel; with his death, the craft that ruled them all broke upon its final posture.
hints: The old soldier stood on prosthetic legs, stamped with the royal seal.
The subjects’ knees were all held by one and the same craft.
The master line controlling every knee lay hidden in the prosthetics; the new king burned them, and every leg locked straight.

title: Door Plates in the Trees
story: Deep in an uninhabited forest, the survey team came upon rows of door plates. We took them all down, numbered them, and crated them up to carry back for study. On the way down the mountain, the town at its foot was gone. From the crates, the knocking never stopped. Why?
answer: The forest could take in the interiors of buildings. Long before, the mountain folk had hung their door plates on matching trees, linking the houses below to spaces inside the trunks, and so rode out the seasonal floods; as long as the plates stayed on the trees, those houses could be seen and entered below, as normal. Take a plate down, and the link was cut: the house and everyone in it drew back into the forest, folding into the sealed entrance the plate marked. Once the survey team had those entrances crated, the residents had nothing left but to knock for help. Finding a tree’s number carved on the back of each plate, the crew hung them back by those numbers — and only then did the streets at the mountain’s foot appear again.
hints: The plates had been holding the link between the forest and the houses below.
The crates held the only entrance to the outside world those residents could still reach.
Taking the plates down pulled the houses back into the forest’s sealed spaces; hanging them back by the trees’ numbers brought the town back.

title: The Letter Reader
story: My employer is a blind old man; each week he has me read him a letter from his dead wife. By the work ledger, I have been reading them for thirty years — yet I cannot even remember his surname. Yesterday he told me to burn the letter, reached out and touched my face for the first time, and called me his son. Why?
answer: With the mail of the dead, every letter read aloud takes its postage from the reader: a stretch of memory shared with the one the letter is for. The old man longed to hear his wife’s voice, but would not bear the postage himself, so he had his son read in his place. At first the son agreed of his own will; as he slowly forgot their kinship, the old man dressed each visit up as employment — paid him a wage, noted in the ledger the date of the next reading. The son still knew his own life, his age, this trade of his; all that bound him to the old man before him was gone. Thirty years on, near death, the old man could no longer bear to let his son keep paying, gave him the unopened letter to burn, and only then told him what they were to each other. The son confirmed it from the household-register paper and the old photograph folded into the ledger — yet he could never summon back the day in that photograph, his father holding him in his arms.
hints: The postage for reading a letter was memory — what the reader and the recipient had lived through together.
The ledger kept the visits coming, but could not keep what the two of them had been.
The old man let his son pay the postage in his place — until the son forgot they were father and child, and still came, summoned as a hired reader.

title: The Second Noon
story: In the colony, noon comes twice a day. When the first sun reaches the top of the sky, we work as usual; when the second one does, everyone must get indoors. The new engineer worked out that the second “sun” was nearer than the moon — and that very night, the roofs came off every house in the city. Why?
answer: The second sun was a scanner the colonial company hung in the sky: at each day’s second noon it read the identity marks on the rooftops into the system, and chose which laborers’ terms were due, to be taken away by force. The deadly sunlight was a rule the company invented, to get everyone indoors on time, inside their numbered houses. From the equipment drawings the engineer learned that the scanner read the rooftop marks alone, and that the craft sent to seize men flew by house coordinates. He reached the laborers, and before the next sweep they stripped away the thin sheet roofs that bore the marks, leaving the system unable to match its list to a single dwelling, while others took the communications station and sent a distress call. The first sun belonged to this planet; the second was a machine, and it watched them.
hints: The second shining body was a machine built by men.
The order to go indoors put every person back in a fixed, numbered place.
The rooftop marks let the scanner locate its chosen laborers; tearing them off left the automatic seizure, for a while, without a target.

title: The Wound Lease
story: I rented out the wound in my chest, and from then on someone else felt the pain for me. Ten years later, I paid off the rent early and went to take my wound back. The man in the room was asleep. He opened his eyes, saw me, and asked: “Why are you still alive?”
answer: Wounds can be rented out; while the lease holds, the injury and everything it does to the body are borne by the tenant. After being stabbed through the chest, the narrator leased the fatal wound away, and his body recovered, while the tenant was kept alive on long-term life support. The company had lied to the tenant, telling him the original owner was already dead, and that if he held out for ten years the ownerless wound would vanish forever. What the narrator paid was the early-termination fee, yet only when he came to reclaim his wound did he learn that the tenant had believed, all along, that he was suffering the last stretch of pain in a dead man’s place. The lease was explicit: while the original owner lived, terminating would simply send the fatal wound back to him whole. He looked at the name on the life-support machine and set down the termination papers, unsigned.
hints: The lease covered more than the pain; it covered everything the wound dealt the body.
The company hid from the tenant the fact that the original owner was still alive.
Ending the lease early would have sent the fatal chest wound back whole; the tenant had believed that surviving ten years would free him of the ownerless wound.

title: After the Applause
story: The sign outside the theater read: “Your applause lights up the whole city.” When the mime collapsed to his knees, the audience took it for another gag and applauded, laughing. He took off his mask and pointed at his sewn-shut mouth. The whole house fell silent — yet not one light in the city went out.
answer: The city’s power ran, by contract, on the suffering of the man on the stage; until the show had officially closed, the actor could not flee it. The operators packaged the power as a reward of the audience’s applause, and forced the actor to perform through the night. He had once tried to call for help; for that his mouth was sewn shut, a mask fitted over his face, and the program changed from opera to mime. That night he sank to his knees, spent, and the audience applauded the performance all the same. He took off the mask to show them his wound, and the applause finally stopped — but the suffering went on, so the lights did not change. Then a spectator from the front row rushed the stage and pulled down the curtain rope that had been tied fast all along; only after the curtain closed did the whole city go dark, and for the first time the actor was carried out of the theater.
hints: The promise on the sign came from the theater’s operators.
The power stayed on even after the audience stopped; the true source remained on the stage.
The electricity was drawn from the actor’s suffering; only dropping the curtain and ending the show could break the contract that kept him on stage.

title: The Pardon
story: Before the hanging, the executioner asked whether I would pay for my crime with my shadow. I agreed at once. The rope caught my shadow and strung it up. I came home alive — but my wife pointed at the floor and told me to get out.
answer: The city’s rite of pardon can strip the crimes a man has committed out of his memory, seal them into his shadow, and put that shadow to death. A pardoned man does not forget the facts; he loses all guilt over those acts, and all restraint. The narrator had lashed out many times before, and at the hearing his wife had insisted that he serve his sentence — precisely because she feared the man he would become without his last scrap of remorse. Once the shadow had been hanged, the first thing he did on coming home was smash open the locks his wife had fitted to protect herself, and calmly announce that no one would ever wring a confession from him again. Seeing that he cast no shadow on the floor, his wife knew which pardon he had chosen; she backed out of the house, took refuge with the neighbors, and called the police. The body that came home alive had left at the gallows the part of him that might still have held him back.
hints: What the shadow carried away was a particular feeling he had about his own crimes.
His wife knew the pardon would strip him of restraint over his own behavior.
The hanged shadow took his guilt with it: he still remembered everything he had done, but no longer believed he had anything to repent.

title: Clouds on the Manhole Cover
story: A deep-sea probe discovered a manhole cover. The robotic arm pried it open, the camera slipped through — and there on the screen was a street in the rain. Passersby with umbrellas steered around the lens; then a hand reached over and clapped the cover shut.
answer: That manhole cover joins two layers of the world: our seabed corresponds to an opening in the sky above a street on the other side. Sealed, the cover holds the sea back; opened, it lets seawater pour through that opening onto the other world’s street as a sudden, local downpour. Only once the probe’s camera had crossed the boundary could it film the pedestrians in the rain. The people over there lived on a street that sprang leaks like this all the time; they knew the opening overhead, walked beneath it under their umbrellas, and pressed the cover back into place with a long-handled tool. The feed’s last frame caught the hand reaching out beside the tool. This so-called relic of the deep is, to this day, somebody else’s city infrastructure.
hints: Past the cover, the camera was filming a different space.
The rain on the other side was the seawater that had just poured through.
The seabed opens into the sky above another city; when the passersby closed the cover, the rain stopped.

title: Land Ahead
story: In thick fog the icebreaker sighted a black cliff wall, and the captain ordered the engines slowed at once. The watchkeeper kept his eyes on the telescope, then suddenly called everyone off the deck. On the cliff face, a line of white was slowly turning sideways.
answer: The black surface was the flank of an iceberg, so crusted with rubble it passed for rock. The watchkeeper saw that a layer of white ice, formed on the berg by nature, was turning against the horizon, and understood the whole iceberg was about to roll. Up close, the crew had at first mistaken it for a stable coastline, and so had thought only of slowing to avoid a collision. His warning got the men on deck inside and away from the rails in time, and the captain changed the order to full speed away. The wave raised by the rolling berg swept the deck soon after; by then the white ice that had stood vertical already lay beneath the water.
hints: The whole of that supposed cliff was changing its orientation.
The black came from rubble frozen to its surface; the mass inside was ice.
The iceberg was rolling over; the turning white ice foretold the great wave right behind it.

title: The First Pot of Rice
story: Thirty days under siege, and we finally saw a grain convoy arrive. The first pot of rice had barely been carried out when the cook charged over and overturned it. The soldiers pinned him down; out of his apron he pulled half of a city-gate seal and said: “Let them eat first.”
answer: The grain convoy had been ambushed by rebels outside the walls. Dying, the escort commander snapped his city-gate seal in two and hid one half in a grain sack. The city’s cook was an old comrade of his, and the two had agreed that only an unbroken seal meant he was handing over the grain of his own free will. The rebels donned the escort’s uniforms, slipped into the city carrying the other half, and laced the relief grain with poison, meaning to seize the gate once everyone had eaten. When the first sack was more than half used, the cook found the broken seal at the bottom, wrapped with a bloodstained slip of warning paper the commander had hurriedly stuffed in; he knew the men who had come in with the grain were impostors, and seeing the first pot already on its way to the soldiers in line, he overturned it and shouted for the granary to be sealed. The garrison matched the two halves of the seal, took control of the convoy, and sent fresh samples for testing, which confirmed the grain had been tampered with.
hints: The cook had found something at the bottom of the first sack of grain.
Beside the broken seal lay the escort commander’s warning note.
The real convoy had been ambushed; impostors brought poisoned grain into the city, and the cook overturned the pot to keep the soldiers from eating it.

title: Welcome Back
story: It was our first landing on this planet, yet the airport loudspeakers said welcome back. Photographs of every one of us hung along the jet bridge, not a single name wrong. Under mine ran one extra line: “Last time: died refusing to disembark.”
answer: The jump corridor the exploration ship passed through splits a single instant of departure into many independent arrivals, each ship unaware of the others. The rescuers on the planet had already received many batches of identical crew members; they knew all their names, and they had learned that after each arrival the hull disintegrated within an hour, undone by the corridor’s residual energy. The previous copy of the narrator, seeing his own photograph, had taken the place for a trap, refused to leave the ship, and died in the disintegration. The rescuers wrote that ending beneath the photo, hoping the next batch would believe the warning. The loudspeakers welcomed the arrivals off a list prepared long in advance, and the jet bridge still bore the burn marks of earlier evacuations, and records marked with different dates.
hints: The locals had met other crews, identical to this one.
Each record matches a separate arrival; the crew members carry no memory of any of them.
The jump copies one same departure again and again; the last batch that refused to disembark died when their hull broke apart.

title: The Expanding Graveyard
story: Only robots dwell on this planet, yet the graveyard grows larger every year. We dug open one of the new graves and found an intact machine inside. It opened its eyes, and its first words were: “Was the update canceled again?”
answer: The colonists had long ago moved their minds into robot bodies. Every major system update creates a new version carrying the complete set of memories, while the old version remains a whole self. To keep two versions from contending for one identity, the administrators power the old body down and seal it away, calling it burial, while telling the outside world only of a lossless upgrade of consciousness. The old version we dug up still stood at the moment before the update began; once repowered, it supposed the upgrade had failed and asked whether it had been canceled. The graveyard expands year by year, and what it keeps count of are the discarded old selves. On the grave markers the explorers found the same name repeated across the years — and in the city they then met the newest one.
hints: The body is a machine, but a whole self is still stored inside it.
Each upgrade begets a new version, and the old version never truly disappears.
The graveyard holds the powered-down old selves; every update adds a batch of people who can still wake.

title: Scratches on the Inside
story: The returnee said something out there had tried to tear open his helmet. We got him into the quarantine bay and found the visor covered in scratches. The technician ran his fingers over the smooth outer face — and quietly locked the second door.
answer: Alien spores had entered the explorer’s body through an open wound and formed, in his head, a parasite that could seize his limbs for short spells. He never saw one of those spells clearly; all he remembered was a suffocating sense of something foreign inside the helmet, so he took the struggle for an attack from outside. The surveillance footage showed him out on the waste pulling his hands back through the inner cuffs, clawing at the visor from inside the roomy old-style pressure suit, trying to tear himself an exit. Every scratch on the transparent visor was on the inner face, which meant the attack he described had taken place inside the protective shell. So the technician kept the suit sealed, had the man isolated, and called in medical robots for a patient already spinning spore-silk inside his helmet.
hints: The returnee’s memory of the attacks is far from complete.
The outer face of the visor is smooth; every scratch was made from within.
A parasite is already inside him, and it once drove his hands to claw at the visor from inside the suit.

title: Don’t Hit Replay
story: The base received surveillance footage from five minutes ahead: a man in the same uniform as mine opened the airlock, and everyone died. I locked myself in the storeroom to wait out the five minutes. When the countdown reached zero, my crewmate asked through the door: “Can the recording be deleted now?” And I suddenly remembered — the man in the footage had no shoes on.
answer: The base’s prediction machine shows only one future — the one that follows if present choices run their course — and any action can change it. The duty officer had secretly stolen the alien samples and gone into the lab wing barefoot; in that future he would open the airlock afterward to dress the theft up as an accident. The prediction footage was low-resolution, and the narrator mistook the man in the same uniform for himself. He hid in the storeroom and left his key with the duty officer. The duty officer knew the plan had been laid bare to the prediction machine, so he set the airlock aside for the moment and waited out the five minutes instead, meaning to destroy the recording once the prophecy failed to come true. Remembering that he himself had never once taken off his work boots, the narrator asked the others to check the duty officer’s feet outside the door, and the sample cabinet. The lab-wing dye on the man’s bare soles, and the missing samples, exposed the plan — and the choice that truly led to the accident was cut off.
hints: The prediction shows a future that can still be changed — and the identity of the man in the footage needs confirming.
The narrator kept his boots on the whole time; someone had walked the lab wing barefoot.
The matching uniform caused the mistake; the one ready to open the airlock was the duty officer who stole the samples and was eager to delete the footage.

title: My Turn to Ask
story: The alien envoy never spoke unless spoken to: we asked one question, it gave one answer. The day the translator broke, it suddenly spoke in fluent human language: “At last — my turn to ask.” The security chief pulled the plug at once.
answer: The so-called translator was the control apparatus of the contact experiment: it turned every question the humans uttered into a binding command laid on the envoy, so that it could only ever respond, never speak on its own. The envoy had long since learned human language; the device had simply held it in check. The malfunction briefly lifted the control, and at last it could ask where it was being held, and what had become of its companions. The security chief saw the device still trying to restore itself, and cut the power to end that control for good. He had believed he was guarding a diplomatic meeting; only when the envoy spoke a plea for help that none of the staff had ever taught it did he realize that the two sides separated by the glass had never once truly spoken.
hints: The envoy itself could already understand and use human language.
The device governed when it was allowed to open its mouth.
The translator in truth forced it to do nothing but answer; pulling the plug stopped the control from coming back, and let it speak freely.

title: The Empty Cage
story: With the war closing in on the zoo, the director ordered us to open every cage — all but the emptiest one, which was to stay locked. The vet cursed him through the bars, calling him a madman. The director took off his coat, and beneath it showed a prisoner’s uniform, the same as the vet’s.
answer: The occupying army had turned the zoo into a makeshift camp for interned laborers. Most of the animals had been moved out; the remaining cages held prisoners forced into old work uniforms to conceal what they were. The director himself had been locked up for refusing to cooperate, and with the shelling drawing near and the guards pulling out, he got hold of the keys and emptied the cages one by one. The emptiest cage held only the overseer posing as the vet — the real vet had been sold out by that man long before. The overseer had changed into prison garb to slip away among the fleeing prisoners, so the director took off his coat to show the others the same serial number they all wore, proof that he had seen the betrayal with his own eyes, and left the overseer locked in the cage for the rescue troops to take over when they arrived.
hints: In wartime the cages had been turned into a place for holding people.
The director and most of the people in the cages were prisoners.
The man calling himself the vet was the overseer trying to pass among the rescued; the director left him behind for the rescue troops.

title: The Anchor in the Sand
story: In the desert we dug up an intact ship, its hold still wet. Someone proposed dragging the anchor out for a souvenir. The guide had barely said don’t touch it when a distant dune rose — and bared a row of pale teeth.
answer: When the great beast of the desert sleeps, its skin secretes fine sand and mantles its body into a dune. It had taken a ship at sea and dived back beneath the ground; the swallowed ship lay wrapped near the stomach wall in a moist pouch, and the anchor had snagged on one of the teeth growing along its gullet. The crew had escaped long before, but the ship stayed moored inside the beast by its anchor chain. Years later the wind thinned the sand over the pouch, and the explorers took the find for the wreck of an ancient ship. The pull on the anchor ran down the chain and wrenched at the tooth, and the beast woke; the “dune” that rose was its head, lifting and opening. The guide knew the local accounts of wet ships and anchor chains — which is why he urged everyone away while the hull was still slick with fresh mucus.
hints: The hold stayed wet because the ship was never truly buried in dry sand.
The anchor chain still ran to something beyond the ship.
The ship lies inside a great beast; hauling the anchor wrenched its tooth, and the head disguised as a dune rose.

title: Returning the Air
story: On the colony, all the air was sold in canisters. I found my younger brother’s name engraved on the bottom of one, and took it straight back for a refund. The shopkeeper asked when he had gone missing. When he heard the date, he opened the cabinet and told me to take away every canister of the same batch.
answer: After the company’s oxygen plant failed, its managers turned to an illegal technology that compresses a person’s mind and body into a gas other people can breathe. What has been consumed cannot be restored; the unopened canisters of a batch, sent back through the device together, can still be returned as one whole person. To keep account of how much of each convert had been used up, the factory engraved the true name on the bottom of every canister. The day the narrator’s younger brother disappeared was the very day this batch of gas was produced. Only at the date did the shopkeeper recognize where the “new raw material” came from; he hurried to gather the whole unsold stock and sent the narrator off with it, to stop the factory from destroying the reversal device. The last canister in the cabinet was still sealed — no one had ever breathed his brother.
hints: The name on the bottom marks the source of the raw material.
All the unused gas of one batch can be restored through the original device.
The company turned the missing into breathable gas; his brother’s batch is still unopened, and he can still be brought back whole.

title: The Bell Rope
story: In the village, the death bell tolls only for those already dead. I climbed the bell tower and saw the keeper hand a noose to a living man. The man slipped it over his neck — but the bell did not ring. The smile dropped from the keeper’s face: “Who exactly are you here in place of?”
answer: The bell tower was bound to the village’s ledger of lifespans: with the noose, the keeper could take the remaining years of anyone entered in it — but only where the wearer put it on of his own will. He gave out the story that anyone who wore the rope and heard no death bell would be granted a year of safety, and by it he picked out the villagers who could be quietly killed. The man who came was an outside investigator who had followed the rumors here; wearing a name tag belonging to one of the village’s missing, he took part in the rite under a borrowed name. He stood nowhere in the ledger, so the noose would not tighten, and the death bell gave no answer. Taking him for a stand-in, the keeper let the question burst out of him — and with it gave away the rule that he killed by registered name. The investigator took off the tag and called up the men lying in wait downstairs.
hints: The bell tower’s power reaches only those entered in the village’s ledger of lifespans.
The man who donned the rope wore a missing villager’s name tag.
The outside investigator stood nowhere in the ledger; the noose could not tighten on a borrowed name, and the keeper’s reaction gave the scheme away.

title: Welcome In
story: A devil may enter another’s home only by invitation. Before I moved out of the old house, I burned the doormat that said “Welcome.” That night, as expected, it did not come. The next day the new tenant brought me the lease I had left behind and asked whose signature that was at the bottom.
answer: For a devil to enter a dwelling, the current occupant must invite it in so many words; a house it rents itself it may enter freely, and the general welcome printed on a doormat carries no force. The narrator’s lease with the landlord was a lease for a shared dwelling, with a blank line for a second occupant. By the time he moved out, the landlord had let that line to the devil; with its own signature it became the lawful occupant of the new term, with no need to ask anyone’s leave. On that first night the term had not yet begun, so it stayed outside. By the next day, when the new tenant came asking the narrator about the strange signature, the devil — as joint occupant, key in hand — had already let itself into the old house.
hints: The words on the doormat decide nothing; standing in the register of occupants does.
There was a second joint occupant on the lease.
The landlord wrote the devil into the new lease, and once the term began it became an occupant of the house.

title: The Last Crane
story: Every paper crane I folded brought my missing older sister one step closer to home. At the ninety-ninth, her footsteps sounded outside the door. But my mother snatched away the last sheet, stuffed it into her mouth, and chewed it to pieces. From outside, my sister said softly: “Mom, you chose her again.”
answer: As children the two sisters wandered into the mountain, and their mother begged the mountain god for rescue, accepting his one condition: only one of them could be brought back. She carried the younger home and left the elder behind. Years later, the elder sister had a passerby carry out a hundred sheets inscribed with the old covenant; folded into cranes, they would lay her path out of the god’s domain, step by step. The covenant held that when the hundredth crane was finished, the other child who had once been spared must walk into the mountain and fill the empty place. The mother had kept all this hidden; only when she saw her own blood-print on the last sheet did she recognize the old covenant her daughter had sent home. She destroyed the final page and stopped the exchange. The sister who had walked all the way to the door was held at the threshold, and knew their mother had saved the younger one — again.
hints: Both sisters were once trapped together; the mother brought back only one.
The sheets carried an old covenant whose number still had to be made up.
The hundredth crane would have brought the elder sister home and taken the younger away; the mother destroyed the sheet and stopped the trade.

title: Seats for the Drowned
story: Every time the river drowned someone, another stone bench appeared beside the bridge. The new magistrate ordered them broken up to pave the village road. The day after the road was finished, everyone who had stepped on the stones was sitting on the ground, unable to stand.
answer: The old bridge had been built from stone lent by the river god, and the covenant held that for every soul the river took off that bridge, the god owed the dead a place to leave the water and sit on the shore. So the benches beside the bridge multiplied, each one bound to one of the drowned. Even smashed, the binding stayed in every fragment; when the living stepped on the rubble, the dead took them for new seats and pressed them down where they stood. Only when the magistrate found the stele at the bridgehead, carved with the covenant, did he grasp what he had torn up: the only seats on shore the dead would ever have. He had the paving stones carried back to the riverside one by one and rebuilt into benches, and only then, one after another, were the people sitting on the road let go.
hints: Each stone bench was bound to one particular drowned soul.
Breaking them into paving stones did not undo the bond.
The dead, with no seats left, pressed the people who stepped on the stones down in their place; restoring the riverside benches released them.

title: The Daytime Lantern Festival
story: The lantern festival in our town was always held at noon; the moment the sky darkened, every lantern had to be put away. A merchant newly arrived in town said they looked better at night, and secretly kept one lit. At midnight his shop door stood open, and on the floor there was nothing but a set of flat clothes.
answer: The town’s lanterns are made of a paper that preserves human silhouettes. Displayed under the sun, the shadows inside are pressed flat by the strong outer light and show only as patterns on the paper; once night falls and a flame is lit within, the paper silhouette gains a solid outline and must borrow thickness from a living person nearby. The merchant did not know that putting the lanterns away meant folding the paper flat to seal off any light inside — he left a whole lantern burning. In the night the silhouette inside propped itself up into a complete body, and the thickness was drawn out of him instead, leaving him a thin shadow pressed against the lantern paper. The open shop door was left by the one who climbed out of the lantern and walked away wearing a body freshly borrowed.
hints: The patterns on the lantern paper are preserved human silhouettes.
Sunlight striking the outside and lamplight burning within produce different results.
At night the inner flame let the paper silhouette borrow the merchant’s bodily thickness, and the merchant was pressed into the lantern paper.

title: Say It Again
story: The priest heard my confession, then locked the door from the inside and told me to say it again. When I finished repeating it, he asked for a third time. Near dawn he finally opened the door. The space beyond it was filled with kneeling people, and every mouth was telling that thing in my stead.
answer: The statue in the confessional can divide a sinner’s memory among those who hear a complete confession; each time the confession is repeated, one more listener truly lives through what the victim endured. The narrator is a torturer brought back under guard to be investigated, who insisted that the torments he inflicted were of no consequence — and the townspeople had long believed his propaganda. The priest locked the inner door so the confession could not be cut short, and had the officials who once supported him listen outside, one by one. By dawn every one of them carried the same memory as if it were their own, and their mouths kept repeating that thing without their willing it. They knelt and begged the victims for forgiveness. What the narrator faced as he stepped out was a congregation of witnesses who knew the truth.
hints: Each repetition passed that experience to one new listener.
What the people outside lived through was the pain the victim had suffered.
The statue turned the confession into lived memory in its listeners; those who had backed the torturer learned the truth.

title: Eyes for a Day
story: With a single decree, the blind king asked the whole nation to lend him their eyes for one day. He finally saw his own palace — and at once ordered the throne torn down. The man beneath it raised his head and said: “Your Majesty, you have finally seen me.”
answer: The king’s eye-borrowing art lets him tap into the current sight of all his subjects while the original owners keep on seeing; he had never cast it so widely before, for fear of drowning in jumbled images. The court ministers had imprisoned the elder brother — the true heir — in a hidden chamber beneath the throne, and set his unknowing blind younger brother to rule in his place. When the younger brother borrowed the eyes of the nation, one of the views he tapped was the elder brother looking up through the air slit, and so from beneath the throne he saw the hem of his own robe and heard breathing close by, in step with that gaze. The chamber’s walls bore the elder brother’s name and reign title; he ordered the throne demolished at once and his brother pulled out. The small patch of palace that for years had been all the elder brother could see was finally seen by the man sitting above it.
hints: The borrowed eyes gave the king every subject’s field of vision.
One of those views looked up at the king from beneath the throne.
The imprisoned brother was a subject too; his sight exposed the hidden chamber under the throne.

title: The Lighter Offering
story: The mountain god accepts tribute and weighs it — weight is all that matters. I carried a basket of stones up the mountain, sure I could muddle through. On the way down, the basket was as light as if it held nothing, yet not one stone was missing. The child at the village gate saw me and called me grandpa.
answer: The weight the mountain god measures is the number of years a tribute has left before it dies. The villagers usually offer fresh fruit, buying a short stretch of peace with the remaining life of the fruit; stone lasts nearly forever, and the narrator thought it the better bargain — he had only missed the rule on the altar: tribute is accepted only while it still holds life. The stones in his basket could pay nothing, so the god took the difference from the carrier. The basket’s shoulder strap is the contact point of the weighing art; once the toll is drawn, the carrier feels the load lighten, the sign that the tribute has been settled. Decades were stripped from the narrator on that mountain; his face and hair aged in a moment, and only on the way down did he see the change — in the child’s greeting and in his reflection in the water.
hints: The weight the mountain god speaks of has nothing to do with how heavy a thing is.
The tribute must be something still alive.
The stones could pay nothing, so the god took decades of life from the man who carried them.

title: The Full-Moon Feast
story: I deliver babies at the edge of town and never take a coin for it. With every child I deliver, my face gains another wrinkle. Yesterday the oldest woman in town brought me an infant, knelt at my door, and bowed her head to the floor. I touched the child’s hand, and every wrinkle on my face was gone.
answer: This is a town that keeps its people through rebirth. Each time the midwife delivers a returning soul she first lends out a year of her own life so the child can live to its first full month; at the full month the child’s mother must bring it back in person to return the life that was lent. The mothers before had believed the midwife meant to take their children, and none would come, and so she aged, delivery by delivery. The oldest woman in town had read the rules in a covenant left by her grandmother; she brought her great-grandson at his full month and made her apology to the midwife. This child is the founding covenant-maker of the town reborn, and his full month also marks the close of a whole cycle of rebirths, when every unsettled loan of life falls due at once. The midwife felt on his palm the same mark as the covenant’s, and took back all the years she had lent out through the cycle.
hints: The midwife lends out her own life so that dead souls can be born again.
The families never completed the rite of returning the life at the full month.
The last child is the founding covenant-maker reborn; completing his full-month rite settled the whole cycle of lent years.

title: The Burnt Bread
story: The bakery caught fire, yet the owner barred the way and would not let the firefighters open the oven. It was all burnt bread inside, he said, long past saving. One firefighter pulled off a glove, pressed his ear to the oven door for a few seconds, turned back, and said: “This bread is crying.”
answer: The bakery owner had shut a child worker — one who had overheard his criminal dealings — inside the decommissioned great oven, to wait for his accomplices to take the boy away. That night the rear storeroom caught fire, and the firefighters came in searching for anyone trapped. Afraid the boy would testify against him once rescued, the owner played the heartbroken merchant, steering the search again and again toward the pantry and away from the idle oven. The oven itself was unlit, but the fire around it kept heating it through. While clearing the kitchen, a firefighter noticed the owner was guarding this one cold oven door alone, called for silence, and heard muffled sobbing behind it. When the door was opened, the boy curled up inside crawled out with his arms wrapped around himself — and the owner’s reaching hand was struck aside by the firefighter.
hints: The shop has a decommissioned great oven.
The owner kept blocking the firefighters from searching it.
The owner had locked the boy who knew too much inside the oven; the oven was never lit, and the child inside was still alive.

title: The Warm Room
story: The blizzard had closed the mountain, and we at last found an inn still open. The owner photographed every one of us before he would let us into the warm room. I had left my gloves at the front desk; going back for them, I saw him ticking the photographs off one by one. On his list, we had been dead since yesterday.
answer: The owner was in league with men smuggling valuable samples; on learning that the survey team was returning through the pass, he had set his accomplices to stage a fatal crash off the cliff road in the night, planning to take the samples and kill them all. The early blizzard shut the road, the team left the vehicle and walked — straight into this inn, which served as the gang’s way station. The confirmation list his accomplices sent had every killing set for the night before marked as done, and now the owner found his targets standing alive before him. He photographed us as a pretext of check-in, matching each face, marking for his partners the ones the plan had failed on. The narrator returned for his gloves, saw last night’s hour of death written beside his own photograph, and led the others out of the warm room on the excuse of fetching luggage, sending the distress call from outside. The police later found the pre-photographed crash scene and the full record of the deal on the owner’s phone.
hints: The owner had received arrangements made about them in advance.
The times on the list came before their arrival; the photographs were to confirm which of the planned targets were still alive.
Someone had meant to kill the survey team for the samples; the blizzard broke the plan, and the innkeeper found his accomplices had reported it done in vain.

title: The Numbers on the Shoes
story: The shoes of the dead lay in rows across the assembly hall; each family could claim one pair only. One woman picked two shoes of different sizes, and the staff at once showed her into a back room. Before the door closed, she lifted the shoes over her head and called out to the reporters: “Photograph these!”
answer: After a factory fire, the management, meaning to undercount the dead, had re-matched the scattered belongings of many victims into fewer sets and told the families that each pair of shoes stood for one person. The woman’s job was issuing safety boots to the workers, and she knew the employee numbers registered one by one inside each boot. The two shoes she chose belonged to two different missing workers — different sizes, different numbers — and that alone broke the pairing story. The staff, under the pretext of further checks, moved her away from the reporters’ eyes; so before the door could shut she held the shoes high, letting the cameras take the numbers. The original issuing ledger was later given to the investigators, and the list of the dead was counted again.
hints: The woman knew how the numbers inside the shoes were registered.
A supposedly matched pair could belong to two different workers.
The factory had re-paired different victims’ belongings to shrink the count; she raised the shoes so the reporters would keep the numbered evidence.

title: The Blank Score
story: The conductor came on stage, set the full score upside down, and the house began to play as usual. The patron in the front row listened and grew more and more afraid, then suddenly rose to leave. The conductor turned to the last page — the page was blank — and the whole orchestra stopped together.
answer: The patron had forced a vanished composer to ghostwrite in his name and arranged this premiere, ready to sign the work as his own. After escaping, the composer had passed his evidence to the orchestra, and they had memorized in advance a vocal work of his, never published, that set down his captivity plainly — and swapped it in at the premiere. The conductor setting the score, printed with the patron’s name, upside down was the signal for the musicians in the know to begin the switch. Hearing in the lyrics the details of a room only he and the composer could know, the patron understood it was over. The last blank page was another rehearsed signal to stop; when the orchestra fell silent, the composer walked out from behind the stage and handed the recording and the manuscripts to the reporters present.
hints: The orchestra had rehearsed another work beforehand.
The inverted score and the blank page were both agreed signals from the conductor.
The orchestra performed the imprisoned composer’s new work in public, forcing the name-stealing patron to face the true author.

title: Step Into the Cage
story: The circus beasts had broken loose; the trainer opened an empty cage and told us to hide inside. Once we were all in, he locked the door from outside and stayed there himself. Only when he threw the key over the bars did we see the man with the gun behind him.
answer: Armed robbers had slipped into the touring grounds for the takings and had opened the animal cages to sow chaos. The trainer first steered the visitors into another empty transport cage — one that could hold back the maddened beasts, stood behind the stage, and lay for now outside the robbers’ sight. He locked it from outside because the latch of that cage faced outward, and the visitors could never have secured it in time. When the robbers came after them and tried to seize the key and hold the hostages inside, the trainer threw it in first, leaving the visitors the means to open the cage themselves once the beasts had passed. He himself stayed outside to hold the robbers off until he heard the sirens closing in.
hints: The cage held off the beasts and, for the moment, kept the visitors out of sight.
The trainer put the only key into the hands of the people inside.
Robbers loosed the beasts to make chaos; the trainer locked the visitors in the safe cage and left the power to open it with them.

title: Tally Marks on the Ceiling
story: The ceiling of the cell was carved full of tally marks. I stood on tiptoe to count them when my cellmate suddenly pulled me down and stopped up the half-dug hole. He pointed at the very last mark: “Yesterday it still had four strokes.” The new stroke was cut deep, and it showed the white of fresh stone.
answer: The two men were held in a dungeon by a private militia, planning to escape along an old drain tunnel. The older scratches on the ceiling were left by prisoners before their time; the cell now had no bed frame to climb, and no one inside could reach those marks. When the two measured the hole the day before, the cellmate had noted that the last tally lacked its fifth stroke. The fresh cut meant someone had brought in a ladder and gone over the cell while they were taken out to labor. That someone had found the hole, added the missing stroke, and lay waiting at the far end to cut them down as they crawled out — two dead escapees, as the record would run. On that, the cellmate gave up the breakout set for that night. At midnight came the sound of a round being chambered at the other end of the tunnel, and then a low voice asking why they had not come out yet.
hints: Neither man in the cell can reach the ceiling now.
A stroke carved since yesterday means someone searched the cell while they were away.
The tunnel has been found and an ambush waits at its mouth; the cellmate sealed the hole and called it off, stepping past the trap.

title: The Mirrored Signature
story: After the painter disappeared, the auction house mailed his family a photograph of a new work. The family knew his brushwork and breathed again at last. The apprentice took one look at the signature and called the police. When the photograph was flipped, the signature read rightly — and every word in the painting turned backwards.
answer: The painter was being held by a partner of the auction house and forced to finish a run of paintings for laundering money. Before signing, he wrote his own name mirrored on purpose and kept the shop signs within the painting the right way round. His apprentice had an old pact with him: a reversed signature was his call for help whenever he could not write freely. The partner sent the photo to quiet the family, taking the signature for an artist’s flourish; when the apprentice kept asking questions, he flipped the whole photograph left to right and tried to pass it off as a camera gone wrong. But flipped, the shop signs turned backwards too — proof that the two texts in the painting had pointed different ways from the start. The apprentice brought the photographs and the pact to the police, and the inquiry turned toward the ones who had sent the painting.
hints: The signature and the words inside the painting face different directions.
No single flip of the photograph can set both texts right.
The painter sent his cry for help in a mirrored signature, and the flip meant to cover it left a new contradiction behind.

title: Brand-New Rust
story: The missing man was last seen at an abandoned mine. I looked at the rusted-dead rails and told myself no cart could ever run in there again. As the guide led us back, his boot soles left a line of red prints. I crouched and touched one — my fingers came up covered in wet paint.
answer: The mine had been turned into a site of illegal confinement, and small carts still ran in it by night, carrying men and supplies. The guide was one of the guards; hearing that the family was bringing searchers up the mountain, he had painted the entry stretch of track rust-red through the night, faking years of corrosion to make them give up on the rails. Hurried to turn the party back, he stepped in the fresh paint, and his boots carried it onto the pale stone. The narrator saw how wet the prints still were, slipped around to the inner side of the track, found the bright polished line of wheel flanges under the paint, and heard a cart rolling somewhere inside the mine. He backed away to where a phone had signal and called the police.
hints: The rails had been freshly treated.
What the guide’s boots carried off was red-brown paint that had not dried.
The entry rails were painted to look derelict, while carts still run inside, hauling the people held there.

title: One Medal Short
story: The memorial hall hung out a group photo of the rescued. The old veteran looked at it a long time, then unpinned his own medal. The curator took him for a donor and held out the register. The veteran pressed the medal against the photograph instead, and asked: “Can what this covers be given back?”
answer: In the war, the veteran had smuggled a prisoner of war out of the camp, and that man had then guarded him across the blockade line. To recast the story as a one-man act of heroism, the memorial had cropped half the prisoner’s body from the group photo and blown up the medal on the veteran’s chest to cover the arm that remained. The veteran kept the original negative and knew that hand had steadied him when he lay badly wounded. He took the real medal from his chest, held it against the photograph, and showed that the medal in the picture broke every true proportion — then drew out the original photo and asked that rescuer and rescued be shown standing side by side, whole. The honor the curator had been ready to receive became the very measure that laid the falsification bare.
hints: The photo on display had been altered; the veteran kept the original.
The enlarged medal hid the other man’s arm.
The memorial cut out the prisoner who had saved him in turn; the veteran brought the medal and the negative and demanded the missing man back.

title: Please Collect Your Effects
story: In the empty station, the ticket machine printed out a ticket to my home town, then pushed out my wristwatch after it. The screen said: Please collect your effects. I stepped back at once. The machine brought up a ring next, engraved inside with a date from next year.
answer: The ticket machine of this derelict station receives the effects no one will claim in a future railway accident and, tracing back the journeys their owners once bought, delivers each thing to the moment of that old purchase. The narrator pressed a button still wired to the old system; the machine read the same route he would ride ten years on, and sent back the ticket first, then the wristwatch and the wedding ring from that future. Next year was the year he had meant to marry, and the date inside the ring told him these things came out of a life he had not yet lived. The machine can only return what the owner leaves behind; it cannot say how the accident comes. He carried the effects out of the station, noted the hour and the train on the ticket, and kept off that train ever after. Ten years later, the same watch lay on the table of his home.
