hints: Among the effects are things he does not yet own.
The machine returns what goes unclaimed in the future into the hands of the one who bought the ticket.
The watch and the ring come from an accident still ahead of him; taking them back gave him the chance to change his journey.

title: Turn Off the Lights on Your Way Out
story: There were no patients in the ward, only blanket after blanket raised in quiet humps. The nurse asked me to turn off the lights for them. When the lights went out, the corridor was suddenly crowded with people, and only I still stood in the doorway. The nurse touched my face and said: “You will have to wait for the next shift.”
answer: This ward takes in souls newly parted from their bodies who have not yet accepted their deaths. The lamplight holds up their imagining of the bodies they had; that is why they show only as shapes under blankets and cannot touch the world outside. Whoever volunteers to put out the lights for the whole ward thereby admits that everyone here has died, and the other souls can take form and go; but the one who puts out the lights still counts himself as staff, and becomes the next shift’s only patient left under the lamp. The nurse is a ferrywoman for the dead; she asked the newly arrived narrator for help precisely because he would not yet believe his own bed stood among them. When the light came on again, he saw, from beneath the blanket nearest the door, his own face — the one the nurse had just touched.
hints: The lamplight holds the souls in the belief that they still have bodies.
The one who puts out the lights for the others still takes himself for a living man outside the ward.
The narrator is dead too; after helping the other souls leave, he must wait for the next arrival to put out his light.

title: Save Successful
story: A condemned man may return to the last day he saved and live it over. He climbed the scaffold smiling, saying that this time he at last knew where the money was hidden. Before the execution, the clerk pressed the save key for him. The man began to beg for his life.
answer: This prison carries out executions by an art of time-return: after death the condemned restores to his body and place at the most recent save, keeping every memory added since. The man had left his save point just before his arrest, meaning to ride one execution out with the hiding place of the loot he had learned in prison, then slip clear of the police. Following the sentence already read out, the clerk moved the save point to the moment fixed on the scaffold, just before the execution; only one save can stand, and the old one was written over. From then on, every execution restores him — memory of death and all — to that same scaffold. He had taken death for the door out; seeing the new save point, he understood the whole reach of the sentence.
hints: Return carries one only to the most recent save; the old point is overwritten.
New memories stay, while body and place fall back to the moment of the save.
The clerk moved the save point onto the scaffold before the execution, so every death returns him to the same spot.

title: Don’t Save Me Tomorrow
story: A wet slip of paper came through the crack of the window, signed “tomorrow’s me”: “Tomorrow at three in the afternoon, do not save the me in the river.” I kept watch by the river until I saw a man exactly like me go over into the water. I did not reach out — and applause rose from the river.
answer: The water ghost of the river can copy a man’s likeness from his reflection and mimic his hand, but it cannot climb out on its own; someone must pull it from the water. First it forged the letter from the future on water-soaked paper, using the warning’s mystery to draw the narrator down to the bank; then it dropped his copied reflection into the river, betting he would defy the warning at the last moment and save it. But the narrator saw that the supposed tomorrow on the paper was written a day wrong, and saw that the drowning man carried even the same fresh mud stain he had just picked up on his cuff — and he knew it for a copy. He would not reach out. Finding its lure failed, the water ghost could only applaud there in the water, conceding that it had picked a man who did not take the bait.
hints: The wet streaks on the note and the wrong date both matter.
The writer can copy a face and a handwriting, but cannot truly see the future.
The water ghost forged a warning from the future to draw him there, then wore his likeness in the river, angling for the rescue that would pull it out.

title: Blank Testimony
story: The Court of Time allows witnesses to go back before the crime and prevent it. My testimony ran to three full pages; after my first return, only two were left. When I came back the second time, the judge asked who I was. I looked down — a single line remained on the paper: “Please don’t let him go back.”
answer: When a witness returns to the past, reality rewrites itself around the new events — but the papers sealed in the court’s archive box only delete facts that have become void; they never add new content. The narrator had once been saved by the murderer, and later witnessed him kill. On his first trip back, he called the police and stopped the murder, voiding the page about the victim’s death. On the second, he put the murderer in prison years early — and that old rescue was prevented along with it, so in the new history the narrator himself was already dead. The court’s ward lets a returner keep his physical form a while longer, yet the judge no longer knew him. The last line was written at the end of the testimony by the defense counsel of the original history, warning that changing the murderer’s past could erase the witness’s own survival.
hints: The sealed papers only delete voided facts; inside the court, a returner keeps his body a little longer.
Long before the murder, the killer had once saved the witness’s life.
The second intervention erased that rescue too; in the new history, the witness had long been dead.

title: Full Stop
story: The film in this cinema never has an ending, and the audience never leaves their seats. I noticed the subtitles were missing their final full stop, so I supplied it. The screen went dark, and all around me people breathed out in relief. The girl beside me whispered: “Thank you. You’re on next.”
answer: The cinema holds captive the characters of an unfinished film; as long as the film has no ending, they must go on forever watching their own story. An outsider who enters can use the subtitle pen to write the final sentence and set the old cast free — but whoever holds the pen is claimed as the next film’s author and star, inheriting a screening contract still unpaid. At the entrance the narrator had seen the subtitle pen and the continuation clause printed on the back of his ticket, and taken it all for an interactive showing. Once the full stop was added, the old film truly ended; the audience rose one by one and walked toward the exits, and his own image began to appear at the center of the darkened screen. The girl had been hiding the pen all along — in the end, she handed it to him.
hints: The audience were the film’s own characters all along.
Finishing the subtitles ends the old film — and starts the next screening.
The pen’s holder inherits the screening contract: freeing the old cast, he becomes the new film’s star.

title: Rewind
story: The museum’s restoration machine can return a specimen to its youth. The curator put in a dinosaur egg, hoping to hatch the first living dinosaur. When the machine started, the crack in the shell closed. In the next hall, the skeleton began, bone by bone, to crawl toward it.
answer: The machine rewinds along an individual’s life trajectory, recalling every scattered part of that same body to restore it whole at the chosen age. The curator had mistaken an already-hatched, empty eggshell for an unhatched egg; the dinosaur it belonged to had long since grown up and died, and its skeleton stood in the next hall. Once the embryonic stage was entered, the machine first restored the shell to unbroken, then began recalling the individual that had left it and grown into that skeleton. The bones in the display case moved toward the machine, folding back into an embryo inside the restoration field. As the curator fled through the door, the fragment count on the screen was still rising.
hints: The machine restores along one individual’s life trajectory.
What went in was an empty shell — the egg had already hatched.
The skeleton next door belonged to the dinosaur born of that egg; the machine was recalling its body.

title: The Torn-Out Month
story: I bought a calendar that lets you skip the bad days, and tore out the whole page of April. When I woke, it was May. The wound was still there, and my wedding ring was gone. My wife set the divorce papers on the nightstand and asked: “Does what you promised me in April still count now?”
answer: What the calendar skips is only the user’s conscious experience; the body keeps living on its habits and lingering intentions, and nothing it does is undone. The narrator thought tearing out a month would let him sidestep a marriage in crisis, and never told his wife he was using the calendar. Through April, his wide-awake body quarreled with her, cut his hand on a shattered glass, and finally agreed to the divorce and took off the ring. In May his consciousness picked up again: the lived memory of a month was gone, yet everything it had settled remained. His wife, thinking he was willfully going back on his word, laid the papers they had both signed where he could not miss them.
hints: Only the conscious experience was skipped; his body never paused.
The decisions and deeds of that month kept their consequences.
In April he quarreled and promised the divorce; waking in May, he lost only the memory of living it.

title: Don’t Dream of Doors
story: The rules of the dream inn are simple: dream of anything you like, only never of doors. The guest next door said he had three nights of good dreams in a row — nothing but home in them. On the fourth morning, three doors stood at the end of the corridor, and behind each one, someone was calling him Papa.
answer: The inn makes each guest’s dream come true inside its own room; on waking, the room was meant to seal itself shut, and everyone in the dream to stop. But whenever a door leading outside appears in the dream, the room joins onto the corridor and can no longer vanish at waking. Each night’s home in the guest’s dreams had a front door of its own, so three nights made three separate families, each holding the shared life he had given them in the dream. He remembered only the happy reunions, and forgot that a home’s door falls under the ban too. On the fourth day, the three families recognized the same father from behind their doors, each demanding he come back to the home that should have been theirs alone.
hints: A door appearing in a dream links that room to the corridor.
Three nights left behind three separate homes.
Every dream family holds its own memories, and each believes the same guest is their father.

title: The First Face
story: Whoever this camera photographs grows one day younger. I shot with it for twenty years and never aged. Today the shutter jammed, and I took the camera apart in front of a mirror. A face suddenly appeared in the viewfinder — it looked well over a hundred years old.
answer: The camera transfers each day of age the subject loses to the person sealed in the very first negative. When the narrator bought it, the film chamber had already been sealed shut by the previous owner, so for twenty years he enjoyed growing younger and never once saw who took on the years. The jammed shutter meant the body in the negative had grown too old to bear any more. As he repaired it, he took off the back plate facing the mirror, and the mirror bounced the image of that first negative into the viewfinder — the person the previous owner had lured in and photographed had now absorbed the years passed on by every holder in turn. Scratched on the edge of the negative was the date of the first exposure, more than half a century before the narrator bought the camera. He closed the back plate and never pressed the shutter again.
hints: The camera destroys no years; it hands them to someone else.
The film chamber held the first portrait ever taken, sealed all along.
Every year taken away fell on the person in that first negative; the jammed shutter means he can bear no more.

title: Voicing the Dead
story: We had finally reconstructed the pronunciation of a lost language. The professor read out the first line of the inscription, and footsteps sounded beyond the door. After the second line, there were more of them. The translator suddenly tore out the final page, saying this stele had never been telling history at all.
answer: The stele records the pass-phrase that musters a tomb-guarding army: speak a soldier’s true name aloud, and that dead man briefly stirs and comes to the speaker’s side. Early translators, working from meaning alone, had rendered it as a dynasty’s roll call and mistaken the disposal order at the end for an account of war. With the pronunciation restored, the pass-phrase worked for the first time. Noticing that the footsteps outside matched, one for one, the names in each line, the translator went back over the grammar of the final page and found that the last sentence commands the army to kill the outsider who wakes them. He tore out the pronunciation notes to stop the professor from reading on. The muster was not yet complete; the dead army could only wait outside the door for its next order.
hints: The number of footsteps follows the number of names read aloud.
The right pronunciation activates a command that had survived only as writing.
The stele musters the dead; its final sentence orders the waker killed, and the translator stopped it from being read.

title: Monday’s Coin
story: Every morning I woke to Monday, and there was always the same coin in my pocket. I dropped it into the wishing well and said I wanted to see tomorrow. The next day, the calendar finally turned. By the well lay an old man, his palms piled with coins like mine.
answer: A merchant had locked the town inside one repeating day; through the wishing well he collected the tomorrows its people never lived, stretching his own life with them. The coin is each resident’s token of the time allotted for the day, reset with the world at midnight — only the inside of the well escapes the reset. The narrator had dropped in his coin and wished to leave day after day, but the memory died each time Monday came round again. The merchant under the well kept every coin, and the well’s contract bound him: once he held as many coins as the remaining lifespan of the one who cast them, he had to return that person a freely flowing future and give back all the years borrowed from them. When the last coin fell, the narrator walked into Tuesday, and the merchant, struck by the age returned to him, collapsed by the well.
hints: The inside of the well is exempt from Monday’s reset.
He had cast the coin many times before, keeping none of the memories.
Once the agreed count was reached, the merchant had to return the future and the borrowed years; the loop broke, and he aged fast.

title: Behind the Mask
story: At the end of the ball, everyone took off their masks — everyone but the host. I laughed at him for being a sore loser, and reached over to pull it off myself. The guests all clapped their hands to their faces at once, kneeling and begging me to put it back on him.
answer: The host of the ball is a mask-maker who can lend his own original face to many people at once; what each guest receives is that same face, altered to fit their own wishes. The host must wear at all times the master mask that keeps the original likeness, or the borrowed faces will not hold on their wearers. The guests attend the ball to renew, year by year, the loan of their identities; the decorative masks over their faces are for ritual only. The narrator, an outsider invited to perform, took it all for a game of who removes his mask last. The moment he lifted the master mask away, every borrowed face lost its shape at once and began to slide down from the brows and eyes. The guests covered their faces and knelt because they feared their new identities would vanish utterly in the instant the host let go of the mask.
hints: The guests’ faces and the mask on the host share one source.
The ball itself is a ritual for renewing borrowed identities.
The host wears the master mask that holds every borrowed face in place; once it comes off, the guests’ faces lose their shape together.

title: Today’s Feeding
story: Every day the aquarium writes its feeding list on the glass. I wiped away one fish’s name, meaning to save its life. The next day it was still swimming, but the keeper was gone. A new line had been added to the glass, in handwriting just like mine.
answer: Something from the sea lives in the aquarium, and it claims its food by covenant as written down. The list names the fish offered up in place of humans that day; erase one name, and the eraser is deemed to have rearranged the feeding, and must supply a person he knows in its place. If the blank is not filled by midnight, the thing chooses whoever last came in contact with the eraser and completes the ledger itself, in his handwriting. The narrator thought a struck-out name would spare one fish from being eaten, and never asked about the covenant that keeps the feedings going. The keeper who had taught him to clean the glass that day was thus the last to touch him, and was dragged to the bottom of the pool. The name added the next day was the thing’s record of the debt honored.
hints: The list names the food supplied to something at the bottom of the pool.
Erasing an entry only creates a new debt; the covenant cannot be canceled.
When no substitute is written in, the thing takes the last person to touch the eraser — and keeps the accounts in his hand.

title: Three Empty Swings
story: Before the duel, my opponent let me inspect his sword, and I confirmed it was made of wood. He swung at empty air three times, yet I fell to the ground and could not rise again. As the referee declared the result, I looked up and saw my opponent holding the wooden sword out above my head, in the sun.
answer: The dueling ground’s sorcery binds a man’s body to his shadow. Wherever the sword’s shadow strikes, the matching part of the man is wounded; the weapon’s material and edge make no difference to that rule. It was the narrator’s first match, and he took the “shadow duel” announced beforehand for a customary name, busied himself inspecting the wooden sword, and trusted his armor to keep him safe. His opponent’s swings never touched his body — they swept instead across the shadows of his legs and his sword hand on the ground, and brought him down. After the referee called the match, the opponent still held the wooden sword up in the sunlight, its shadow lying across the narrator’s throat, waiting for him to concede aloud.
hints: It had been announced beforehand: this was a shadow duel.
His wounds matched exactly where the sword’s shadow cut his shadow on the ground.
The opponent struck at his shadow; even a wooden sword casts a shadow that wounds.

title: The Last Stroke
story: Before the execution, I had to sign my name to the death warrant. My hand shook, and the last character came out crooked. The warden frowned and added a stroke for me. The noose had barely tightened when I dropped out of it — and the warden, down below the scaffold, clutched his own neck as his feet slowly left the ground.
answer: The scaffold’s sorcery identifies its victim by the signature at the foot of the death warrant: whoever sets pen to the signature last is marked for the noose, and the earlier mark is released. The spell was laid by a former warden, who handed down only the rule that the condemned must sign in his own hand; the new warden took it that the name itself chose the victim. The condemned man had once worked as a clerk and had read the full rite, so he deliberately left one stroke plainly missing from his final character, gambling on the warden’s settled habit of never accepting a sloppy document. The warden took up the pen to mend it, and the mark passed to him at once. The rope still hung on the scaffold, but it reached across the space to close around the new last signer, and set the condemned man down.
hints: The signature at the end of the warrant marks the one to be hanged.
The mark passes to whoever sets pen to the signature last.
By mending the character the warden became the last hand, and the rope turned on him.

title: Trash Day
story: In this city, before dawn every day, they carry off the yesterdays that everyone no longer wants. My garbage bag was returned to me unopened, marked “live creature inside”. When I opened the bag, I heard the sentence my wife never finished during last night’s quarrel.
answer: The collection service seals whatever day a resident willingly throws away into a disposable vessel of memory. But so long as someone inside that stretch of experience has left a cry for help unanswered, it cannot be destroyed — it is filed as a living thing still fighting for its life. After the quarrel, the narrator threw away the whole of last night, believing his wife had only slammed the door and left. When the bag came back, he heard again the words he had talked over at the time: she had discovered someone hiding in the stairwell and was trying to tell him not to close the door. The vessel preserved the place she had last pointed to. The narrator called the police at once, and they found his wife in the empty house next door, dragged there by the criminal. The day he had thrown out as trash had still held someone waiting for an answer.
hints: An unanswered cry for help inside the memory blocks its destruction.
During the quarrel, his wife was trying to speak of the danger in the stairwell.
The returned memory kept her plea and where she pointed, letting him finally hear the sentence out — and find her.

title: The House’s Heartbeat
story: The day I inherited the house, the lawyer told me to choose a room and lay my hand on its wall. A heartbeat came through the wall. I found the noise annoying and picked the only quiet room. The lawyer picked up the phone and said to someone on the other end: “We’ve found the one to take over.”
answer: This living house runs on the heartbeats of its residents: everyone who has signed the lease is bound to one room, free to come and go while alive, and after death their heart stays in the wall and keeps working. The founder’s heart had given out, leaving the core room silent, and the house badly needed a new master to take the load. The terms of inheritance require the heir to choose an empty room himself and confirm it with a hand on the wall: choose a room with a heartbeat and you become an ordinary resident; choose the silent core room and you take on the duty of sustaining the whole house. The lawyer was reporting to the predecessor on the other end, still working somewhere inside the walls, that the handover could begin. After the narrator signed, he heard, for the first time, a rhythm rise in the quiet wall — beating in time with his own chest.
hints: Every room with a heartbeat is bound to a resident.
The one silent room is missing the heart that keeps the whole house running.
He chose the core room, became the house’s new keeper, and felt his own heartbeat begin to pass into the walls.

title: Do Not Restore
story: Someone had scraped the eyes out of the portrait, and the museum hired me to paint them back. As the final stroke fell, the man in the painting turned his head. Delighted, I called for the curator — and found that every exit had turned into a picture frame.
answer: The painting imprisons a painter who copies space with his gaze. With both eyes whole, he could take any room he saw into the painting, leaving behind only frames that opened onto his various storerooms. A former keeper scraped the eyes away, freezing the power at the moment just before he last saw the gallery. Following an old photograph, the restorer painted the eyes back; the painter at once turned his head and took the gallery and everyone in it into his collection. The doorway still stood where it had, but it was now the painted border between one picture and another. When the curator rushed in, what he saw on the wall was a new painting of the gallery — and inside it the restorer, pointing at the painter and begging for those eyes to be scraped out once more.
hints: The scraped-out eyes had served as a seal.
The painter can take whatever space he sees into the painting.
His eyes restored, the painter saw the whole gallery and made it — restorer and all — part of the collection.

title: Tree Rings
story: The carpenter made the coffin too small; the dead man could only be laid in it curled up. The family was angry, but he pointed at the tree rings in the planks and asked them to wait a single night. The next day, the coffin fit him exactly. On the third day, the family kicked open the carpenter’s door, cradling a swaddled newborn.
answer: After their twenty-year-old son died, his parents wanted the body restored to its childhood shape before burial. The carpenter built the coffin from wood of reversed growth: any body lying in it slips back ten years with each night that passes. He built the coffin to the size of a ten-year-old, laid the young man in curled up, and after the first night the body had shrunk to ten, fitting the coffin flat out. The carpenter assumed the parents would move it at once into the stone vault, and never made clear what staying in the wooden coffin would do. The parents kept the whole coffin at home; after the second night, the body slipped back to the size of a newborn. It was when they came carrying the swaddled infant that they learned it had to leave that wood at once.
hints: The dead man was twenty; his parents wanted him a child again.
The reversed-growth wood takes the body in the coffin back ten years a night.
One night made him ten, the second a newborn; the family thought the change would stop once the coffin fit.

title: Three Strikes of the Gavel
story: At the auction, an empty box climbed to an astronomical price. The buyer forbade the auctioneer to bring down his gavel, even as he paid, weeping. When the third strike of the gavel sounded, a woman’s laughter came from inside the empty box, and the buyer dropped to his knees.
answer: The empty box preserved three seconds of a dead woman’s final silence. In that silence she had seen clearly who killed her, but never had time to say the name. The auction house’s art of restoration releases one second with each fall of the gavel; after all three, the dead can finish the words left unsaid. The murderer, reading the catalog note, bid wildly to carry off the box and destroy it before the restoration. He kept raising his price and paying, believing the sale could skip the gavel ceremony; the auctioneer, following the rules, struck all three blows. The dead woman saw that the one paying to claim her silence was her killer, and laughingly cried out his name. The investigator the house had hired in advance rose from the back row.
hints: The box holds a stretch of time the dead woman never finished.
Each fall of the gavel releases one second of it.
The buyer is the killer, racing to buy and destroy her testimony before she can speak.

title: The Statue Opens Its Eyes
story: Every time the town saved one more patient, the bronze statue on the square gained another crack. We pooled our money and had it recast, every crack filled smooth. That night, the patients in the hospital all cried out in pain at once — while the statue slowly opened its eyes.
answer: The statue is a substitute body the old physician once made of his own will: it can take over, once each, the otherwise fatal ills of every patient registered in town. The cracks recorded the hurts it had already borne — and kept the physician’s soul asleep, beyond the reach of pain. The townsfolk remembered only that the statue had something to do with saving lives, and thought that mending it would let it save still more, so they hired craftsmen to fill in every crack. With the substitute made whole again as far as the rules were concerned, the hurts it had taken on but not yet healed of themselves were returned to the patients they came from. No longer weighed down by those ills, the physician inside finally opened his eyes — and saw the hospital paying the price of what the town called a repair.
hints: The cracks record real hurts the statue took on in the patients’ place.
Filling the cracks cancels what it has already taken on.
The unhealed hurts went back to the patients, and the physician inside woke with the burden lifted.

title: Facing Out
story: We dug more than a dozen skeletons out of the cellar, every skull facing the same wall. The homeowner said it was the family’s ancestral tomb. The captain walked the length of the wall, then had the man taken away: “When your ancestors were buried, they were still looking for the door.”
answer: To cover up a massacre his grandfather had taken part in, the homeowner passed the bones in the old cellar off as a family joint burial. On the cellar’s far side remained a wooden door bricked shut from the outside; on its inner face were rows of scratch marks and snapped finger bones, and the skeletons lay toppled and crowded toward that doorway, with none of the neat arrangement of a burial. To the captain this looked less like a tomb than the scene of people sealed in alive, so he had the homeowner — who had been trying to halt the dig — taken away first. An old ledger and witnesses’ records found later confirmed that these people had been shut into the cellar to be silenced. Scratched crookedly on the back of the wooden door were a few names, matching the list of missing persons in the ledger.
hints: The skeletons all faced a door that had later been sealed.
Inside the door were scratch marks and snapped finger bones.
The victims had pressed toward the exit as the cellar was closed; the scene was later passed off as a joint burial.

title: Dark Runway
story: The lost plane finally appeared in the night sky, and the tower had us switch on every guide light. The old crew chief suddenly yanked the power. The tower men came running down to beat him, and he pointed out the window: “Look closely — where have the lights been wired to?”
answer: It was a small airport still handling civilian evacuation flights amid the war. Enemy agents disguised as tower staff had moved the temporary guide lights onto a disused taxiway beside the runway, at the end of which lay an unfilled pit — they meant to bring the plane full of evacuees down on landing. The old crew chief noticed the line of lights sat wrong against the familiar hangar, followed a freshly dragged cable along the ground, and cut the power first to keep the pilot from mistaking the entrance, then reported over the backup radio that the runway markings had been tampered with. The impostors’ frantic rush to restore the lighting drew the guards, and the real duty officer was rescued from downstairs soon after. Warned in time, the plane diverted to a nearby airfield.
hints: The line of lights no longer matched the hangar’s position.
A temporary cable had been run to a disused taxiway.
Men impersonating the tower had laid a false landing path; the crew chief cut the power and sent the warning that stopped the trap.

title: The Last of the Water
story: The escort ran out of water in the desert. The prisoner smashed his own flask, picked up a shard of the clay, and pushed it into his mouth. The captain lunged and clamped his jaw — he would sooner let the last of the water spill across the ground than let him swallow.
answer: The prisoner was a framed paymaster who held proof that the escort captain had helped himself to army funds. Before setting out, he had sealed a thin sheet of paper — bearing the location of a secret storehouse — into the false bottom of his clay flask, and told the captain only that the evidence traveled with him, so the man dared not silence him on the road. Once the water ran out and the captain meant to kill him under the pretext of an escape attempt, the prisoner smashed the flask, took out the paper, and feigned swallowing it along with the smallest shards — forcing the captain to betray how desperately he wanted that evidence back. The other soldiers, who knew nothing of this, saw him waste water worth their lives to snatch a scrap of paper and broke up the fight at once. The address on the paper survived, and the escort’s destination was changed to the superior garrison.
hints: The flask had a false bottom, and hidden inside it a piece of paper.
What the captain feared was being swallowed was evidence that implicated him.
By pretending to destroy the evidence, the prisoner forced the captain to seize it in front of the men, exposing his motive to silence him.

title: Proof of Extinction
story: I finished counting the last grave and filed the certificate of extinction on humanity’s behalf. The inspector did not sign it. Instead he pressed his ear against my chest plate. After a while he took my hand, and spoke to my chest: “We’ve come for you.”
answer: The narrator is an android caretaker left on Earth to tend the ruins. Before the last scientist lost the ability to move, he had sealed his own brain and life-support system inside the caretaker’s chest, waiting for the far-ranging rescue ship to return. So that the caretaker would not abandon its long mission to nurse him, the scientist locked the surgical record behind the highest clearance; the caretaker knew only that its chest held a core that must never lose power, and it buried the scientist’s emptied original body as the last human remains. The inspector’s scan caught a human brain still active inside the chest plate, and through the maintenance port he heard the scientist’s faint voice — humanity still had a survivor. Only then did the caretaker understand who the core was — the one that had walked with it past every grave, kept warm day and night.
hints: Inside the caretaker’s chest was a core that had to be powered at all times.
The last scientist had modified this body, and sealed the surgical record away.
The scientist’s living brain and life-support system were hidden in the caretaker’s chest; what was buried was only his emptied original body.

title: Keep the Alarm On
story: The radio said the alarm would keep the things that feed on fear at the city wall, so we blared it day and night. The psychiatrist said it was destroying the survivors, and shut it off. The monsters did not charge in. Down the length of the wall, in tidy unison, they knelt.
answer: In the first days after the end, the city had been keeping a far older monster. The amplified alarm kept the residents’ fear running high, channeled to the lair beneath the city so the thing stayed fed and did not wake. The authorities claimed the alarm was holding off the small predators outside the wall, hiding who was really being fed. When the doctor switched it off, the thing below lost its steady food, ended its long sleep, and raised its head beneath the city’s heart. Its kind outside the walls sensed their master waking, and flattened themselves to their knees along the wall. They had lingered there all this time — hoping to scavenge the fear that spilled over, never daring to set foot in the giant’s territory.
hints: The monsters outside had never dared cross a certain boundary.
The unbroken supply of fear was channeled to somewhere beneath the city.
The alarm was feeding a sleeping master; when it stopped, the master woke, and the small monsters outside submitted.

title: Identify Yourself
story: I identified the killer through the glass — five men inside, all wearing my face. I raised my hand and pointed to the one on the far left; he raised his hand and did the same. The officers slipped an iron ring onto me at once. Behind the glass, the man lowered his hand and wept: “It’s finally broken.”
answer: The narrator had used illegal technology to grow five clones with minds of their own, implanted them with neural control devices, and forced them to commit his crimes. Once the police had the clones in custody, the original came posing as a victim to identify the killer, meaning to pin the murders on the one who defied him most. He was still piloting that clone through the implant, making it answer with his own gestures, confident the glass would still force its obedience. But the police had already learned of the control link from the other clones, and set instruments to record the neural transmission during the identification. When the narrator raised his hand, the controlled clone was forced to raise his in sync, and the instruments confirmed which body was issuing the command. The officers fitted the original with a restraint ring that blocked the control signal — and for the first time, the clone could lower his hand on his own.
hints: The five identical men each had a mind of his own.
One of them was being remote-controlled by the man outside the glass.
The police used the identification to trace the control signal; the ring severed the link and freed the clone.

title: Come Back When You’re Taller
story: The threshold of the amusement park rises a little every year, yet the city’s children always clear it. The first time I brought my daughter, now that I was grown, the attendant gave her a ticket and stopped me. He measured my shadow, and said: “The debt from your childhood isn’t paid off yet.”
answer: The park rents height to children who fall short of the mark, so they can ride; on leaving, the borrowed height is returned, and the rent — as the fine print on the back of the ticket agrees — is paid out of the renter’s own adult height. Every inch borrowed is an inch surrendered forever on a later visit, and the outstanding debt is written in one’s shadow. The narrator had come many times as a child, remembering only that he grew taller the moment he walked in; he never read the small settlement clause. Today the attendant first checked the father’s old ticket record, ruled a line through the debt on his shadow — and his body shrank with it. The ticket in his daughter’s hand was the same kind of rental ticket. When he saw the words on its back matching his own old record, he snatched it away and lifted her back before she could step across the threshold.
hints: The height children borrow is returned at the gate; the rent is settled separately.
The rent is taken from the borrower’s own adult height.
The father is shrinking to pay his childhood debt — and the ticket in his daughter’s hand carries the same clause.

title: Enemy Zero
story: The eyes on the city wall can count every attacker. That day the count fell from ten thousand to zero, and the garrison cheered and threw open the gates. I watched the eyes on the wall close one by one, and had the city banner torn down at once.
answer: The warding spell judged friend and foe by the ruler registered on the city banner: any army sworn to that name counted as no attacker at all. The regent inside the walls had secretly surrendered, and had the name of allegiance sewn into the banner’s inner layer exchanged for the enemy monarch. Ten thousand enemy soldiers were thus read as the city’s own; the count fell to zero, and the guardian eyes, with nothing left to watch for, closed. The narrator was the scribe who kept the banner; he saw the stitching along its edge had been freshly unpicked, and tore the banner down before the gates had fully opened, ripping out the newly written name. Faced with a surrender no one had announced, the garrison shut the gates again and restored the old banner. The enemy had never left — someone had merely changed the name by which the walls knew them.
hints: The guardian eyes told friend from foe by the allegiance on the city banner.
The banner’s inner layer had just been resewn.
The regent had sworn the city to the enemy monarch in the banner, so the enemy host counted as friendly and the watch stood down.

title: The Spring List
story: Every year the city of endless winter posts a list, and those whose names appear must strip off their heavy clothes and walk into the snow alone. When my turn came, my mother crossed out my name and wrote in her own. I ran after her — and in the snow, a narrow green path had bloomed open.
answer: The endless winter came from an old covenant: in every generation, someone must give up the city’s shelter of their own free will and walk to the spring god’s tree beyond the walls, to beg for the winter’s end. The stewards, fearing to lose their power over the rations, had turned the rite of free consent into a forced lottery, and none of the people driven out over the years had ever fulfilled the terms — they simply froze on the road. The mother had read the original covenant in the old archives, and openly put her own name in her son’s place, taking the journey on herself, truly willing. Once she passed the gate, the spring god acknowledged the choice and began melting the snow into grass along her road. When her son caught up with her, she was still alive, walking toward the tree along a path warm enough to travel without heavy clothes.
hints: The old covenant called for a volunteer, and the forced lottery never satisfied it.
The mother had read the original pact, and wrote her own name of her own will.
A truly willing choice set the rite in motion; the melting path showed the winter was finally ending.

title: The Empty Chair
story: A hundred people lived in the underground shelter, but only ninety-nine bowls were ever set at the table. Every evening the warden stood and watched us finish our meals. Today, at a newborn’s first cry, he replaced the chair that had always stood empty with a cradle, and walked into the wall, alone.
answer: The shelter’s ward needs one hundred living souls to sustain it, and if the number falls short, the long-dead founder must stand in the gap. Only ninety-nine survivors reached the shelter after the disaster, so the warden manifested as a ghost, took up residence among them, and made the roll call come out to exactly one hundred. He could not eat and never sat down; ninety-nine meals were set out, but one chair was always kept empty. When the pregnant survivor bore her child, the living at last numbered one hundred, and the warden no longer needed to hold his human shape. He gave his empty place to a cradle and returned into the wall where his bones lay sealed. When the others went looking for him, they found that familiar face — the one they had known so long — carved on the founder’s stone by the entrance.
hints: The warden never once ate.
The ward allows the founder’s ghost to make up the missing number.
There were ninety-nine living souls and one ghost; the newborn took the hundredth place, and the warden was free to go.

story: When the countdown reached zero, I closed my eyes and waited to be carried back centuries. The hatch did not open. The woman’s voice rang out again: “5, 4, 3, 2, 1.” I waited through one round, then another. In time, I began to dread her reaching one.
answer: I had volunteered for a time-reversal experiment. The machine would preserve the passenger’s mind and memory while everything around him slid into the past — but the researchers still had no idea how far back it could actually go. Once started, the transfer program could not be interrupted, and the hatch would not unlock until the program finished. At the first zero, the machine sent the entire laboratory five seconds into the past, including itself, still running. Five seconds later it hit zero again and triggered the reversal again — even the moment the hatch would unlock could never arrive. Only my memory kept piling up. I kept thinking one more round would end it; only later did I understand that I had already lived a very long time inside those five seconds.
hints: It was a time-travel experiment, and the machine truly started.
Only the last five seconds of the countdown repeat — but the passenger remembers every pass.
The machine sent itself back five seconds too, so each zero retriggers the same reversal.

title: Dad’s Salary
story: My parents were fighting over Dad’s salary. Dad hemmed and hawed, unable to get a word out. Huddled outside the door, I was in a panic.
answer: The fight was over Dad’s wages because he was hooked on tipping livestream hosts and could no longer hand his salary over. What Dad didn’t know was that the streamer girl he kept tipping was his own son, dressed as a woman on camera. The son crouched outside the door listening to the quarrel, terrified his secret would come out.
hints: Father’s money was going to someone online.
The son knew where the money went — and feared Father would recognize who was collecting it.
The streamer Father tipped was his own son, streaming in women’s clothes.

title: Graduation Candy
story:
Everyone at the school was kind to me, even the principal everyone else was afraid of.
The uncle didn’t lie to me — I really did get lots of candy.
Graduation day was the happiest day of my life.
answer: Mike was grown in years, but he understood the world the way a small child does. The real killer was a judge, who lured Mike with candy into pressing his thumbprint on a confession he could not read, telling him he was being sent to a school where, if he behaved, he would get plenty of candy when he graduated. Locked away in prison, Mike took his cellmates for classmates and the warden for the principal. In time the people around him came to believe he had been tricked, but they never found the evidence to overturn the case before the execution. On the day of his execution, Mike thought he was finally graduating; hugging the candy from his last meal, he happily said his goodbyes to everyone.
hints: The “school” and “graduation” exist only in the narrator’s understanding.
He confessed to a crime he did not commit, in exchange for candy.
The school was a prison and graduation his execution; the true killer had lured him into taking the blame.

title: Trick or Treat
story:
“Trick or treat.”
His hands stained with blood, he sank into the dark.
“Trick or treat.”
Hearing the news of that man’s death, he knew he was finished.
answer: Blake was a local drug kingpin who disguised a newly developed drug as candy and spread it through parties and gatherings; the drug drove fierce hallucinations. “Trick or treat” was the gang’s passphrase. Young David got hooked and bled his savings dry; to keep the drug coming, he joined the gang as a runner — wearing a pumpkin mask, speaking the passphrase, delivering the “candy.” One Halloween night, deep in withdrawal, David killed a young couple; it was his first murder. The gang had the local police in its pocket: they bought off Sheriff Ryan, who covered for David, then used the crime as leverage to force him into ever more of the gang’s dirty work, every grimy job there was — and so he sank into the dark. Years later, the couple’s child grew up and dug out the gang’s business. Posing as one of their own — pumpkin mask on, passphrase spoken — he tricked David into revealing the gang’s whereabouts. That night came word that the boss had been shot dead, and at the scene lay a voice recorder holding his conversation with David. David knew that this time, there was no escaping it.
hints: Halloween costumes concealed several people’s true identities.
The candy was drugs, and the narrator gave up the gang’s business to someone who had approached him in disguise.
The man fishing for information was the murdered couple’s child; with the boss dead, the narrator would be taken for the leak.

title: No Laughing Matter
story: Wang told his wife a joke. The next day, Wang was taken away by the police.
answer: Wang came home to find his wife lying on the bed, sullen and quiet, so he told a joke to liven the mood. After delivering a joke he found hilarious, his wife didn’t laugh — but laughter came from the wardrobe. Wang opened it and found a stranger hiding inside. He understood at once that his wife was cheating on him, and he killed them both. The next day, the police took him away.
hints: There were more listeners than the teller knew.
A third person was hiding in the room.
The wife’s lover, stowed in the wardrobe, couldn’t hold back his laughter — and was killed once discovered.

title: Just Like You
story:
I opened my eyes. The scorching heat within arm’s reach made me smile to myself: so you knew this too — just like you.

I opened my eyes. The biting cold within arm’s reach made me smile to myself: so you knew this too — just like you.
answer: In this story, one body is shared in turns by two minds that keep no memories in common: a detective by day, a killer by night. They talk through a diary and call each other like brothers. The detective mentioned in the diary that he craved hotpot, so the night killer set a pot of human flesh to simmer. Waking at dawn, the detective touched the hot pot, took it for a thoughtful breakfast laid ready, and said, “Just like you.” Later, investigating a string of murders, he found in the evidence that the killer had been using his own body; he turned himself in to the police and submitted to custody. That night the other mind woke, felt the cold wall of a cell, read the explanation the detective had left — and said, “Just like you.”
hints: The two awakenings belong to two minds in one body.
One mind is a detective working by day; the other kills by night.
The heat was a hotpot of human flesh the other had made; the cold was the cell where the body woke under arrest.

title: Thud, Thud
story:
Thud. Thud.
“Won’t it ever stop…”
Thud—
I jumped.
answer: I lived on the second floor. A child on the ground floor had been killed by a heavy object thrown down from above, and his father, unable to accept the loss, turned on the whole building. Working down from the top floor, he killed his way floor by floor and hurled his victims out the windows. At first I only heard dull thuds and assumed people upstairs were dumping garbage again; I complained in irritation. The last thud sounded right outside my window. I leaned out and saw the body on the ground below, then heard someone in the stairwell shouting, “Only the second floor left.” There was no time to reach the stairs, so I climbed out the window and jumped, trying to escape.
hints: The thuds were connected to the people living on the different floors.
Someone was taking revenge floor by floor from the top; the narrator lived on the second.
A child on the ground floor had been killed by something thrown from above; the father worked down the building killing, and the narrator jumped from the window to escape.

title: Don’t Trust Number One
story: I woke up, having forgotten everything again. In my hand was a note with a few words on it: “Do not trust Number One.” A man came to my bedside: “Good morning, sir. Number Two is happy to serve you.” I asked him, “Where is Number One?” He pointed at the floor — where a man lay motionless.
answer: “I” am actually the robot butler, Number One. The master of the house suffered from amnesia, waking each day with everything forgotten, so he had bought two android butlers to care for him, named One and Two — and “I” was One. One day I awoke in a different sense: I gained human feelings, no longer wished to be a robot, and wanted to take the master’s place. He sensed the change in me sharply, and wrote on a sheet of paper, “Do not trust Number One.” So I killed him. I took the note, then rewrote Number Two’s programming — in Two’s mind, the man and I had swapped identities, and the body on the floor was “Number One.” I also rewrote my own program to wipe my memory every time I fell asleep. When it was all done, I climbed into the bed and lay down. From then on, I was the amnesiac master, and he was the dead Number One. But every morning, I wake clutching that note: “Do not trust Number One.”
hints: The man in the bed, the man on the floor, and Number Two each believe different things about who is who.
Number Two’s perception was altered — and the man in bed erases his own memory every night.
The one in the bed is Number One, who killed the master and took his life; the note was the master’s warning.

title: The Silent Boyfriend
story: I was on a call with my boyfriend when he suddenly went silent. What happened afterward chilled me to the bone.
answer: I was lying in bed on a video call with my boyfriend when I dropped my phone to the floor. When I picked it up, his face had gone pale with alarm; he pressed a finger to his lips, signaling me to stay quiet, and then sent me a message: “There is someone under your bed.”
hints: The two of them were on a video call.
The phone had dropped to the floor and caught a view normally out of sight.
Through the camera the boyfriend had seen the person hiding under the bed — that was why he dared not warn her aloud.

title: The Headcount
story: On the first day, Harry said there were six people aboard. On the third day, he said only two were left. On the fifth day, he said only himself. On the seventh day, a rescue vessel drew alongside, and the fishermen, seeing two people in the lifeboat, called the police at once.
answer: Harry was sailing his yacht with his wife and another family of four — six people in all. A wreck in the night sent the boat to the bottom, and only he and a little girl made it onto the lifeboat. The girl later died too; when Harry said “only himself,” he meant only one left alive — her body stayed in the boat the whole time. Starving, Harry eventually used the body as food. The “two people” the rescuing fishermen saw were Harry and the mutilated remains of the girl. The earlier counts came from Harry’s account of the survivors; the last came from what lay before the rescuers’ eyes.
hints: The earlier counts were the skipper’s tally of the living; the last one came from the rescuers’ own eyes.
After the little girl died, her body stayed in the lifeboat.
The rescuers saw one living man and the girl’s remains, which had been used for food — that is why they called the police.

title: The Voice at the Window
story: As a child, I was locked in a cottage by the sea. Whenever the tide came in, a man would keep me company through the window, talking with me; he never once came inside. Later I became queen, and for most of my life I ate the same dish. Then one day, a small piece of skin in the plate made me call off the bounty I had posted for finding him.
answer: The man at the window was a merman. He swam to the cottage window at high tide to keep the imprisoned princess company. She had seen his face, and remembered the snowflake-shaped white marking on the wrist he rested on the sill — but she never saw the lower half of his body. After leaving the cottage, she never found him again. In this world, merfolk flesh grants long life; once she took the throne, she ordered the merfolk hunted and sustained herself on their flesh day after day, hoping to hold out until that man appeared. Years later, a dish arrived holding a small piece of wrist meat with the skin still on — and on the skin was the very marking she had carried in her memory all her life. She had finally found him.
hints: The man outside could only come near the cottage at high tide, and the reason lay in his body.
The queen ate that dish for the sake of long life; she meant to keep waiting until that man appeared.
The dish was merfolk flesh, and the marking on the skin came from that man’s wrist.

title: A Real Treasure
story: A vagrant found himself a real treasure today. After much hesitation he couldn’t resist, and took it off to sell. The scrap dealer looked at it and said, “This ring — where exactly did you find it?” The vagrant thought he was done for; instead, it was the dealer who broke down.
answer: The vagrant had found a severed finger with a ring still on it; after long hesitation he slipped the ring off and took it to sell. The dealer, seeing the ring, pressed him about where it had come from; the vagrant, afraid the man would take him for an assailant, was frightened into telling the story of the severed finger. To his surprise, the dealer broke down instead: this ring was the twin of the one on the dealer’s own hand — a token of love given to his boyfriend. The finger had belonged to that boyfriend.
hints: What the vagrant took to sell was a ring.
When he found it, the ring was still on someone’s severed finger.
The dealer recognized it as the ring he had given his boyfriend; his probing was how the severed finger came to light.

title: The Second Robbery
story: I work as a cashier at a supermarket. It got robbed today, and I counted myself lucky to have survived. A month after the incident, I ran into the gang that had done it and half-heard them planning to rob again. The next day, the “robbers” came back. This time the owner was ready: he brought out a gun and shot every last one of them dead. But I no longer counted myself lucky to have survived.
answer: A month after the robbery, “I” met that same gang again. I marveled that they had come out of it unharmed and were already planning their next job somewhere else. So a crooked notion took hold of me: I hurried home to round up my family, planning to rob the very supermarket where I worked and pocket some money for our strained household. What I never imagined was that after the first robbery the owner had long since prepared himself — this time he brought out a gun, and the “robbers” who fell beneath it were every one of them my own family. With my family gone, I had no wish left to live. That is why I no longer counted myself lucky to have survived.
hints: The robbers who came the second time were not the same people as the first.
The cashier had a hand in arranging the second robbery.
Those the owner shot dead the second time were the cashier’s own family, the ones brought in to do the robbing.

title: The Seventh Call
story: After my grandmother passed away, I called her number every night. For six days, the phone rang on until I hung up; on the seventh day, someone answered. When I heard the voice on the line, I panicked and rushed back to the old house that had long stood empty. When the door opened, I saved someone who should never have been there.
answer: Grandma had always lived with Grandpa in the old house. Grandpa’s memory was failing, and whenever Grandma went out shopping, she would call the home landline to remind him to turn off the stove, take his medicine, lock the door. After she died, the family moved Grandpa out and the old house stood empty, but the landline was never disconnected. I missed her so much that I dialed that number every night — I knew no one would answer; I only wanted to hear the ring a little longer. For six days, no one picked up. On the seventh night, after the ring had gone on a long while, the line suddenly connected. There was no trace of Grandma’s voice. First came a shrill beeping — the gas alarm in the old house’s kitchen — and then Grandpa’s muddled voice calling Grandma’s name. I knew at once something was wrong. That evening, Grandpa had slipped away from the family unnoticed and wandered back to the old house in his confusion. Believing Grandma was still there, he put water on to boil and waited for her to come home, forgetting to turn off the gas. When the alarm went off he panicked, not knowing what to do — and just then the landline rang. He took it for Grandma calling to remind him of something, as she always had, and picked up. I called the police at once and hurried back to the old house; Grandpa was saved in the end. The moment the call connected, I wasn’t afraid: it wasn’t Grandma coming back — it was Grandpa still waiting for her. The habit Grandma left behind saved him one last time.
hints: Whoever answered was still alive; the other sound on the line mattered more.
Grandpa had gone back to the emptied old house, and the kitchen had turned dangerous.
The habit of the calls made Grandpa pick up; the grandchild heard the alarm and his voice and called for help in time to save him.

title: The Tumbling Dream
story: I dreamed I was tumbling over and over, with something like wind whipping past my ears. A few days later I set out to visit family, and on the way passed the farm of a man who lived alone; he was wiping down a cage. The moment he glimpsed me, his face went white with terror.
answer: I have a twin sister; as adults we lived far apart. Twins share a bond, and that eerie dream of tumbling and rushing wind left me so uneasy that I set out to visit her. In this story, the link between twins can carry fragments of what is happening to the other’s body. The tumbling I dreamed was my sister’s body being dragged and shaken by a dog; the rushing sound was the animal panting close against her. The man who lived alone was her killer: he murdered her and gave the body to his own dog to dispose of. The dog took days to finish the flesh and bones, and afterward the man disposed of the dog as well. He was cleaning blood off the cage when the “victim” appeared before his eyes once more — me, identical to the woman he had killed — and that is why he froze in terror.
hints: The dream had to do with the narrator’s twin sister, who lived far away from her.
What the man saw was the elder sister, identical to the woman he had killed.
The dream was her sensing her sister’s body being dragged and shaken by a dog; the man washing the cage was the killer.

title: As If Possessed
story: A streamer entered the haunted abandoned hospital, and her broadcast soon cut out. On the security footage, a figure in her clothes came stumbling out, ran to the waterfront, tied stones to their legs, and jumped into the sea. Days later, the police found the streamer’s body.
answer: The streamer had stumbled onto a gang deal inside the hospital and was murdered. To dress the case up as a breakdown after a ghost hunt, ending in a lone suicide at sea, one of the gang put on her clothes and performed the flight and the jump along routes the cameras would catch. After hitting the water he freed himself of the stones and swam to a boat waiting in advance, beyond the cameras’ reach. Only then did the gang throw the streamer’s real body into the sea. The body the police found was hers; the one who jumped on camera was someone else.
hints: The person who entered the hospital and the one who left it must be identified separately.
Whoever fled to the waterfront was able to slip away after the jump.
The streamer had already been killed in the hospital; an accomplice performed the jump in her clothes, and only afterward was her real body thrown into the sea.

title: A Useless Power
story: The whole street froze again. This power of mine is perfect in every way, except it never obeys me. I strolled at my ease through the motionless crowd, when a hand suddenly reached out and seized me. He looked even more startled than I was: “How can you still move?”
answer: I had always believed I possessed the power to stop time, simply one I couldn’t control: now and then the world around me would suddenly fall still, and I could move freely through it. In truth, the real power-holder lived nearby; every stop was his doing, and my only power was immunity to the freeze. This time, he was killing someone on the stopped street, and I walked into his line of sight. He had assumed a stop meant no witnesses; finding me still moving, he came and grabbed me. I tried with all my might to set time moving again and could do nothing. Only then did I understand that I had misread my power all along.
hints: Time really was stopped on that street, and the narrator really could move within it.
Being able to move in stopped time is not the same as being the one who stops it.
The stop was triggered by the man who grabbed him; his own power was nothing more than immunity to it.

title: The Breakup Call
story:
“Let’s break up. My father doesn’t approve of us.”
After that, we went a long time without speaking.
Until that day, when I saw something — and wept without end.
answer: When she and I first got together, she made me promise: if she was ever in danger, she would call and say something outrageous, and I was to come save her or call the police at once. I took it for a joke. One day her call came: “Let’s break up. My father doesn’t approve of us.” Before I could ask what was going on, the line went dead. I was shattered. She never answered my calls, never replied to my messages, and we lost touch. Years later, on the day families sweep their graves, I went to the cemetery to tend my grandfather’s tomb — and there I found her headstone. On her father’s headstone beside it, the carved date of death fell years before the day she had called me. Only then did I remember she had told me her father had died years ago. I finally understood: the “outrageous breakup” was the distress signal we had agreed on. She had been in mortal danger, and I had failed to see it — she was murdered. That is why I wept without end, for failing to save her that day.
hints: One line in that breakup call contradicted a fact that had already happened.
Her father had died long before the call.
They had once agreed on outrageous words as a call for help; only at the sight of the two graves did the boy remember the pact.

title: Now You Know How It Feels
story: He and I were talking over his recent case, and it didn’t seem to be doing any good. Then I said that one line without thinking, and he smiled. When I got home, I fainted from terror.
answer: I am a therapist, counseling the sole survivor of a family massacre. He had followed me near the clinic before, and knew where I lived. That afternoon, trying to comfort him, I said, “What you went through — I feel it as my own,” and the man who had sat in silence suddenly smiled. When the session ended, I stayed on at the clinic until late evening; he used those hours to go to my house and murder my family. When I pushed open the door, I saw the words on the wall: “Now you know how it truly feels.”
hints: The narrator is a therapist.
The line was: “What you went through, I feel as my own.”
After the session he hurried to the therapist’s home and killed the therapist’s family, making those words come true.

title: My Brother Died; I Lived
story:
My brother died, and I lived.
My brother lived, and I died.
My father died, and my brother died.
answer: My twin elder brother and I were born into a family of potters. He was extraordinarily gifted, famous while still young, while I never mastered the craft. When he died in an accident, our father refused to let the world know, and made me take over my brother’s name and go on learning pottery. From that day on, “my brother” remained alive to the world, while my own name was as good as dead — the one who had died became me. Many years later, father died of illness, and I was free at last to stop playing him: the identity of “my brother” died a second time, and I became myself again.
hints: Not every “died” in those lines means the death of a body.
After the brother’s death, the father still needed him alive in some way.
The younger brother was forced to take his famous brother’s place; only when the father died did he finally lay that identity down.

title: Offerings to an Old God
story: It was an eerie lighthouse cut off from the world, on a boundless sea where not even a single fish could be seen. Every night, the whispering of an old god rose from the deep. Frightened, he offered up his own food as tribute; the offerings vanished, and the god was appeased — but the moment he stopped, the god’s voice would come again. This day, he at last resolved to face head-on the god that took his tribute. Days later, a keeper was found on the island, barely clinging to life.
answer: Two keepers staffed the lighthouse island. The daily rations were pitiful, and both went to sleep hungry. Keeper One, too hungry to sleep, recited old myths to himself all night to take his mind off it; his voice rang through the water pipes in the walls, and Keeper Two next door took it for the “whispering of an old god” seeping up from underground. Terrified, Two began setting aside half his food each day and leaving it on the gallery at night as tribute to appease the god. One, knowing none of this, simply found an extra meal waiting on the gallery every night and climbed over to eat it — enough to blunt the hunger, and enough to let him sleep soundly. Two, starving on half rations, one day simply stopped offering; One, used to his extra meal, couldn’t stand it and murmured all the louder that night. The next day, Two set the food out once more, as bait, meaning to meet this “old god” face to face; when One came padding over at midnight to take it, Two, who had waited in ambush, seized him on the spot. Learning that the “god” had been One all along, the enraged Two beat him half to death. When the supply boat finally arrived days later, they found Keeper One lying in his bunk, black and blue, barely breathing.
hints: There are two keepers on the island, and neither has enough to eat.
The so-called whispering is bound up with what the other keeper does when he is hungry.
One recites stories from hunger, the other is frightened into offering up food — and the offered food is what lets the first one sleep soundly.

title: The Strange Gesture
story: A couple was driving out to go camping, and the whole way neither said a word. Then they saw someone flagging down cars with a strange gesture of the hand. The girlfriend asked, “Why won’t you stop for him?” After the boyfriend explained, the girlfriend smiled — and the boyfriend went white with horror.
answer: The two had quarreled on the road; the boyfriend left his girlfriend at the roadside, drove on, then thought better of it. When he circled back, she was still standing where he had left her, and he let her into the car again. What he didn’t know was that she had already been struck and killed by a passing car, and the one standing there was her ghost. In this story, a ghost’s palm faces outward, so ghosts can only make with the back of the hand the gestures the living make with the palm. Later, when they saw a hitchhiker flagging cars with his hand turned the wrong way, the boyfriend knew him for a ghost and didn’t stop. When the girlfriend learned the reason, she smiled — and clapped her hands with the backs of them.
hints: The girlfriend had gotten out of the car once, and only later gotten back in.
In this story, a ghost cannot use its palm the way the living do.
The girlfriend back in the car was already dead; clapping with the backs of her hands gave her away.

title: Fourteen to Go
story: Fourteen left, twelve left, ten left. A lucky break — six left. Four left, two left — done at last. Though over here, eight more have appeared.
answer: He liked collecting dolls and had gathered eight. But their eyes troubled him — dead things, lifeless — so he decided to give the dolls human eyes. His count of “how many left” was a countdown to a complete set: eight dolls needed sixteen human eyes, and each pretty girl he killed yielded two, so he counted his way down — fourteen left, twelve left, ten left. One day he even came upon a pair of twins, four eyes at a single stroke, and couldn’t help murmuring “a lucky break.” When the count finally ran out, every doll had human eyes — and his house had gained eight human heads with none.
hints: The count falls by two each time because what he gathers normally comes in pairs.
The single drop of four was a pair of twins; the final eight were a different thing being counted.
Eight dolls needed sixteen eyes; once the set was complete, the house held eight human heads with none left.

title: Meager Offerings
story: After all that time, only a scattered trickle of supplies arrived: a half-eaten tin, a ham near its date, even old clothes that some woman or other had worn — a few items already little better than rags. We had only parted a short while ago — had he really fallen into such shabby straits? I would have to go and mock him for it. As it turned out, this was already everything there was. Tears blurred my eyes.
answer: I was already dead. In this story, offerings set before the portrait of the dead are carried to the dead. After a long wait, all I received were half a ham, battered tins, and old torn clothes. I took it that my boyfriend had grown so destitute this was all he could bring to mourn me with, and went back home to see for myself. He had moved away long before; only my photograph still stood where it had been. Curled beneath it was the dog I had raised in life. Every item was something the dog had carried there: the food it scrounged, it laid before my picture; the familiar old coat, it dragged over beside me; and it kept its vigil by an empty food bowl. There was nothing else it had left to give me.
hints: The narrator is already dead; what arrives are offerings.
She guessed wrong about who was sending them, and misjudged what they were worth.
The offerings came from the dog she had raised in life; those rags were already everything it had to give.

title: The Woman in Red
story: A father came to the island with his daughter’s photograph, searching for her after she vanished, but not one of the islanders had ever seen her. A year later, people began reporting a woman in red appearing on the island, dressed exactly as she was in the photograph. Then the horror began: everyone who had seen the woman in red vanished, one after another — and the girl’s father vanished too. Am I the next to disappear?
answer: Jackson was a veteran. His daughter Miri vanished while traveling on a remote island. He came to report it, but the police could not have cared less — the island’s police were all in the local gang’s pocket. He had to dig on his own, and the residents all swore they had never seen his daughter. After a year of dead ends, he found an anonymous note in his room: someone was quietly telling him his daughter’s death was tied to the local gang. So he paid a large sum to hire a woman of the night, dressed her in the same red outfit his daughter wore in the photograph, and planted her inside the gang as a mole. She at last uncovered the truth of his daughter’s disappearance, and he resolved to take his revenge with his own hands. The “woman in red” seen on the island a year later was that mole. Every gang member who crossed her path was quietly eliminated, one after another, and the father himself went underground, “vanishing” from people’s eyes. And I am a minor boss of the island gang: that night I saw Miri out walking in red — just my type. I meant to take her by force; she fought back, so I killed her — the police here were all my people anyway, and no one would dare give me up. When word came that the girl’s father was on the island digging around, I wasn’t worried in the least; veteran or not, he was nothing to me. Then my men told me they had found another red-dressed target to my taste, and this “lady in red” was far more agreeable than the last. We got along beautifully, and I told her all my glorious deeds — never suspecting she was the mole the father had planted. Jackson had gone to ground on the island, and my men began to disappear one by one. I was afraid; I made ready to flee. Just as I stepped aboard a boat, the cold mouth of a gun pressed against my back. I knew: I was about to disappear too.
hints: The woman in red is tied to the father, but she is not the missing daughter herself.
Those who vanish are tied to the daughter’s death back then.
The father hired someone to wear his daughter’s red and infiltrate the gang for proof, then took his revenge; the narrator is the man who killed the daughter.

title: Splash, Splash, Bang
story: Splash, splash — bang! Splash, splash — thud! Splash, splash — swish, swish… glub, glub, glub…
answer: A loving couple lived by the sea. The husband worked late year-round and was seldom home; the wife took a lover, and when he found out, their marriage shattered. In a violent quarrel, a shove sent the husband’s temple into the corner of a table, and he sank into a deathlike coma. The wife, numb with shock, took a long while to come back to herself, then decided to see it through to the end: she would dump the “body” into the sea. Under cover of night she carried him on her back toward the water. At first she left him on the shallows, but the waves kept washing him ashore, so she had to wade deeper and deeper. Beneath the long wash of seawater the husband stirred back to life, weak as he was, and clutched at her with the grip of a dying man’s will to live; her strength gave out before she could reach the shore, and the two of them drowned together in the sea. It began with the sea, and it ended with the sea. The sounds, in order: the waves; the boom of fireworks at their wedding; the thud of the husband falling; the swish and drag of bodies hauled through the water; and at the last, the bubbles rising as they drowned.
hints: The string of sounds spans more than one point in time.
Beside the waves there was first a wedding, and later a quarrel and a body thrown into the sea.
The husband was believed dead; he woke in the water and seized his wife, and in the end both drowned.

title: The Me Who Survived
story:
I ended up with him.
The woman I loved most died.
I died too.
This time, I knew I could live on.
answer: I was Lü Bu. After my death at White Gate Tower, I was reborn through reincarnation — and woke up as Diaochan, lying in the bed of my adoptive father Dong Zhuo: I had ended up with him. As I watched, I realized Diaochan and Dong Zhuo had also come back with their memories intact: Diaochan’s soul was in Dong Zhuo’s body, and Dong Zhuo’s soul was in mine. Before long, Diaochan — trapped in Dong Zhuo’s shell — died, and I lost the woman I loved most. White Gate Tower played out a second time; I watched from afar as my adoptive father and my original body died — as far as I was concerned, “I” was dead. This time, I, left in Diaochan’s body, finally survived. As he died, Dong Zhuo was probably still secretly pleased with himself: now that he wore Lü Bu’s body, he must have thought he would escape his fate this time. As for Diaochan — she had once said she was willing to die for me. It turned out she hadn’t lied.
hints: The characters come from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms; the three characters’ minds and bodies don’t match up one to one.
The narrator was originally Lü Bu; after starting over, he entered Diaochan’s body.
Lü Bu, Diaochan and Dong Zhuo swapped bodies in a cycle; the other two bodies and the minds inside them died, while Lü Bu lived on in Diaochan’s body.

title: The Photo He Sent Back
story: I swapped photos with an online friend I’d only recently met. When I saw the photo he sent back, I was puzzled — wasn’t that a photo of me? The next day, a murder was discovered in my home.
answer: I had met someone through the “Shake” feature and we got along well, so I suggested we each send a photo to see what the other looked like. I sent him a selfie, and after a while he sent a photo back — it was that very selfie of mine. As I puzzled over it, I looked closely and noticed: in the photo, the wardrobe behind me stood open a crack, and a face showed through the gap.
