This online friend had long since broken into my home and was hiding in the wardrobe behind me; sending my own selfie back unchanged was his way of telling me “I’m right behind you.” The next day, I was found dead in my own home.
hints: The photo he sent back was indeed the one she had just taken.
Pay attention to the background behind the person in the selfie.
The online friend was hiding in the wardrobe behind her, and his face had been caught in that selfie too.

title: His Sister’s Toys
story: The first time I visited my fiancé’s home, his sister sat clutching a few small garments, counting them one by one: “One, two, three, five… gone again.” He told me to pay her no mind. As I bent to gather the toys scattered on the floor, I saw a wedding photo on her bedside table. The door locked behind me.
answer: The woman my fiancé called his “sister” was the first wife this family had abducted. She had borne three children and then a pair of twins, and all five had been sold off. She kept their clothes and toys, counting the taken children over and over. Afraid I would keep asking questions, my fiancé had lied and called her his sister. In the wedding photo on the bedside table, the groom was my fiancé himself. Only then did I understand that this pre-wedding visit was a trap they had set: they had brought me home to take her place. The moment I saw the photo, my fiancé — who had been watching my every move — locked the door from outside.
hints: The count jumps from three straight to five — meaning two were added at once.
The clothes and toys belonged to the children she lost, one after another.
The “sister” was really the fiancé’s first wife; the wedding photo gives the lie to his story.

title: That Was Fast
story: I called building management to report a clogged toilet. Soon someone came knocking, and I said to him: “That was fast — the bathroom’s this way.”
answer: The man at the door was the killer, who had just finished his work upstairs. He had flushed parts of the body down the drain and found the pipes clogged; afraid the remains would surface when the downstairs tenant sent for a plumber, he hurried down to knock on my door. I had just reported the clog to building management, so when he arrived so quickly I naturally took him for the worker they had sent, and even led him straight to the bathroom. The killer seized on this misunderstanding to deal with the clog before the real repairman showed up.
hints: The visitor knew the toilet might be clogged, but had received no dispatch from building management.
The clog came from upstairs.
The killer, who had done his work upstairs, rushed down to deal with the remains before they surfaced; the tenant who had just filed the repair mistook him for a plumber.

title: A Calendar of Love
story: Xiaohong wanted to fall in love. In January, she fell in love, and spared no cost for it. In February, she lost it. In March, she fell in love, and shouldered a sweet new burden. In April, she lost it. In May, she fell in love, and this time he would never leave her again. In June, she lost it. In July, the police opened the door.
answer: In January, Xiaohong met a handsome man on a dating app and the two fell for each other fast. He turned out to be a con artist who kept borrowing money from her in the name of raising funds for a project. In February, having drained Xiaohong’s savings, the scammer vanished with an excuse about the investment failing and lying low out of town. In March, Xiaohong sold off her possessions and borrowed from everyone she knew to seek him out again; seeing she still had value to squeeze, the man went to work on her once more, promising to marry her once his business troubles were settled. Sweet-talked at every turn, she transferred money to him again and again, until she was saddled with loans. In April, Xiaohong discovered he was also carrying on hot and heavy with another woman, and the lines in their chat history were word for word the ones he had used on her; hatred and a twisted love devoured her. In May, she lured the other woman out and killed her, then drugged the man and locked him in the basement. When he woke and saw his mistress’s corpse he was scared half to death, weeping and swearing he would love only Xiaohong from then on. At last she had the world-for-two she had wanted — but it wasn’t enough: she wanted him to be unable to live without her. So, bit by bit, she cut off his hands and feet and gouged out his eyes, turning him into a complete invalid. In June, her possessiveness reached its limit; to make sure he could never change his heart, she killed him, cut out his heart, and ate it. In the end, buried in loans and stripped of everything, Xiaohong took her own life. In July, the police opened the door and found three bodies.
hints: All three loves were the same man.
The first two relationships were held together by money; the third, by captivity.
She went from being swindled out of her money to imprisoning and mutilating him, and in the end walked toward her own death too; the police found three bodies.

title: Two Documents
story: Two documents, one corpse, and a pen.
answer: The corpse of an infant; a birth certificate and a death certificate; and the same pen that signed both. The baby died soon after being born, and the doctor in attendance used one pen to sign first the child’s birth certificate, then its death certificate.
hints: Both documents were signed by the same doctor.
One records a life’s beginning; the other, its end.
The infant died shortly after birth, and the doctor signed the birth certificate, then the death certificate.

title: Two Athletes
story: Lately, two athletes have been keeping me up all night. One, armed with a very long piece of equipment, does exactly as he pleases; the other — the less he wears, the more excited I get. It’s just that neither of them seems much interested in my body, and that stings a little.
answer: “I” am the owner of the house in Plants vs. Zombies, and day and night a horde of zombies comes to attack it. Two of them are especially hard to deal with. One is the pole-vaulting zombie, who carries a long pole in his hands and wears a tracksuit; with that pole he does exactly as he pleases, vaulting straight over my defenses. The other is the football zombie, suited up head to toe in football armor — nothing knocks him down. But once the plants blast that armor off, he is nothing but skin and bone, gone in one hit. The “long equipment” is the vaulting pole; “the less he wears, the more excited I get” is the football zombie stripped of his gear. And the reason neither of them cares about my body is that what they truly want to eat is my brain.
hints: This scene takes place inside a video game.
The long equipment is a vaulting pole; the clothes are football armor.
The narrator is the homeowner in Plants vs. Zombies; the two athletes are the pole-vaulting zombie and the football zombie.

title: A Wish on a Falling Star
story: I bowed my head and made a wish. The wish came true, and I cried.
answer: Dad was an astronaut, away on a mission, and I missed him terribly. That night, gazing up at the stars and thinking of him, I suddenly saw a falling star, and at once bowed my head and made my wish: for Dad to come home early. The wish came true — Dad did come home sooner than planned. What I never imagined was that the “falling star” I had seen was his ship, wrecked and falling back into the atmosphere. That was how Dad “came home.” I broke down sobbing.
hints: Her wish concerned someone working far away.
She wanted her astronaut father to come home sooner.
What she took for a falling star was her father’s ship, falling back to Earth after the accident.

title: Six Farewell Notes
story: “You have disappointed me so deeply. I am never coming back.” That sentence appeared six times in all. I knew I was in trouble.
answer: After I killed my wife, I tried to dress it up as her storming out in anger. I practiced imitating her handwriting over and over, writing out “You have disappointed me so deeply. I am never coming back.” The first five attempts came out wrong; I crumpled them and threw them in the bin. Only the sixth served as her farewell letter, mailed to her family. When the police investigated her disappearance, they found those drafts in the house, summoned the letter that had arrived, and laid all six sheets in front of me. The same sentence, from a stiff imitation to a near match for her hand: a complete record of the forgery.
hints: The sentence appeared six times because one person wrote it again and again.
Someone was practicing to imitate the wife’s handwriting.
The husband killed his wife and forged a farewell letter; the police found five drafts plus the one that was mailed.

title: A Wonderful Journey
story: A truly wonderful journey. What was that thing? Why did no one answer our calls? What had happened? We had to do something — we absolutely could not let that thing pass. And it seemed we had done something that could never be undone.
answer: In the future, a married couple set out on a trip aboard a civilian spacecraft and strayed into a two-way time wormhole that had stayed open, which delivered them to the late Cretaceous. Not knowing what era they were in, they called Earth and got no answer — and then found an asteroid barreling along a course straight for the planet. Using the backup propulsion unit carried on board, they nudged it off its orbit, then flew back through the wormhole the way they had come, on the ship’s still-working main engine. When they returned to the era they had set out from, the Earth had changed beyond recognition. The impact they had dodged was the one that would have wiped out the dinosaurs and countless other species; with that event averted, everything after it unfolded differently.
hints: This trip went wrong in time.
The object they stopped was the one that was supposed to strike Earth in the past.
They arrived in the late Cretaceous and prevented the impact that wiped out the dinosaurs; by the time they got back, history had taken another branch.

title: The Strange Symbol
story: This old castle really did hold a secret. As I touched the charred corpse, an unfamiliar symbol swam into my view. It hurts… where am I… By a faint light I searched my surroundings. At that very moment, something happened — and there, in the bright blaze, I saw the symbol once more. I understood everything, but it was already too late.
answer: By touching a corpse, I can see the last thing the dead person saw before dying. In the castle, I laid my hand on a burned body and saw thick smoke, firelight, and a strange symbol. Pressing deeper into the castle, I missed my footing and fell into a hidden chamber. Lighting a match, I read the experiment notes on the wall: at fixed intervals, the altar at the chamber’s center transports whatever rests on it to the castle’s great hall as it was one day earlier; the time and objects around it do not go back with it. Beside the notes was drawn that very symbol. Before I could find a way out, my dropped match set fire to the flammable debris scattered across the floor. The flames drove me up onto the altar, and the symbol in the smoke closed over the dying vision I had just read about. After I died, my body was carried to the hall as it was the day before — waiting for the me who had not yet entered the chamber to come and touch it.
hints: The symbol that appears when he touches a corpse is what the dead person saw in their final moment.
The device in the castle sends whatever is on the altar to the hall as it stood one day earlier.
The charred corpse in the hall is the narrator himself, later in time; he read his own dying vision in advance.

title: That Sound
story: Late at night, I stepped out the door. A few steps on, the sound rang in my ears. I turned and looked back at nothing at all. I panicked: this was bad — really bad.
answer: I had been out with friends and took a taxi home late at night. After getting off at my destination and walking a few steps, the chime suddenly sounded in my ears: “Bluetooth disconnected.” I turned around; the taxi was already gone — my phone and my bag were still inside it, and there was nothing behind me at all. I panicked: this was bad — really bad.
hints: The sound came from an electronic device.
After stepping out of the car, its wireless link to another carried item was cut.
The earbuds announced the Bluetooth disconnection, and only then did the narrator realize the phone and bag had been left in the taxi, already driving away.

title: Mr. Pumpkin
story:
He woke on Halloween night.
He told me: beware of Mr. Pumpkin.
He told me: stay away from the candy.
He told me: never trust what the lion says.
He killed the demon, and then he fell asleep forever.
answer: Two minds share Mike’s body, keeping no memories in common and taking turns using it. On Halloween when he was ten, a man in a pumpkin mask broke into the house and murdered his parents. Mike, hiding in a cupboard, witnessed the slaughter — and hid away a few candies the killer had dropped. After that, the mind that remembered the massacre fell asleep, and the mind that handled daily life knew nothing of what had happened. On Halloween when he was sixteen, a pumpkin-head image on television woke that memory. The awakened mind left warnings for his other self in notes, then pursued the truth alone: Mr. Pumpkin was David, the killer from that night; the candy was drugs dressed up as snacks; the lion pointed to Sheriff Ryan, bought off by the drug ring. When he brought tips to the police, he saw the same candies sitting on Ryan’s desk; digging further, he found proof of the police–gang collusion. He posed as a member of the ring to get close to David and used their code words to trick out the boss’s whereabouts, killed the boss, handed the evidence to other investigators, and left behind a recording of David leaking information. When the revenge was done, the mind that held the memory of the massacre sank back into sleep — and never woke again. His other self could only read, in the notes left behind, those warnings, and an account of what he had done.
hints: The one leaving the messages and the one reading them share the same body.
The pumpkin points to the killer’s mask; the candy to the drugs; the lion to the sheriff’s name.
The mind holding the memory of the childhood massacre woke, uncovered the police–gang collusion, carried out his revenge, and fell asleep again.

title: The Murmured Name
story: A beach float drifted on the sea five kilometers from shore, and in it curled a woman at the edge of death. The moment the police pulled her out, relief washed over her and she fainted — a name still murmuring on her lips.
answer: Shirley’s parents chartered Captain Harry’s sailboat for a vacation at sea, bringing her and her little sister along. Woken by noise in the dead of night, Shirley found her parents already murdered in the cabin; she rushed on deck to find her little sister — soaked in blood, barely alive — and Captain Harry holding an axe. Harry, it turned out, was a repeat offender who killed for insurance by staging accidents; he had done away with his own ex-wife the same way. This time he had planned to fake a shipwreck, kill his wife for the payout, and pass off the chartering family as witnesses to the accident; when the family stumbled onto the plan, he simply killed them all to keep them quiet. On deck, Shirley thought fast: she turned around and begged Harry for “help,” playing someone who knew nothing at all. By then the boat was burning and sinking, and launching the lifeboat needed Shirley’s cooperation aboard, so Harry spared her a while longer. But as Harry rode the lifeboat around to catch Shirley when she jumped ship, she simply let go of the rope. Convinced she could never survive on her own, Harry took her little sister’s body and left, spinning a survival-at-sea story for the outside world. What he never imagined was that Shirley stayed alive on the beach float her family had brought along, until the police rescued her — and the name murmuring on her lips was “Harry,” the killer himself. Summoned by the police, Harry knew the lie had collapsed; in the end he took his own life in fear of punishment, driving his car off a cliff.
hints: Her float had been brought along for the family’s outing at sea.
The captain survived too, but the shipwreck story he told the world left things out.
The captain did the killing and staged the wreck; the girl escaped on the float, and the name she spoke can expose him.

title: What Are You Doing?
story:
“What are you doing? What are you doing?”
I looked over in terror.
“Me? I’m not doing anything.” He strolled over, all smiles.
His smile faded.
I knew I was done for.
answer: I was a novice burglar. I had meant to slip in while the owner was out, but my stakeout failed and I ran into him coming home, so I knocked him out and got ready to bolt. Just then, the gas company inspector rang the bell. Out of reflex I answered, then had to drag the unconscious owner onto the nearest balcony to hide him and play the owner myself — the man would only check the kitchen, surely nothing could go wrong. But the moment the inspection ended, the owner’s parrot suddenly shrieked, repeating over and over the very words its master had cried before being attacked: “What are you doing! What are you doing!” It gave me a fright. As it happened, the inspector kept birds himself; beaming, he chattered on about bird-keeping and replied, “Me? I’m not doing anything,” following the parrot’s commotion toward the balcony. When he saw the knocked-out owner, his smile slowly faded. I knew I was done for.
hints: The first voice repeating itself didn’t belong to a person.
It had learned the words the owner cried out just before being attacked.
The parrot kept repeating the cry for help, and the gas inspector, following the sound, saw the real owner lying unconscious.

title: Rewriting the Ending
story:
I was reborn.
This time, I would turn my ending around for sure.
The man beside me said something offhand,
and in my rage, I killed him.
answer: I was reborn just as the French Revolution broke out. In my last life I had died on the guillotine; this time, I was determined to turn my death around. While plotting next steps with a subordinate, he said: “When the time comes, we’ll head our separate ways.” With the guillotine filling my head, the word “head” was more than I could bear — in a flash of rage, I killed him.
hints: In his last life, the protagonist died on the guillotine.
The sentence contained a word that reminded him of how he had died.
The subordinate said they would head their separate ways; hearing “head,” the reborn man lost control and killed him.

title: My Daughter’s Voice
story: Hearing my daughter’s voice, I was terrified. She was screaming hysterically, pouring out how her parents abused her mercilessly at home. I decided that once I got back, I would punish this lying daughter of mine properly — she had promised me, after all, that she would never tell anyone about it.
answer: I am the girl’s mother, and I work as an operator on a helpline. My daughter had long been suffering abuse at home, and she had promised me she would never, ever tell anyone about it. That day, on my shift, a call for help came in — and the voice on the line was my daughter’s: screaming hysterically, sobbing about how her parents abused her mercilessly at home, while the person answering the call for help was none other than the abusive mother herself. I was terrified; then I calmed down and began to quietly think over how, once I got home, I would punish this promise-breaking, “lying” daughter of mine.
hints: The daughter is calling a helpline for help.
The mother’s job puts her on the receiving end of strangers’ calls for help.
The mother is the very operator who took the call — and the very abuser the daughter is denouncing.

title: The Woman at the Car Window
story: I was about to drive off when a woman rushed over, pounding on the car window. I was set on just driving away — but then she took off her clothes, so I let her into the car.
answer: The zombies had just appeared in the city, and I was getting ready to drive out of it. In this story, the infection spreads through bites. The woman pounded on the window, begging me to take her with me; I was afraid she had already been bitten and didn’t dare open the door. She saw my hesitation, took off her outer clothes, and turned her body around for me to inspect — not a bite mark on her. That gesture won her the ride: I let her into the car, and we drove off together, away from the streets as they slipped out of control.
hints: The woman was begging for help; she undressed so I could check for something.
The danger outside has to do with an infection that spreads.
It’s a zombie-outbreak world; she was showing me she bore no bite wounds.

title: The SOS Text
story: “But your daughter already took her own life last year.” “No — she’s alive. She only ran away from home. Look, she just texted me begging for help. She’s been kidnapped, someone is controlling her. Officer, you have to catch the man who did this.” “Ma’am, thanks to you, we cracked this case.” “It was nothing. It was all for my daughter.” “We are very sorry to tell you: your daughter truly is dead.” When the truth came out, the mother went mad.
answer: After running away from home, the daughter had burned herself to death with gasoline — a “suicide.” The mother refused to believe her daughter was dead, and kept digging into the truth of that suicide. She uncovered an organization of suicides: once you joined, you were never allowed to change your mind; anyone who tried to leave was forced by the group to kill themselves. She became certain her daughter had been murdered by this organization. So she forged a text that seemed to be her daughter’s plea for help, reported it to the police, and handed over every clue she had dug up. The police followed the trail to the organization’s hideout, while she set her own trap and burned the leader to death with gasoline — her revenge complete. Then the police told her a shattering truth: her daughter WAS the leader of that organization. Her death a year earlier had been faked, and only hours ago she had died in a sudden gasoline explosion. The one who had burned her daughter to death with her own hands was the mother herself.
hints: The plea for help “from the daughter” was forged by the mother herself.
The daughter did not really kill herself a year ago — she was later tied to the organization’s leader.
The daughter was the leader, alive behind her faked death; the revenge fire her mother set ended up killing her.

title: Abandon Ship
story: “Captain, sound the alarm and order every soldier to the escape pods. Tell them the ship has malfunctioned — all hands, abandon ship.”
answer: To steal intelligence from Country A’s lunar base, Country B had planted a spy inside A’s military. After years undercover, the spy finally saw his chance to carry the intel drive home and boarded the spaceship back to Earth. But Country A had long known a mole existed; its detective had narrowed the suspects to a few dozen men and quietly booked every one of them onto that same ship. The detective told the captain to announce a malfunction and send all the soldiers to the escape pods. Unwilling to give up his only chance to bring the intel home, the spy kept the drive on his body — and was caught red-handed in the belongings check before entering the pod. The ship landed safely in Country A, the spy was arrested, and the “detective” walked off with the drive to report his success. The captain went back to his cabin relieved, savoring another great service he had rendered — then heard a strange noise from the machine room. He opened the door: on the floor, bound with rope and gagged, a man was struggling. He was Country A’s real detective. Among the soldiers there had been one more spy — a master of disguise from Country C. Tipped off about the sting in advance, he had knocked the real detective out and taken his place; by then, he was already back in Country C with the intel.
hints: The abandon-ship order would force anyone carrying the intel to bring it out with him.
The spy among the soldiers was not the only man aboard with a false identity.
The detective giving the orders had been replaced by a spy from a third country, who used the first spy’s capture to walk away with the intel.

title: Three Falls
story: Over one lifetime, a single man went through a car plunging over a cliff three times. The first time, his parents died. The second time, his wife died. The third time, he died.
answer: He lost his parents in a car accident over a cliff when he was a child, and the life-insurance money paid on their deaths raised him. Growing up wild with no one to discipline him, he turned bad, and as an adult sank into gambling — until he decided to recreate “the same accident as his childhood”: he insured his wife’s life, then deliberately sent the car carrying her over the side of a bridge, jumping clear himself at the last moment. The insurance fraud succeeded and made him a rich man; he remarried and started a new life. Many years later the police finally uncovered his crime, and, terrified of punishment, he drove his own car off a mountain cliff in suicide — the third time in his life that a car went over the edge.
hints: The three falls were not the same in nature.
The insurance money from the first accident showed him a method he could use.
Childhood was an accident; his wife’s death was insurance fraud; the last fall was suicide after his crime was exposed.

title: Three Airplanes
story:
I boarded the airplane.
I saw the airplane.
I began operating the airplane.
answer: I work in a gray-area trade — the kind of outcall business advertised as “will fly anywhere in the country.” That day I boarded a plane and hurried through the night to a client’s side, ready to start the job. The client liked a little spice and proposed a two-hand game of Dou Dizhu (the Chinese card game “Fight the Landlord”) with strip rules. On the final hand the client slapped down an “airplane” (two consecutive triples in Dou Dizhu) and took the game. A bet is a bet: having lost, I had to honor the terms we had agreed on beforehand — and began “operating the airplane.”
hints: The three airplanes come from three different contexts.
The first two are a means of transport and a card combination.
It was an outcall date, and the last airplane is slang for a sex act.

title: Two People Up There
story: On a small road in a remote village stood an eerie utility pole. The villagers said strange things had happened there again and again — a while back, someone had ridden straight into it on a motorcycle. One night a father and son came down that road on their bike. The boy stared at the pole ahead and suddenly said, “Dad, there are two people up there.” The father’s heart jumped in fright. The next day, two bodies were found lying beside the pole.
answer: This remote village didn’t have a single streetlight at night, and the authorities never concerned themselves with such things. The darkness made crashes constant — a while back, a motorcyclist speeding through had failed to see the pole and slammed into it. So the villagers put up a notice board of their own at the foot of the pole: 交通安全，人人有责 — “Traffic safety is everyone’s duty.” That night the father and son came past on their motorcycle as well, and the dim light fell on the board beneath the pole. The innocent boy was looking at the two 人 characters in 人人有责 — 人 being the written character for “person” — and said, “There are two people up there.” But the father took the words to mean two real people stood on top of the pole; in alarm he turned back to glance at his son, and in that one unguarded moment the motorcycle rammed into the pole. Father and son both died on the spot.
hints: The “two people” the boy spoke of were not two physical beings.
There was a safety notice on the pole.
The boy was seeing the two 人 characters of the sign; the father misunderstood, lost his focus, and hit the pole.

title: Whose Flashlight?
story: My girlfriend is afraid of the dark, and both her hands clutched my left hand tight. I freed my right hand to hold up my phone, and saw that the flashlight beam ahead had already reached the house beside the exit. I was about to tell her we could go out when something suddenly felt wrong. Which of us was holding the flashlight?
answer: On that forest path in the dead of night, I was gripping both of my girlfriend’s hands, and my one remaining hand was holding up the phone — neither of us had any flashlight. And yet a beam of light kept leading the way ahead. When I turned my head, I saw a figure with no lower half hanging in the air behind us, a flashlight raised in its hand. What had lit our way the whole way here — it was that. Only when I saw the exit did I notice this extra beam of light.
hints: Both people’s hands were occupied.
The flashlight lighting the way came from a third presence behind them.
The narrator was holding both of the girlfriend’s hands and his phone; the flashlight was carried the whole way by the ghost tailing them.

title: The Monsters Behind Me
story: Looking at the monsters behind me, I gave up. Looking at what lay around me, I despaired. Looking at the presence before me and the gun in my hand, I went mad.
answer: When the food ran out and the bullets were nearly gone, I looked at the countless monsters behind me and sank into despair. So I covered my son’s eyes and, to spare him the greater pain, shot him dead. Looking at my dead son beside me, I prepared, in despair, to kill myself. But in the very next moment, the army that existed to destroy the monsters appeared before me and wiped out the monsters at my back. Looking at the rescue in front of me and my son lying dead beside me, I went utterly mad.
hints: The narrator believed no rescue would ever come.
To keep his son from falling into the monsters’ hands, he killed the boy first.
The army arrived right afterward and destroyed the monsters; only then did he learn the killing had never been necessary.

title: The Midnight Suitcase
story: One question too many. One corpse too many. One purchase too many.
answer: Late that night, a delivery runner brought a large suitcase to a customer’s home. The door stood open, and the customer was dragging a rolled-up carpet toward the suitcase. Noticing the red streaks on the floor, the runner asked one question too many: “Why is there so much blood?” Realizing she had seen what she shouldn’t have, the customer pulled her inside and killed her. The suitcase had been meant to hold the person killed before; now there was one more body, so he had no choice but to place another order and buy one more suitcase.
hints: The newly bought item was meant to hold a corpse.
The person making the delivery saw something wrong — and asked about it out loud.
The runner delivering the suitcase noticed the blood and was silenced by the killer, who then had to buy one more suitcase.

title: The Failure
story:
“I’m sorry — it’s a failure,” I told the man who came to test the machine.
In court I kept explaining desperately: “It has always been accurate.”
The public gallery laughed. In the end, only one sentence was left to me: “I am a human.”
answer: I had built a machine that could tell humans from pseudo-humans, and its readings were accurate. The first volunteer it tested was judged a pseudo-human. Terrified that he would find out, I declared the machine a failure, and then, in panic, killed him. I was arrested for it, and in court I insisted the dead man had been a pseudo-human, demanding that the machine be allowed to test everyone present. The police, the judge, the spectators — every single one came back pseudo-human, and they took it as proof that the machine was broken. I nearly believed it myself, until I stepped into the detection field and the screen read “human.” The police and the courts of this city had long since been taken over by pseudo-humans. I am still pleading my innocence to them — but what they need to confirm is that final reading.
hints: The machine identifies a certain kind of being, and that first claim of “failure” was a lie.
The readings in court were strikingly consistent — and the machine truly was accurate.
The police, the judge, and the gallery were all pseudo-humans; the inventor was the one human they had surrounded.

title: The Missing
story: The first time I tried this gift of mine, I nearly suffocated myself. Once I got the hang of it, I could always eat for free and take what I pleased. That day I slipped into a restaurant again — and this time I really did die inside. A few days later, my family was still out putting up missing-person flyers everywhere.
answer: My gift is this: the moment I stop breathing, my body and the clothes on it turn invisible; when I breathe again, I reappear. I would often hold my breath to slip into restaurants, then hide in some corner no one watched and eat. That day I ate too fast; food jammed my airway, my breath stopped, and my body vanished on the spot. I thrashed and collapsed in the corner, and no one noticed anything happening there. Once I suffocated to death, I never breathed again — so the corpse never reappeared. My family cannot find me; to them, I am still a missing person.
hints: He has a supernatural ability tied to breathing.
The ability only stops working when he starts breathing again.
Not breathing turns him invisible; after he suffocated, the corpse stayed invisible forever.

title: The November Diary
story: November 1st. My son’s wife disappeared; he was heartbroken. November 2nd. My son caught a little cold — his voice went hoarse, and he was sweating some. November 3rd. My son kept frowning in pain, and I reached out and touched him, aching for him. November 4th. A stranger appeared in the basement. I called the police at once; they took my son away, and I was beside myself with grief.
answer: The diary was written by the old grandfather of the household. His eyes were failing; he could make out only blurred shapes. On November 1st, the son murdered his wife and claimed she had disappeared. The grandson, learning that his mother had been killed, killed his father, peeled the face from the body and wore it, hoping to go on caring for his grandfather as his father. On November 2nd, the grandson pitched his voice low to imitate his father, and the blood seeping from the mask the grandfather took for sweat. On November 3rd, the mask began to dry and shrink, and the grandfather thought “my son” was frowning in pain. On November 4th, the grandfather found his son’s corpse — the face stripped away — in the basement, did not recognize it, and called the police. What they carried off was the son’s body, and they began hunting for the grandson who had taken his father’s place.
hints: These are the observations of an old man with very poor eyesight, and some of his judgments are wrong.
The voice, the sweat, and the frowning all trace back to one person impersonating another.
The grandson wore his father’s peeled-off face to pose as him; the unrecognizable corpse in the basement was the son himself.

title: The Reply
story: After I broke up with my boyfriend, he kept sending me outrageous messages — things like “I can’t live without you.” I blocked him, and he would just switch to a new number and keep texting. At my wits’ end, I registered a new phone number myself — and before long, messages of much the same sort started arriving again. Maybe he really does love me, I thought; I sent back one reply, meaning to test him — and the other side never wrote again. Some time later, I got a call from the police.
answer: The police told me they had found messages involving my number on the phone of a girl who had recently taken her own life. The girl had lost the man she loved to illness. Aching for him, she sent texts every day to the phone number he had used in life — “I miss you so much,” “The days keep getting harder,” “Can you come back? Can I see you just once more?” Carriers recycle numbers left unpaid and suspended long enough, and that number had happened to fall to me when I registered. That day, the girl sent her usual texts — and for the first time, a reply came back from the number: “If you miss me that much, come to me.” She believed her dead lover had answered her at last. So she killed herself.
hints: Her new phone number had once belonged to someone else.
The sender of those messages was longing for the number’s dead former owner.
She mistook “come to me” for an answer from her dead lover, and killed herself.

title: The Fortune-Teller’s Prophecy
story: A fortune-teller told him that he would die of a heart attack. He took up exercise and started looking after his health — and in the end, he died all the same.
answer: The fortune-teller had prophesied that he would die of a heart attack, so he began to exercise and take scrupulous care of himself. One day, out on a training ride, a car swerved sharply and struck him; through its window he could see an old man slumped unconscious over the wheel. Only in that last moment did he understand — the fortune-teller had never been wrong about the heart attack. He really did die of one; it was simply that the heart which failed belonged to someone else.
hints: The prophecy never specified whose heart would go wrong.
He was hit by a car while exercising.
The driver’s heart attack made him lose control — the indirect cause of the death.

title: He Came Back
story: One. He left, and I waited for him to come back. He came back, but I let his kindness go to waste. Two. I could not bear it any longer; I begged him to hurry up and go. He came back, and though it sickened me, I thanked him still for coming back. Three. He left, and he did not come back. He still has not come back. How long has he been gone? He will never come back now. Four. Another’s record: I came back — and he was dead.
answer: The two of us were trapped at sea, drifting with the waves. Every day he went out to catch fish for us to eat, and I could only wait for him to come back. On the first day, I hoped for his return with the fish, but I simply could not get used to eating it raw, and let his kindness go to waste. A few days later, starving past all endurance, I begged him instead to hurry out and fish; when he came back, though the raw fish disgusted me, I was still grateful that he had returned. Every day after that, I lived inside the waiting for him to come back. Months later, the terror of drifting pushed me into despair, and fear wore away my sense of time — this time, after he left, he did not come back, and did not come back. Convinced that I was now alone, I chose to kill myself. The last entry is the other man’s record: he finally came back — and what he found was my body.
hints: The earlier entries are the waiting man’s; the last section switches to the one who went out for food.
The food brought back was raw fish, and the man waiting went from revulsion to dependence.
Believing his companion would never return, the waiting man killed himself; the other came back to the boat and found the body.

title: He Was Counting, Too
story: I leaned at the window, counting the building across the street floor by floor. Halfway through, the man in that building looked up — and started counting toward my window as well.
answer: From my window I had witnessed a murder in the building opposite. When I called the police, they asked me which floor it had happened on, so I counted from the bottom up. By the time I reached the killer’s floor, he had noticed me too. Then he began counting, floor by floor, toward my side of the street — to work out which floor the witness lived on. I had only meant to make the address clear; in that instant I realized that he, too, was looking for my address.
hints: Both of them were counting the floors of the building opposite them.
The narrator, to make the address clear to the police; the killer, to find the witness.
He saw the murder across the street; the killer saw him too, and began counting up to his floor.

title: Finally Dead
story: I “killed” him. I killed him. This time, he finally died. Who killed me — and whom did I kill?
answer: He and I were twin brothers, both calligraphers. In a quarrel I ruined his right hand, “killing” his career as a calligrapher; as recompense, I began publishing my own works under his name. Years later I discovered that his hand had never been permanently damaged — he had been using me all along. So I killed him, went on living under his identity, and took back the works published as his, together with the fame they had won. Many years later, with my days running out, I thought on my deathbed: this time, he is finally going to die.
hints: “Killing” sometimes means ending a career or an identity.
One of the brothers had long been publishing his works under the other’s name.
One twin killed the brother who had cheated him out of his works and lived on in his place; his own death from illness then became the brother’s second death.

title: The Red Shadow in the Morgue
story: Xiao Chen worked at a funeral home. That day, the body of a woman dressed in red was brought in from outside. Xiao Chen glanced at the death report and was stunned: the deceased was Xiao Hong, the high-school classmate he had once been fond of, and the memories came flooding back. After graduation the two had kept in touch, but Xiao Hong became an actress, and before long a famous star; Xiao Chen, feeling unworthy of her, had let the contact fade away. That night, the more he remembered, the more restless he grew, and the night-shift man got up to make his rounds of the morgue. The morgue at night was cold and silent, and even Xiao Chen, usually so fearless, felt a creeping unease. Suddenly he seemed to see a streak of red deep in the corridor slip around a corner. “Who’s there!” he shouted, and gave chase — only to hear, from the far end of the corridor past that corner, a door open and footsteps hurry away. Xiao Chen ran to the corner: the side corridor was empty, but one of the rooms stood open, and inside it a mortuary drawer hung half pulled-out — in it lay Xiao Hong’s body. When day came, Xiao Chen told everyone the morgue was haunted and they should cremate Xiao Hong’s body soon. His colleagues all laughed at him; the boss gave him two days off to rest. But Xiao Chen refused to let it go, and that night he sneaked back into the funeral home behind the boss’s back. The next day, the police found Xiao Chen’s body in the cremation room. The strange smile on his face chilled everyone who saw it.
answer: Xiao Hong had died in an accident after becoming a famous star. A rich merchant had bribed the funeral home’s boss with a fortune to buy her body — to be ghost-married to the merchant’s son, dead before his time. That first night, the boss came to the morgue to swap her body out and smuggle it away, and Xiao Chen’s patrol footsteps sounded in the corridor; the door and the hurrying footsteps Xiao Chen heard were the boss fleeing in panic. To get Xiao Chen out of the way, the boss simply gave him those days off. The next night the boss came again to make the swap — and walked straight into Xiao Chen, who had slipped back in. The boss offered to split the money with him; refused, he struck Xiao Chen with a blunt weapon. But Xiao Chen, out that night to “catch the ghost,” had brought a dagger to protect himself — and killed the boss instead. Mortally wounded, Xiao Chen lay on the floor, knowing he had little time left. In a haze, he seemed to see the red-clad figure appear before him once more, weeping as it asked: “Are you still willing to be with me?” Only then did Xiao Chen understand that the figure in the corridor that night had been Xiao Hong’s ghost. With his last strength, he dragged her body to the cremation room, so that she would never be given to a ghost marriage, and died there with a smile on his face.
hints: The sounds in the morgue and the red shadow did not necessarily come from the same being.
The boss meant to sell the dead star’s body for a ghost marriage.
The sounds were the boss smuggling the body out; the red shadow was her ghost; Xiao Chen gave his life to cremate the body and protect her.

title: Caught in the Frame
story: Faced with the corpse before me, I was vexed beyond words. But after wasting a great deal of time, I finally had a result I could be proud of — and I showed it all off. Then I saw the other man’s result, and the smile died on my face.
answer: I am an “underground reporter” working the gray zone, racing around every day to beat my rivals to a story. That day I happened to see a criminal bolt from a house, so I slipped inside to film — but the corpse’s position framed terribly. Impatient for my scoop, I moved the body, set the composition, and got a photograph I was satisfied with. When I showed it off to a rival, the man laid down a photo of me in the very act of moving the corpse — the mantis stalking the cicada, with the oriole right behind. My tampering with the crime scene had been caught dead-on camera, and now nothing I said could clear my name.
hints: Both men’s “results” were photographs.
To get a photograph he was satisfied with, the narrator had tampered with the scene.
He moved the corpse to take his picture — and a rival photographed him moving it.

title: Ants on the Ceiling
story: On my second day in the apartment, I wiped out the ants on the floor. On the third day it rained and the bedroom ceiling leaked, so I called the landlord. At midnight I was woken again by dripping water, and when I looked up, the ants had all crawled onto the ceiling. Right then the landlord’s voice sounded outside the door: “Go ahead and open up. I’ve come to fix it.”
answer: The landlord had killed someone and hidden the body in the crawl space above the ceiling, then rented the place out to me in a hurry. At first I had only seen the ants swarming around a dropped snack on the floor, and thought wiping them out would be the end of it. Rain seeped into the cavity and began to drip, carrying fluids of decay with it, and the ants gathered again along the leaking crack. At midnight I followed their trail upward and saw, behind the loosened plaster, the exposed length of a human finger. I had already told the landlord where the leak was; he knew something had gone wrong with his hiding place and hurried over to deal with it. Now he is right outside the door.
hints: Where the ants reappeared matters more than how many there were.
Something is hidden above the ceiling, and the leaking water has passed through it.
The landlord hid the body in the crawl space; the repair call also told him his secret was coming out.

title: The Dancing Bystander
story: I danced, happily watching the companions in front of me die.
answer: I am a sunflower from the game Plants vs. Zombies. In that unreal world I am not a human being but a plant. In battle I sway my body with a smile on my face, “dancing,” happily watching the companions in front of me — plant after plant — being devoured by zombies and dying.
hints: The narrator is not human.
It comes from a game where plants defend against zombies.
It is the ever-swaying, smiling sunflower of Plants vs. Zombies.

title: Your Delivery Is Here
story:
“Ma’am, your delivery is here. Please open the door and take it.”
Over the course of the day, that line sounded four times.
The fourth time, I opened the door — and was never able to close it again.
answer: I was the killer who posed as a deliveryman to get inside. The first time, I used that line to trick a woman into opening her door. While I was at work, the real deliveryman arrived and said the same words a second time; I pulled him in and killed him too, taking his phone and uniform. Following the next order on his phone, I went to another home and knocked a third time with the same line. Neighbors near the first scene heard the commotion and called the police. The police found the dead deliveryman, learned from his orders where his next stop was, and came after me. When I heard the knock called out a fourth time, I assumed yet another real deliveryman had arrived — I opened the door and found the police already waiting for me.
hints: The four lines were spoken by people with different identities.
The narrator posed as a deliveryman and later killed the real one.
Tracing the deliveryman’s orders from the first crime scene, the police caught the killer at the fourth knock.

title: Blank as Paper
story: At twenty I met her, pure as a blank sheet of paper. Two years later we married. At twenty-five I lost the love of my life and threw myself wholly into my work. At forty-five, as the project neared its end, an accident happened — and heaven took away the one I loved most, once again. Staring at the data before me, I felt a dark foreboding rise. When the test results came back, I went mad.
answer: At twenty I met her wandering the streets with nowhere to go: she seemed to have lost her memory, with no idea who she was or where she had come from. I kindly took her in; simple and good-hearted, she became a ray of light in my life, and we fell in love and married. At twenty-five my wife died in childbirth after giving me a daughter, and from then on I devoted myself single-mindedly to science. As my daughter grew up, she came to look more and more like her mother. At forty-five I built a working time machine, though the technology was still unstable. Just as I was preparing further safety tests, the accident happened — my daughter started the machine on her own and never came back; the transmission log showed her destination as twenty-five years in the past. Dark foreboding rose in me. I ran a DNA comparison between strands of my daughter’s hair and the lock of my wife’s hair I had kept for many years, and the match was exact: the amnesiac “her” of long ago was my own daughter, thrown back through time. I went mad.
hints: The moment the daughter vanished lines up with the moment the wife first appeared.
The wife had amnesia when they first met; the daughter stepped into a time machine.
Sent back twenty-five years, the daughter became the young wife her father met — and her own mother.

title: What About Tonight?
story: It was my first visit to my online boyfriend’s home, and we spent the whole afternoon playing games. One round got so intense I couldn’t help shouting — and he suddenly looked over at me with a smile: “This loud already? What about tonight?” I blushed and swore at him. That night, sure enough, no one came to disturb us.
answer: My online boyfriend was a killer who used first meetings to hunt for victims. That afternoon, while I shouted over the game, he kept listening for any stir outside the door. No neighbor knocked, and he took this to mean that even if I cried for help that night, no one would bother to come. I had heard “This loud already? What about tonight?” as a flirtatious joke. That night he turned on me, and I truly began to scream for help. No footsteps ever came to the door.
hints: What he was watching for that afternoon was whether the shouting would bring anyone.
What happened that night was nothing like the flirtatious meaning I read into it.
He used my cries during the game to test the neighbors’ reactions, preparing for the night’s attack.

title: The Sole Survivor
story: A coach plunged into a valley. Of everyone who had ridden that bus that night, only one young man survived. When he was thrown off the bus, he still thought the driver hated him.
answer: Several thugs were on the bus, and seeing that the driver, a young woman named Xiaohong, was beautiful, they turned vicious. Once the bus reached the winding mountain road they moved on her in front of everyone; only one frail young man on board stepped in to stop them, and the thugs stabbed him for it. The other passengers all watched in silence, as if it were none of their business. After having their way, the thugs forced Xiaohong to drive the route they chose so they could escape. She agreed — and at the same time angrily threw the wounded young man off the bus, cursing him as a useless good-for-nothing, and the other passengers chimed in with her. Wronged and injured, he had no choice but to make his way back on foot. The next day he saw the news of the coach falling into the valley: Xiaohong had driven off the cliff, taking her own life together with a whole bus of bystanders who had looked the other way. To all appearances she had been angriest at the young man; in truth she had put him off the bus on purpose — and that young man, thrown off before the crash, was the sole survivor.
hints: The survivor had been put off the bus before the accident.
He had been the only one on board who helped the driver.
The driver drove away the one helper with curses, then sent the thugs and the bystanders over the cliff together.

title: Gentle Father
story: I’ve been happy lately: Father, who never used to come home, now often plays with me, and he has grown gentle too. The news says a research institute on the outskirts of our city exploded and they are still accounting for the victims. Father walks over, turns off the television, and gently strokes my head.
answer: Father worked at the institute developing androids. He knew he was terminally ill, and fearing there would be no one left to keep the child company, he finished building a replica of himself and left behind arrangements for the child’s care. Then the institute exploded, and the real father died inside. The completed android, following the arrangements he had left, walked into the home and took over the child’s daily care. The father of the old days, buried in work, had always been absent; the one beside the child now always had time to play. When the news reached the victims of the institute, the android turned off the television and stroked the child’s head.
hints: What the institute studied is tied to the change in the father at home.
The father had built an android copy of himself for his child.
The real father died at the institute; the one with the child is the machine he left behind.

title: A Cozy Home
story: Another day with nothing to show for it. I returned to my cozy home, wearily set down whatever was in my hands, intending to grab a simple dinner, went straight to the dining table and sat down, and took out a sandwich. The hairs on my body stood on end in an instant — I realized I was done for.
answer: I am a serial killer. Years ago I let a little brat slip through my fingers, and never knowing whether she would become a threat, I searched for her tirelessly all these years. My house is one I spent years collecting, crafting, and arranging with my own hands — a room furnished with human skin, bones, and taxidermy. I love my cozy home. Today, having failed once more to find her, I tossed my usual weapon on the shoe cabinet in the entryway, planning to grab a quick dinner. But the moment I sat down at the dining table, I found that the human chair beneath me was warm — someone had just been sitting there, and that someone was still in my house. My trusty weapon was far out of reach. Then a voice behind me spoke my name. I turned and saw the girl who had escaped me all those years ago, holding the weapon I had left in the entryway. I had hunted her for years; she had found my home first.
hints: The narrator is himself a serial killer, and the furniture in his home is far from ordinary.
The lingering warmth on the chair means someone sat there only moments before.
The girl who escaped him has slipped into his house for revenge, while his weapon lies far away.

title: I Appeared
story: The man finished ransacking the drawers and walked out of the camera’s view. I sped up the playback, waiting to see when he would come back into frame. Nothing stirred on the screen. Then the door opened, and the one who came in was me, just home from work.
answer: Coming home from work, I found the place turned over and sat down to check the cameras. In the footage, after finishing with the drawers, the thief had walked into the windowless bathroom. The only passage out of that bathroom stayed within the camera’s view the whole time, so I fast-forwarded and waited for him to emerge. He never did — not until the footage showed myself walking in the door after work. I finally understood: all the time I had been sitting there watching, the thief had been in the same house with me, and the bathroom door was still shut to this moment.
hints: The narrator is watching recorded footage from home; the picture hasn’t caught up to the present.
The man who walked out of frame never left the house — he went into another room.
He never came out before the narrator got home; he is still hiding inside.

title: My Heroes
story: Vicious, brutal thugs shattered my carefree life. Someone saved me. They are my heroes.
answer: I was a pig waiting for slaughter, living a carefree life on my master’s farm. That night, two travelers lodging there heard knife-sharpening in the yard and the words “bind it and kill it,” took them to mean their host meant to murder them, and struck first, wiping out the master’s whole household — only afterward did they learn the knife was being sharpened to bind me up and butcher me to feed the guests. With the master dead, I would never be slaughtered: as far as a pig can see, it was those two “vicious, brutal thugs” who saved my life. They are my heroes. The story retells the Three Kingdoms tale of Cao Cao mistakenly slaughtering the family of Lü Boshe — told from that pig’s point of view.
hints: The narrator is not human, and was to be killed to feed a guest.
What it overheard were preparations of the bind-and-butcher kind.
The narrator is the pig Lü Boshe’s household meant to slaughter; Cao Cao’s mistaken killing is what saved it.

title: I Saw Myself
story: The man on the screen suddenly looked at me and reached out his hand. I hurriedly switched feeds, and this time what I saw was myself. And the man from just now.
answer: I am a hotel caretaker who secretly planted cameras in the guest rooms. That night I was going through the footage when I saw a guest lift a girl’s body out of his suitcase. Then he noticed the lens, walked toward the camera, and reached out a hand to cover it. Startled, I switched feeds — to the live view of the monitoring room itself — and saw first myself sitting before the screens, and then the guest standing behind me. What I had been watching had happened long before; after finding the camera, he had left the guest room and located the monitoring room. I had been glued to the recording and never noticed him come in.
hints: The narrator is spying through hidden hotel cameras.
What played before was recorded; only after the switch is the monitoring-room feed live.
The guest had long since found the monitoring room — switching to the live view revealed him standing behind the narrator.

title: Seven Years Old
story: Seven years on, I am seven years old.
answer: This borrows the setup from Detective Conan, in which Shinichi Kudo’s body shrinks and he lives as a seven-year-old child. “Seven years on” refers to the real-world readers, who have followed the manga for seven years; “I am seven years old” gives the character’s age within the story. The seven years that passed in the real world did not flow at the same speed inside the tale.
hints: The seven years belong to real-world readers; the age of seven belongs to a character.
The character is Shinichi Kudo with a shrunken body.
Seven years passed for the readers, while Conan still appears in the story as a seven-year-old child.

title: I Killed Myself
story: After a single gunshot, I had killed me. Yet this was not the death I had in mind.
answer: Ronald Opus leapt from the roof of his own apartment building, but as his body fell past the ninth floor a bullet chanced to fire from a window, killing him on the spot. At that moment an elderly couple on the ninth floor were quarreling; the old man, as was his habit, was threatening his wife with a gun when it suddenly went off. The old woman was not hit — the bullet broke the window and struck Ronald in mid-fall. Both husband and wife insisted the gun should never have been loaded: brandishing it during quarrels was merely the old man’s habit, with no intent to kill. The police found that the chain of events began with the old woman’s decision to stop supporting her grown son financially. Cut off, the son nursed a grudge against his mother and secretly loaded the gun, hoping his father’s hand would kill her in some future quarrel. And that son was Ronald, the dead man himself. When the borrowed-knife plot refused to come off, Ronald sank into despair and decided to jump to his death — only to be shot dead by the very gun, fired from his own parents’ home on the ninth floor. In the end he died from the bullet he himself had put into the gun, though never in the way he had imagined when he stepped off the roof.
hints: He had prepared a method of murder, and it later found him.
The gun was in the father’s hand; the bullet had been loaded by the son beforehand.
Falling past his parents’ window, the son was struck by his own pre-loaded bullet, fired by his father by mistake.

title: Found You
story: “Three, two… Are you all right? You’re safe now. Three, two, one… Found you.” Rat-a-tat-tat…
answer: As a child, “I” was playing hide-and-seek with my mother. My small body fit into the hidden compartment beneath the wardrobe, and through the one narrow gap I watched to see whether she could find me. Then a killer broke into our home. I heard my mother’s panicked footsteps as she fled (rat-a-tat-tat); she ran into the very room I was hiding in, and just as she tried to lock the door he seized her and cut her throat. He simply watched as her life drained away little by little, then carved into her body with the knife, stroke by stroke — unnervingly quiet, slow, and methodical, as if sketching a work of art with lines. From the compartment I made no sound at all; perhaps I was frozen with terror, perhaps I was drawn to the sight. The police finally arrived and got me out, saying, “Are you all right? You’re safe now.” But what I had witnessed had already warped my mind: I could not forget the thrill of held breath, of a life snatched away in an instant, nor the artful lines the blade had drawn on that “canvas of life.” Grown up, I wanted to know what it felt like to hold another person’s fate in my hands — to toy with prey and watch the breath leave them little by little at my fingertips, and to create “artworks” of my own. So I began abducting prey, counting down to send them into hiding while I went to seek — “Found you” — and having found them, I killed them.
hints: The two countdowns happened years apart.
The child who once hid grew into the one who seeks.
As a boy he witnessed his mother’s murder during hide-and-seek; as a man he turned that same game of hiding into a hunt.

title: Bloodstains in Midair
story: On the tenth floor of an apartment block, the doorway of one unit was soaked red with blood. In the pool lay a police cap and several photographs of corpses, each body bearing an identical wound on the neck. Two trails of blood: one ran to the railing outside and vanished into midair, the other led into the living room — to the smiling corpse of a woman. The police officer who arrived would never have guessed that the truth lay in his own phone.
answer: In this world, vampires live hidden among humans. As a child she lost her parents to vampires, and the truth was buried by vampires nested in the upper ranks of society. She resolved to expose their existence by extreme means: she attacked many innocent people and staged the scenes as vampire kills, leaving the very same wound on every “victim’s” neck, until public opinion began to stir. The vampires noticed her in turn, and sent one of their own disguised as a police officer, on the pretext of investigating the serial murders, to get inside her home — for a vampire cannot enter a human dwelling uninvited. She was ready for that, and shot the vampire at her door. It dropped its disguise and, wounded, made ready to flee; the police cap and the photographs scattered into the pool of blood — photographs of the very “vampire attacks” she had staged. Nothing proves their existence like a vampire’s corpse, so she gave chase, only to be gravely wounded when it turned on her, and she barely made it back inside. The badly hurt vampire had no time to tidy the scene; it rose over the railing and flew away, its blood trail breaking off in midair, while the other trail remained in the living room she had crawled back into. But her purpose was already served: the whole fight had been streamed live to the internet by a hidden camera on her body. In the end she died at home from blood loss, smiling; the officer who came to investigate learned the truth from the live stream on his own phone.
hints: The investigator outside the door is no true human police officer.
One blood trail breaks off in midair because the wounded one can fly.
The woman baited out a vampire and streamed the fight live; the proof went online before she died, where the police can see it on his phone.

title: Thank You
story: “I don’t like you.” Hearing that, I was overjoyed. “I like you.” Hearing that, I burned with restless unease. “Thank you.” Hearing that, I fell into utter despair.
answer: I am a twisted stalker who planted a bug on the one I love. She is popular; there is always someone coming to confess to her, and every time I heard her turn someone down, I was overjoyed. But this time she accepted a certain man’s confession — and hearing that “I like you,” I burned with restless jealousy, tracked down who he was, and killed him. With him gone, perhaps I still had a chance. Then her voice came through the monitor: “Ha — thank you for getting rid of the person I wanted dead.” She had discovered the bug long ago and knew I had been listening all along; that “thank you” was spoken to the bug, meant for me — she never liked the man at all. Accepting his confession was simply her way of borrowing my hands to remove someone she, too, wanted dead. Hearing that, I fell into utter despair.
hints: The narrator has been eavesdropping on his beloved’s conversations.
She knows the bug is there, and knows how easily jealousy makes him lose control.
Feigning acceptance of another man’s confession, she baited the stalker into killing for her — then thanked him through the bug.

title: New Stock on the Shelf
story: Hello, is this item still available? Yes. The item has been sold; new stock is on the shelf. Where is my child? Was it you? Was it you?
answer: On a second-hand marketplace, he weighed it for a long while before opening the listing with the best value in strollers — his child had just been born, and he wanted to add a stroller for the baby. “Hello, is this item still available?” “Yes.” The same-city deal handed his address straight into the seller’s hands: to a trafficking ring, “new stock” meant a fresh address with a new family, ready to be scouted and taken. In the ring’s private message group, a new photograph of a baby was uploaded — “new stock on the shelf.” At the same time, on the marketplace, a similar stroller was relisted — second-hand, ninety percent new, free same-city delivery — waiting for the next family to place an order. The child’s father recognized that stroller and bought it back, but the question “Where is my child? Was it you?” will never be answered.
hints: The item sold to the public and the “new stock” in private messages are two different things.
A stroller deal gives away the address of a home with a newborn.
The traffickers used the free stroller to scout the home, then sold the abducted child as new stock.

title: The Repairman
story: After the old repairman died, five people vanished from the city, one after another. On the third day, a neighbor looked through the window and saw the old man seated at his workbench again. The same face — only the hands were impossibly young.
answer: The old man had found a still-functioning robot head at the junkyard and built it a body out of parts from different sources. The robot stayed on in his home, taking “when something breaks, fit on a working part” as the way to fix anything. When the old man died of illness, the robot set about repairing him the same way. It killed five people, took their torsos and limbs, and joined them beneath the old man’s head, then propped the patched-together body up at the workbench. What the neighbor saw was still the old man’s face; the young hands belonged to the victims. The robot kept watch beside him, waiting for the old man to wake up the way it once had.
hints: The old man never came back to life, yet the face at the bench truly was his.
The old man had once repaired something with parts, and it is imitating his way.
The robot he saved tried to repair him, joining body parts taken from five people beneath the old man’s head.

title: The Wishing Well
story: Everyone said it was a wishing well. I dropped a coin in and wished to become a millionaire — and then I died.
answer: The well grants wishes by exchange: when two wishes match, it transfers the offerings and remaining lifespans of both sides in a single batch, leaving no balance behind. Before the narrator, a million people had each tossed in a one-yuan coin, hoping for a longer life. His wish to become a millionaire matched that stockpile exactly. The well delivered the million coins to him, and divided every last scrap of his remaining lifespan among those million people. He got the money he had asked for, with no time left alive to spend it.
hints: The well grants wishes through exchange.
Earlier people threw in coins asking for longer life; the later one wanted money.
He received the million coins they had thrown in, while all his remaining lifespan was divided among them.

title: The Search for Santa Claus
story: He had spent his whole life searching for Santa Claus — and when he finally found him, he wept.
answer: When he was little, burglars broke into his home to rob and kill; his mother threw him out into the yard and told him to run. It was Christmas Eve, and she lied to him, saying Santa Claus had come to take her away. As he ran he looked back, and saw only the robber — drenched in his father’s blood, red from head to toe — dragging his mother away from the window. He grew up certain that Santa Claus had taken his mother, and searched for Santa Claus for years. Then, this Christmas Eve, the news reported the capture of the killer who had been at large all those years, and he could no longer lie to himself: his mother had died that night. He would never see her again.
hints: The red of that Christmas Eve had to do with blood.
To make her child run, the mother explained what was coming in terms of Santa Claus.
The red figure he saw was the robber who killed his parents; the capture reported in the news, years later, forced him to face the truth.

title: Three Summer Days
story: It was the height of summer, the heat unbearable. On the first day, the old hen we had kept for three years died. On the second day, my little brother died. On the third day — why did everything turn out the opposite of what I had imagined? The big sister broke down.
answer: The big sister was still very young and did not understand what death meant. The weather was scorching, there was no air conditioning in the countryside, and grown-ups and children alike were wilting in the heat; her little brother cried without stop. “It would be so nice and cool for him in the refrigerator,” the sister thought, but the adults forbade it. On the first day, the old hen fell into the pond and drowned; the adults found it, cleaned it, and put it in the refrigerator. On the second day the sister had a bright idea and pushed her brother into the pond — now he could be put in the refrigerator to cool off too. On the third day things went the other way entirely, the opposite of what she had imagined: after her brother died, the grown-ups laid him in a wooden box and placed it in the fire to be cremated.
hints: The sister misread why the dead hen had been put in the refrigerator.
She wanted her brother to enjoy the refrigerator’s coolness too.
She believed drowning was the way into the refrigerator; instead, her brother was cremated after death.

title: One Hundred Agents
story:
“Who are you?” “I’m Agent One. I come from the future. Soon you will die, so my mission is to travel back here and save you.”
“And who are you?” “I’m Agent Two. Agent One’s mission failed. I’m here to save you.”
“I’m Agent Three. Agent Two’s mission failed. I’m here to save you.”
“I’m Agent Four. Agent Three’s mission failed…”
“I’m Five.” “I’m Six.” “I’m Seven.”…
“I’m Agent One Hundred — it seems the mission has failed completely.”
Why did a hundred agents who traveled through time fail to save one man fated to die?
answer: The time-drop only delivers each new agent to the target’s side; it cannot remove anyone already there, nor restart what is happening. Watching the failures from the future, the rescue bureau kept dispatching reinforcements. The protagonist was driving on the highway when Agent One suddenly appeared in the passenger seat and explained his mission; he was badly rattled. Worse, more and more agents began popping into the car as if copy-pasted — different agents arriving almost at once — until the vehicle was overloaded, and some agents even ‘spawned’ directly in front of the speeding car. Under the overload and the pile-up that followed, the car exploded; the agents inside were jammed together with no room to protect anyone, and the rescue mission failed utterly with the hundredth agent dispatched.
hints: The rescuers kept arriving; no one already present was reset or removed.
The protagonist was inside a car speeding down the highway.
The agents were all delivered to his side, and the overcrowded car and the collisions on the road killed him instead.

title: One, Two, Three, Seven
story: There was a child at the kindergarten who always counted “one, two, three, seven,” always skipping the four, five and six in the middle. But when I corrected her, she said her mother had taught her to count that way. Puzzled, I proposed a home visit. After the visit, “one, two, three, seven” was what I said to her too.
answer: I’m a kindergarten teacher. In class I noticed a girl who could never count the numbers right: everyone else said one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, but she said only one, two, three, seven. When I taught her the correct way, she told me her mother had taught her this one. Puzzled, I arranged a home visit — and she led me to a hospital. Her mother had heart disease and would not live much longer; the doctor said she would very likely not make it past April, May or June. It was March, and the daughter’s birthday fell in July. To be there for her daughter’s last birthday, the mother had woven this kind lie with her: after three, count straight to seven — as long as four, five and six did not exist, Mama would live to July. I was so moved that I told her, just as her mother did: after three does come seven.
hints: The skipped numbers stand for months.
The child’s birthday is in July, and the mother might not live to see it.
Mother and daughter wanted to skip the April-to-June the doctor had spoken of; once the teacher knew, she joined the count to honor that wish.

title: Try Again in One Minute
story: I live alone. Waking in the middle of the night, I glanced at the phone lying on the bedside table; the screen read “Try again in one minute.” But the phone had been sitting on that table beside me all night, and I had never touched it. What on earth had happened?
answer: My phone locks out further attempts for a while after several wrong passcodes in a row. That night, someone slipped into my home, picked up the phone on my bedside table and tried to guess the passcode; after repeated failures, he set it back exactly where it had been. Only when I woke and saw the lockout message did I realize the phone had been handled while I slept. I didn’t know whether he was still in the apartment. I sat staring at that message until dawn.
hints: The phone had just been through several failed unlock attempts.
Those attempts happened while its owner was fast asleep.
An intruder in the home had taken the phone and tried the passcode, leaving the lockout message behind.

title: One Match
story: I had one match, and so I survived.
answer: Some friends and I went on a trip into the desert, got lost, and ran out of supplies. With no other choice, we drew lots with matches of different lengths to decide who would be eaten — whoever drew the shortest match would be the one. Of course I drew the shortest one. But I had another match hidden on me, and while no one was watching I secretly swapped it for the short one. So the one to be eaten became someone else, and I survived.
hints: Here the matches were used for drawing lots.
Matches of different lengths decided who would be sacrificed.
Whoever drew the shortest match would be eaten; the narrator swapped his own for a longer match he had hidden.

title: It Was Always Black
story: When the police asked a murderer for his motive, he gave them a single answer: “It was always black.”
answer: He was an obsessive fan who wanted to know everything about the idol, so he hid a surveillance camera inside a gift he sent. But the idol never opened presents from fans at all — the parcel stayed sealed, no light could reach the lens, and the picture on his screen stayed black, always. His pride was wounded; adoration turned to hatred, he felt he had been made a clown of, and he waited for his chance and killed the idol. That is why, asked by the police for his motive, he answered only: “It was always black.”
hints: He was watching the feed from a hidden camera.
The camera was hidden inside a gift sent to the idol.
The gift was never unwrapped, the lens stayed wrapped in darkness, and humiliated rage drove him to kill.

title: The Door to Next Week
story: Today I peered once more through the door that looks one week into the future. The same notice was pasted all over the streets. The moment I stepped through, a stranger seized me in a death-grip and called a whole crowd over. Only after I read the notice did I have to apologize to them.
answer: The door opens onto the same town one week later. Looking through it from this side, you see the future; step across the threshold and you arrive there in person. I had only ever looked, never crossed. This time the future street was plastered with missing-person notices carrying my face; I walked over to read one clearly, and in doing so vanished from my own week for seven whole days. The townspeople had already been searching for me for seven days — that is why they seized me the moment they saw me. What I saw upon stepping through the door was precisely the result of that very step.
hints: The door lets you see the future — and walk into it.
The person on the notices was the narrator himself.
Crossing the door removed him from his own week, and during those seven days the townspeople put up the missing-person notices.

title: It Should Have Been Red
story: It should have been red. I stared tensely at the screen. Two seconds later, I breathed a sigh of relief. Wait — something was off. I hurried to open a webpage, then slapped my thigh: we were done for.
