story: The beef noodles at this shop were delicious — remarkably like the ones Mom used to make for us when we were little. I happily brought my older brother along: “Big Brother, have a taste — do these noodles have the taste of Mom?” He took a bite of the noodles, frowned, and shook his head.
answer: We were very poor growing up. Mother raised my older brother and me on her own, and only made us beef noodles when she had earned some money, or on holidays. Ten years ago she vanished without warning, and my brother told me that Mother had come to see us as a burden and left home for good. I believed him all those years, and I never forgot that bowl of noodles. Later I found a shop whose noodles tasted just like hers, and I brought my brother there in high spirits. He shook his head: what the taste brought back for him was Mother herself. Ten years ago, it was he who killed her and ate her remains. The story of Mother abandoning us was simply a lie he told me.
hints: I missed the noodles Mother made; what my brother remembered was a very different taste.
Mother disappeared ten years ago, and my brother kept what happened from me.
My brother had eaten Mother’s remains; for him, ‘the taste of Mom’ was literal.

title: Mama and the Old Uncle
story:
She held the hand of the woman beside her and asked softly, “Mama, who is that old uncle?”
A week later, she passed away. The woman she had called Mama, and that old uncle, both wept bitterly.
answer: She was an elderly woman with Alzheimer’s disease, and in those days she often believed herself still a child. The woman at her side was in fact her daughter, and the aged man was her husband, but she could no longer recognize them as they were now: she took her daughter for her mother, and her husband for a strange old uncle. A week later, the old woman died a natural death. The ones who lost her were her daughter, and the husband who had walked through all those years beside her.
hints: ‘Mama’ and ‘old uncle’ were just what she called the people in front of her; the real relationships were something else.
She was very old, and after falling ill she often felt she was still in her childhood.
The ‘mama’ was really her daughter, the ‘old uncle’ really her husband; she could not recognize them, yet the two stayed by her side all along.

title: The Nuisance
story:
The nuisance on my door had to be cleaned off every day. Today I came home and the door was finally spotless.
But the moment I pushed it open, I believed it: the man’s steep quote really did have something behind it.
answer: Locksmith flyers were pasted onto my door every single day; I would tear them off and they would go right back up, and it drove me crazy. I had once called the number on one to ask about lock-opening prices — the quote was steep, and the man on the phone said there was no lock he could not open. Today every flyer outside was gone, and only after stepping inside did I discover them: all pasted on the inner side of the door. The locksmith behind the ads had quietly picked open my lock, moved his flyers indoors, and in just this way put his skill on display.
hints: The nuisance on the door was something people kept sticking there.
Today, those things moved from the outside of the door to the inside.
The man sticking the ads was a locksmith; he had entered the home uninvited, and the flyers inside the door were his way of showing off his skill.

title: The Slow Race
story:
My father arranged a race between my older brother and me, with his entire estate as the prize.
Pointing at our cars, he said: “Whoever’s car reaches the finish line last, wins.”
The starting signal had barely sounded when my brother and I both floored the gas at the same instant.
answer: My older brother and I both loved racing, and Father wanted us to learn to slow down, so he offered the estate to whichever of our cars crossed the line last. Before the race, we had quietly swapped cars, each of us driving the other’s. That way, driving to the finish as fast as possible would push the car under the other man’s name across the line first, leaving one’s own car behind. Each of us wanted the car he owned to be the last one in, so we both slammed the accelerator to the floor — and the slow-car race turned into an ordinary sprint.
hints: Father’s condition for victory was who owned the car that crossed the line last.
The two of us had swapped cars before the race.
If I drove my brother’s car across the line first, my own car would be last, and I would take Father’s prize.

title: The Mango
story:
On the bus, I scooped up a handful of mango flesh and stuffed it into my mouth.
I had meant to clear things up; the passenger beside me threw up instead.
answer: I had taken an overripe mango to work. Fiddling with my phone, I slipped it into the back pocket of my trousers, and when I sat down the mango was crushed — yellow flesh squeezed out from under my bottom and smeared across the seat. The passenger next to me took it for excrement. Desperate to prove it was only fruit, I scooped up a handful and ate it in front of him. He thought I was eating that mess, and was so disgusted that he vomited.
hints: The problem lay in where the mango got crushed.
The overripe mango was in my back trouser pocket, and sitting down squeezed the yellow flesh out from under my bottom.
The passenger took it for excrement, and my eating a mouthful to prove the point only deepened the misunderstanding.

title: His Own Kind
story:
He used to be too frightened to turn off the light for the whole night after watching a horror film. Later, though, he could not stop watching zombies, smiling as he said how familiar they felt.
He lived alone in a big house, the refrigerator packed full. The next time anyone came to see him, the food had all gone bad, and he had starved to death.
answer: He had developed the delusion that he was already dead, and was certain that he himself was now a corpse. Watching zombie films, he felt the dead on the screen were his own kind, and his fear gave way to fondness. He believed just as firmly that the dead have no need of food; he refused to eat for a long time, and finally starved to death in a house that still held plenty of food. This nihilistic delusion of being dead is seen in Cotard’s syndrome; the warm familiarity the man felt toward those films came from his own association of himself with the zombies.
hints: The change in how he reacted to horror films came from a mistaken belief about what he himself was.
He felt he was already dead, one of a kind with the zombies on the screen.
His living body still needed food, but holding to the belief that the dead do not eat, he refused food and starved to death.

title: A Feast
story:
Crunch, crunch.
“Wow, so much food! Hot, hot… every single time there’s this much good stuff to eat.”
“Where am I this time?”
Crunch, crunch, crunch.
answer: A rat had long been foraging near the cells. The jailers would eat their meals in front of the starving prisoners and toss the still-warm leftovers on the ground, so the rat fed well on the scraps. The crunching at the beginning was the sound of it eating. That day it slipped inside a cell, and a prisoner who was never given any food seized it in one grab. The rat took this for just another strange new place — and was then eaten by the prisoner. By the final crunches, the eater had changed: it was the prisoner eating the rat.
hints: The one eating at the start was very small, and lived on scraps others dropped.
It was a rat that had slipped into a cell, where a prisoner had gone hungry for a long time.
The two rounds of crunching belonged to the rat and then the prisoner; the rat that had just enjoyed its feast became the food.

title: My Little Sister’s Secret
story:
Only my little sister was with me on my tenth birthday. Mom was still lying in the bathtub, much fatter than before. Dad’s face was turned toward my sister, his eyes stretched wide.
Stroking my face, my sister said: “When you come of age, you’ll have to marry me.”
answer: My little sister was in fact a grown woman. Because her body had stayed child-sized, she dressed in children’s clothes under a forged identity, and my parents adopted her as a little girl. She was obsessed with her adoptive father; while he was away on a business trip she killed our adoptive mother and left the body in the bathtub. When Father came home and uncovered both her true identity and how his wife had died, he tried to subdue her — but she had set a trap in advance, and killed him too. On my birthday, Mother’s body had already swollen, and the head she had left of Father still wore a look of terror, positioned facing my sister. Looking at me, she decided that I might grow up to look like Father, and planned to make me his stand-in.
hints: On that birthday, the child did not truly understand the state Mom and Dad were in.
The little sister was a grown woman disguised as a small child, and she had been obsessed with her adoptive father.
She had already killed our parents — the bathtub held Mother’s body, and Father’s head was turned toward her; next she fixed her eyes on me, who might grow up to resemble Father.

title: Dreaming of a Plane Crash
story:
An employee said to his boss: “Whatever happens today, do not get on a plane. Last night I dreamed that the plane you are taking would crash.”
The boss asked a single question in return. The moment he heard the answer, he fired him.
answer: The employee was in charge of the factory’s night patrol and should have been at his post the entire night. The boss asked him where he had had the dream, and he answered: while dozing off in the factory guard booth. That one answer exposed that he slept on duty, and the boss dismissed him for it. What the boss cared about was a night with no one on patrol — whether the plane in the dream would really crash never entered into it.
hints: What the boss cared about was how the employee had spent the previous night at work.
The employee was in charge of the night patrol and should have been on duty all night.
He admitted the dream had come while he dozed in the guard booth; the dismissal was for sleeping on duty.

title: The Keypad Lock
story:
Beep, beep, beep… It sounded like someone kept pressing the keypad lock on my front door.
I opened the door, and there was not a soul outside. The beeping of the keys went on.
answer: A toad was squatting on the keypad panel of the lock outside my door, and every shift of its body and feet set off the touch-sensitive keys. Hearing the beeps, I assumed someone was entering a code and opened the door from the inside to look. There really was nobody at the door — but the toad was still sprawled across the panel, so the beeping never stopped.
hints: The beeping of the keys was real; the one pressing them was not a person.
The door was opened by me from the inside, and had nothing to do with the right code being entered.
A toad crouched on the panel, and its movements kept triggering the touch keys.

title: A Keen Eye
story:
A man walked past me with a dog on a leash. The dog wagged its tail, a bone held in its mouth.
One glance was all I needed: I pulled out my phone, turned around, and followed them.
answer: I am a forensic pathologist and know human bones well. As the man brushed past, I saw that the bone in the dog’s mouth was shaped very much like a human femur, and I suspected it came from human remains. I took out my phone to alert colleagues at the police, then followed the man at a distance while reporting our position, so my colleagues could find the bone and investigate where it came from. A bone that would normally pass for a dog’s chew toy was what had put me on alert.
hints: The work I do let me see a detail ordinary passersby would miss.
The key is the bone in the dog’s mouth; I have experience identifying human skeletons.
The bone looked like a human femur. I called the police and followed him so its origin could be traced.

title: It Was There All Along
story:
After Father’s affair, I left home with him. As we walked out, Mother shouted one sentence after him.
That night, I wanted to prove Mother wrong.
The next day, Father was dead. And I had confirmed it: it was there all along.
answer: My parents divorced over Father’s affair, and he took me with him. In her anger, Mother shouted at him: “After all these years, do you even have a heart?” She meant his feelings and his conscience, but I took her words literally, as a question of whether there was truly a heart in his chest. To prove Mother wrong, I waited until Father was asleep and went at him with a knife, trying to find that heart. It cost him his life, yet I stubbornly believed I had my answer: Father did have a heart.
hints: Mother was asking about Father’s feelings for the family; I took her words literally.
Her exact words were: do you even have a heart.
I tried to cut my father open to find his heart and prove he had one, and killed him.

title: The Enchanted Ranch
story:
After Mother died, she left me a run-down ranch. The next day a chicken arrived; on the third day, a cow; on the fourth, a sheep. A month later I found the pattern behind their appearances and decided to bring Mother back too.
The next day, a young woman was standing on the ranch. When I saw her face clearly, I did not dare walk over.
answer: The ranch carried a magic: if the owner ate the meat or the bone ash of some animal during the night, then the next day a young copy of that animal would appear. I watched and tried different meats, and found that every newcomer matched what I had eaten the night before. The rule held for humans too. To bring my mother back, I swallowed some of her ashes. The young woman who appeared the next day looked exactly like me. I searched through the diary my mother had left and found an entry: years before, she had eaten some of her own flesh, and the next day a little girl had appeared on the ranch; she raised that girl and gave her my name. Only then did I understand that I myself was a copy my mother had made through the ranch. This time, in trying to find my mother again, I had created yet another young individual identical to myself.
hints: Each animal that appeared matched what I had eaten the night before.
Meat or bone ash makes the ranch produce a young copy of the original creature, and it works on people too.
I ate my mother’s ashes and got a woman identical to myself; her old diary recorded how she had once generated me from her own flesh and raised me.

title: The Magician
story:
On a cruise ship, a magician was rehearsing a vanishing act with his three assistants. When the door opened again, only four corpses remained inside, dismembered and pieced back together — and one of them wore the magician’s stage costume.
Everyone said the magician had died too. But the examination found that parts of the bodies had already decomposed while the rest were still fresh.
answer: The magician meant to kill his assistants and erase his own identity along with them. Before boarding, he had murdered a man whose build and features closely resembled his own and smuggled the body aboard in his luggage. During the rehearsal, using a moment alone with them, he killed the three assistants, then took their bodies and the double’s corpse apart, mixed the parts, and reassembled them into four bodies, dressing one in his own stage costume. He wanted the body count, the costume, and the double’s face to convince everyone that the dead were the entire magic troupe, himself included. He had already changed clothes, slipped in among the passengers, and was ready to leave the ship. But the two rounds of death lay far apart in time: the double’s decomposition did not match the freshly killed assistants, and that exposed the four bodies as the product of two separate killings. The real magician was still alive.
hints: Four bodies for a four-member troupe is exactly the impression the killer wanted to create.
The body in the stage costume came from another man of similar build, one who had died before boarding.
The magician killed his three assistants, mixed in the double he had killed in advance to fake his own death, then changed clothes and escaped.

title: The Photo Over My Heart
story:
The six of us lay pressed into the grass, not daring to move a muscle.
I wanted one more look at my wife’s photo, and reached toward my chest.
The instant the photo came out, gunfire rang out. None of us made it back.
answer: We were the last six soldiers of our unit, lying hidden in the grass near enemy positions, where silence meant survival. I was afraid, and I wanted to look at my wife’s photo to keep myself going. The photo lay in a chest pocket sealed with Velcro, and when I peeled the seal open, the ripping sound reached the enemy soldiers close by. They fired toward the noise, toward our hiding place, and all six of us died there. What truly gave us away was the sound of taking out the photo.
hints: The enemy was close by, and we had to stay silent.
Before looking at the photo, I unsealed the pocket at my chest.
The pocket was fastened with Velcro; the ripping sound of peeling it open led the enemy to our position.

title: Doomsday
story:
When the white light flared, I covered my eyes and rushed into the underground shelter. A tremendous blast followed.
I hid inside for ten years.
When I pushed the door open again, people were out buying groceries and children were laughing. I sat down in the doorway and cried for a long time.
answer: I was obsessed with doomsday survival: I had stockpiled ten years of supplies and turned my cellar into a shelter fit for long-term living. That day, a blinding white light and a roar convinced me the catastrophe had finally come. Without checking any news, I followed my own contingency plan, cut off contact with the outside, and lived down there alone until the supplies ran out. Outside, the city was as ordinary as ever. I later found the reports from that year: the flash and the boom had come from a meteor exploding as it entered the atmosphere, and it had destroyed nothing. I had hidden from ten years of normal life behind a disaster that existed only in my own conviction, and at last I wept for all the time I had thrown away.
hints: The shelter and the ten years of supplies were prepared in advance; the hiding was my own choice.
The white light and the boom brought no global disaster, and I never verified anything.
It was a meteor airburst. Mistaking it for doomsday, I hid alone for ten years and came out to find the world had gone on as always.

title: The Destination
story:
He gave his destination, urged the cab driver to go faster, and made a phone call.
After the call ended, the car turned off toward a remote spot instead.
He never reached the house where he had arranged to meet her.
answer: The passenger was on his way to his lover’s home, and by chance he had gotten into the taxi her husband drove. The driver had long suspected his wife had another man; when he heard the passenger state his own home address, his suspicion rose. Then the passenger put the call on speaker and asked the woman on the line whether her husband was still out driving. The driver recognized his wife’s voice, and heard her tell the passenger to hurry over. That settled it. The driver took the car to a secluded spot and killed the passenger. The man’s urging to go faster had been to reach the affair while her husband was still away.
hints: The address the passenger gave was one the driver knew very well.
The person on the phone was making sure her husband was still out driving.
The driver was that woman’s husband; the taxi was carrying her lover straight to his own home.

title: The Underwear
story: My underwear was stolen. The thief died that same day, and I was shattered with grief.
answer: I had bought a pair of red underpants, and my son secretly took them from the wardrobe. He wore the red underpants over his blue trousers, dressed up as his beloved Superman, and believed that dressed this way he could fly too. While the family wasn’t watching, he imitated flight and leaped from a high place, falling to his death. The one I called the underwear thief was my own child.
hints: The one who took the underwear was someone close to me in the family.
It was a pair of red underpants, worn on the outside of blue trousers.
My son was imitating Superman, believed he could fly, and fell to his death from a height.

title: The House Phone
story:
At the inn I tossed and turned, unable to sleep. In the small hours I dialed a number; the instant the call was answered, I hung up without a word.
Once it was done, I finally fell asleep.
answer: The guest in the next room was snoring so loudly that sleep was impossible. Using the inn’s internal line, I dialed the room next door; the ringing woke him, and the moment he picked up, I hung up. His answering meant he was awake, and for a while the snoring stopped. I hurried to fall asleep before he drifted off again.
hints: The sound keeping me awake came from the next room.
The purpose of the call was to wake him; once he answered, that purpose was served.
The neighbor kept snoring; I let the call wake him, then fell asleep in the quiet that followed.

title: Your Name
story:
When I was a child, a high monk said to me: “One day, one called Guan Yangqing will be the death of you.”
I spent my whole life avoiding that name — until my child’s parent-teacher meeting.
The teacher walked me downstairs, then called out behind me. I turned my head, and fell from the staircase.
answer: The monk had foreseen the shout that would come just before my death, and left behind that ambiguous warning. I took “one called Guan Yangqing” to mean a person named Guan Yangqing, so I stayed away from that name all my life. My own name is Zheng Qing (郑晴). My child had done badly on an exam and dared not show me the paper, so he signed my name for me in a sprawling hand, pulling the strokes of the characters wide apart: in written Chinese a character can come apart into components, and 郑 (Zheng) fell open into 关 (guan) and 阝, while 晴 (Qing) fell open into 日 (ri) and 青 (qing) — and the middle 阝 and 日, pressed side by side, looked merged into 阳 (yang). Read that way, my name became Guan Yangqing (关阳青). The teacher misread the forged signature on the paper. After the meeting, as I was on my way down the stairs, the teacher called me “Guan Yangqing,” going by the name written there. The name I had dodged all my life was suddenly being applied to me; I panicked, turned my head, missed my footing, and fell to my death. The “calling” in the prophecy referred to the teacher calling that name aloud.
hints: In the monk’s words, “called” also carries the sense of calling a name aloud.
My name is Zheng Qing; my child spread the components of the two characters apart while signing the exam paper for me.
The sprawled components of Zheng Qing were misread as Guan Yangqing; the teacher called that name, I turned in panic and missed my footing — the prophecy pointed to the one who calls the name.

title: A Warm Winter’s Tale
story:
“I have an idea. Say that my business is booming — say it, quick!”
“Your business is booming...”
She raised the hand saw. The fire burned brighter and brighter, and even the falling snow melted.
answer: On Christmas Eve, the Little Match Girl had not sold a single box of matches and was freezing, close to the end of her strength. She came upon Pinocchio, the wooden puppet, suffering in the same snowstorm. In this fairy tale, every lie the puppet tells makes his wooden nose grow a little longer. The girl had him say that her business was booming; that was the opposite of the truth, so the nose kept stretching. She sawed off the new growth, used her matches to light a bonfire, and had him repeat the same lie to keep the firewood coming. That was how the two of them kept warm and got through the freezing night.
hints: This is a meeting that rewrites fairy-tale endings; the girl is the one selling matches.
Her business is dreadful, and the puppet traveling with her grows a longer nose whenever he lies.
Pinocchio keeps saying business is booming; the growing wooden nose becomes firewood that carries the two through the cold night.

title: The Auction
story:
At a secret auction, a tycoon paid an astronomical price for something he had no interest in whatsoever.
Years later, he learned that the other buyers from that night had been killed, one after another — he alone was still alive.
And what he thanked his luck for was precisely that the money had been well spent.
answer: What was auctioned that night were young women being sold as slaves. The tycoon could not stand by and watch one of them fall to the other buyers, so he paid a fortune to win her, took her home, settled her in, and told her plainly that she was free to leave. The woman had been trained as a killer by a criminal syndicate; the auction was the syndicate’s way of placing its women inside buyers’ homes, under orders to seize valuables and kill. But she saw that this tycoon did not treat her as property and was willing to let her go, so she gave up the mission to kill him and fled alone. The killers taken home by the other buyers carried out their missions in turn. Years later, when the case was solved, the tycoon learned that every other buyer from that night was dead, and realized that his decision to save someone had saved his own life as well.
hints: What was auctioned off was in fact a human being.
The auction placed the syndicate’s killers inside the buyers’ homes.
The tycoon gave the woman he bought her freedom, and she gave up her mission to kill him; the other buyers met a different end.

title: The Cards Are Fine
story:
“There’s something wrong with these cards!” I pounded the gambling table.
“There is nothing wrong with the cards.” The next day, the dealer laid out that same deck again.
“There’s something wrong with the cards.” Later, the police slid it into an evidence bag.
answer: After losing my money, I discovered the dealer was cheating with cards that bore secret marks. Burning with resentment, I secretly poisoned that same deck. The next day, the dealer checked the marks, judged the deck still fit for his cheating, and declared in front of the gamblers that there was nothing wrong with the cards. He had a habit of licking his fingers before flipping the cards; the poison on their faces got into his mouth, and some time later he died of it. When the police examined the deck left at the scene and found the poison, they spoke the last “something wrong with the cards.” The first complaint pointed to the cheating; the second was the dealer’s denial, covering up his cheating; the last pointed to the poison.
hints: The three lines come from a gambler, a dealer, and a police officer, each with a different “problem” in mind.
The dealer had been cheating with marked cards all along, and the gambler separately poisoned that same deck.
The dealer licked his fingers to flip the cards, was poisoned, and the police found the poison on the deck; the second line was his own defense.

title: Pour Some More
story:
I poured the water right to my friend’s mouth, and it streamed down all over his face.
Yet he refused to let me stop, frantically signaling me to pour a little more.
answer: It was a cold winter day outdoors, and my friend had licked a metal railing; his wet tongue had frozen fast to it. I fetched warm water and poured it over the place where tongue met rail, melting the ice that bound them. The water ran all over his face, but he still wanted me to keep going, because his tongue had not come loose yet. I was rescuing him — of course he hoped I would pour a little more.
hints: My friend’s mouth was stuck to something.
In the cold, his tongue had frozen onto a metal railing.
I melted the ice at the stuck spot with warm water; he wanted me to keep pouring until his tongue came free.

title: A Broken Home
story:
Dad is good to me: I have a warm room and more snacks than I can ever finish.
Mom wants to take me away from this place, but I don’t want to go.
Only when I saw Mom’s dead body did I understand — it was already far too late.
answer: I am a puppy, and I took the man who fed me for my dad. He runs a dog-meat restaurant; the warm quarters and the endless food were meant to raise me big. The mother dog heard the slaughter of her own kind in the yard, and time and again she clawed at the door and tried to drag me away — but the food in the man’s hand always lured me back. Then she was killed, and when I saw and smelled her body, I went looking for the door in fear. The door was locked. I was still shut inside the kennel where the man was fattening me for sale.
hints: “Dad” and “Mom” are the narrator’s names for two different relationships.
The narrator is a puppy; Dad is the man who feeds it, Mom is the mother dog.
The owner runs a dog-meat restaurant and fed the puppy to fatten it; the mother dog tried to take it away and was slaughtered herself.

title: Breaking the Curse
story:
Master Li broke a taboo: he crafted a paper effigy for a living man. Word came that the man had died suddenly — and then an effigy exactly like Master Li himself appeared at his own door.
He went up the mountain to copy sutras and ward off the calamity, and came down only months later.
The lock on his house had been changed. The stranger who opened the door said: “I’ve rented this place.”
answer: Master Li was a craftsman of funeral paper effigies, and he held firmly to the rule of never making one for the living. His apprentice wanted to swindle rent money out of his master’s house. He found an accomplice to pose as a rich client and paid an exorbitant price to make Master Li break his rule, then reported the client dead. The apprentice set an effigy made in the master’s own likeness at his door, so that the master would believe the curse had turned on him. The calamity-warding master up the mountain was in on it too; under the pretext of keeping Li on the mountain to copy sutras, he detained him for months. As required, Li wrote his name at the end of each sutra he copied and pressed his fingerprint below it. The apprentice scraped away the sutra text on the pages, leaving only the closing signature and fingerprint, and doctored them into a house-rental agreement; with his master’s keys he rented the house to someone else and pocketed the rent. The tenant, trusting the documents, moved in and changed the locks. Coming down the mountain and seeing the contract the tenant produced, Master Li finally recognized his own closing signature left there from copying sutras. His journey to break the curse had supplied the scam with exactly what it needed: the time, and his name.
hints: The so-called curse was fear manufactured by someone exploiting his taboo.
The rich client, the bearer of the death news, and the master on the mountain all belonged to the apprentice’s plan.
The signature and fingerprint left on the copied sutras were turned against him: the apprentice forged a rental agreement and rented the house out while keeping him on the mountain.

title: Grapes
story:
One grape, two grapes, the juice running all over the inside of my mouth.
Dad handed me another and said: “Eat a few more — soon you’ll be able to see.”
answer: I lost my sight early in childhood. My father believed a folk remedy that eating eyeballs could restore vision, so he took a job at a funeral home, secretly took the eyes of the dead, and fed them to me, calling them grapes. I had never seen them, so I took my father’s word for what they were. My sight did not improve, but he decided the dead men’s eyes were not fresh enough, and he began to seek out living people, kill them, and take their eyes to keep feeding me. “Eat a few more and you’ll see” was the promise he made me in his certainty about the remedy.
hints: I had never seen those grapes; I simply believed what my father called them.
Father wanted to cure my blindness and swore by the folk remedy that eating an organ heals that organ.
The grapes were actually eyeballs, at first taken from the funeral home; later he began killing living people for the sake of what he called freshness.

title: My Wife Fell in Love with Him
story: My wife fell in love with him, and he and my wife both wanted me gone. To stop the two of them from being together, I killed myself.
answer: After an experiment on my brain, a second, independent consciousness arose inside my body. We took turns controlling the same body, and whichever of us was not in control sensed nothing of the life outside. At first I took him for someone who shared my workload, but he occupied the body for longer and longer stretches, and my chances to wake grew fewer and fewer. Somewhere along the way, my wife fell in love with him. The time I regained control, I found the body admitted to the experimental hospital, and I heard my wife and the doctors discussing a plan to delete the original consciousness: they meant to remove me for good and let him live on alone. I confronted my wife, and all she said was that I should disappear quickly. In the end I chose to end this body’s life, taking him — the consciousness dwelling inside it — down with me. He and my wife wanted to keep the same body and be rid of one consciousness; my death destroyed the very body they meant to keep.
hints: My rival and I shared something that could not be taken apart.
We were two independent consciousnesses in one body, and my wife chose the other one.
My wife backed the plan to delete my consciousness; I destroyed the body, and both consciousnesses died with it.

title: The Strange Incantation
story:
To get away from my former landlord, who would not stop pestering me, I moved into a place my best friend had recommended. The old landlady next door smiled and said, “Live here in peace.”
That very night, she hummed a strange tune, and a familiar figure flickered past my window.
The odd smell in the room kept getting stronger. On the seventh night, I could swear something was brushing against my skin.
When day broke, I lifted my pillow, screamed, and ran out.
answer: Hidden inside my pillow and quilt was fatty tissue reeking of decay, and the fly eggs laid in it had hatched—the larvae were crawling onto the bed and onto me. I called the police, and the old woman confessed everything: she was the former landlord’s mother, and she believed in a dark folk practice—place a son’s bodily tissue near a woman, and she would fall in love with him. She had paid my best friend to steer me into this room, then arranged for her son to have liposuction so she could take some of his fat and hide it in the bedding she had prepared for me. Flies had laid eggs in the tissue while it was handled and stored, and once hidden it slowly rotted. Her humming at night was the incantation of her ritual, and the figure peering in through the window was the landlord who had been pestering me. The safe new home I thought I had found was a place his mother had arranged for him all along, and what I rested my head on every night was his own bodily tissue.
hints: Both the strange smell and the touch on my skin came from what was hidden inside the bedding.
The old woman was the former landlord’s mother, and she had also paid off the best friend who recommended the place.
Fat taken from the former landlord’s liposuction was hidden in the pillow and quilt; it rotted, fly eggs came with it, and at night the larvae crawled onto me.

title: The Wallet
story:
I was sitting on a park bench with my dog on its lead when I suddenly stood up and groped my way out.
I had not gone far before I saw a black wallet lying on the ground, and I bent down and picked it up without thinking.
Behind me, the man who had stopped began walking toward me again. My hand froze in midair.
answer: I had witnessed a murder from that bench, and the killer had noticed me. My dog was a guide dog, so I pretended to be completely blind—kept my eyes away from him and groped my way out. He hesitated and stood watching, and I believed I had slipped past him. A little way on, I saw a wallet lying on the ground and bent to pick it up without thinking, forgetting to keep moving as though I found my way by touch. The killer saw that and decided I had been faking blindness all along, and he came toward me again. I froze with the wallet in my hand because I knew I was exposed.
hints: Before I abruptly left, I had seen something I could not let him know I had seen.
I witnessed a murder and used my guide dog to pass as fully blind, trying to escape the killer’s notice.
When I picked up the wallet I had plainly seen, I forgot to keep groping my way; the killer decided I was faking blindness and closed in again.

title: The Submarine Chess Match
story:
In a small submarine lying sunk on the seabed, the two pilots played their game of chess out to the very end.
The winner picked up the pistol from the table.
In the end, neither of them came out alive.
answer: The submarine had broken down; it could not surface, and no rescue came in time. The two pilots knew the air was running out, and there was only one gun aboard, with a single bullet left. Rather than fight over it, they played chess to decide who would get the bullet—and here the prize for winning was to end one’s life early with the gun and be spared the long suffocation ahead. The winner shot himself; the loser stayed behind in the submarine, where no breathable air remained, and in the end he died of suffocation too. The game never decided who would live; it only decided who would stop waiting first.
hints: After the breakdown, the air the two men were waiting on kept running lower.
The gun held a single bullet—enough for one man.
What they played for was an early death that spared them suffocation: the winner died first, and the loser died in the sub soon after.

title: Blood on the Walls
story: The man lay on the bed with his eyes shut tight, and blood covered the walls all around him.
answer: The man had been bitten by a swarm of mosquitoes in the night. After he had swatted nearly a hundred of them dead on the walls of his room, not one mosquito was left to trouble him, and he fell asleep exhausted but content. The blood on the walls was what was left behind each time he slapped a mosquito dead.
hints: His eyes were closed because he could finally rest.
The walls were covered with small blood spots left by many swats.
He had spent the whole night slapping dead the mosquitoes that had fed on blood; only when they were gone did he fall asleep, satisfied.

title: The Music Stopped
story:
I watched them circling around me, and the whole time no one touched me.
The music suddenly stopped.
Several people lunged this way at once, and I had no time even to get away.
answer: I was a small bug resting on the seat of a chair. At the party, people were playing musical chairs: while the music plays, everyone walks around the chairs, and the moment it stops they scramble to sit down. The ones circling me were the players circling this chair. When the music stopped, someone seized the chair and sat, crushing me where I lay on the seat.
hints: The circling crowd and the stopping music belonged to one and the same game.
They were playing musical chairs, and what they raced for was the very spot where I rested.
The narrator is a small bug on the chair’s seat, crushed the moment a player sat down.

title: The Proposal
story:
He proposed to her in a restaurant.
He finished a dinner with a client at that same restaurant.
The next day, he asked her for a divorce.
answer: She had a boyfriend outside her marriage. He proposed to her in the restaurant, not knowing she was already married. That same day, her husband happened to be dining with a client in that very restaurant, and he witnessed the proposal. The next day, he asked her for a divorce. Of the three lines, the “he” of the first is the boyfriend and the “he” of the last two is the husband; the “she” is the same woman throughout.
hints: Across the three lines, the same pronoun points to two different men.
The one who proposed was her boyfriend; the one dining with a client was her husband.
Already married, she was also seeing another man; her husband witnessed the proposal at the same restaurant and asked for a divorce the next day.

title: The Human-Skin Drum
story:
During the Wanli reign, an old farmer’s daughter went missing. Before that, the village strongman had kept coming to their house to pester her.
The farmer went to the county yamen to press his case. He raised the drumstick to beat the grievance drum—and suddenly found himself staring at the drumhead.
He never brought it down, and he never left the yamen alive.
answer: The strongman had abducted and murdered the old farmer’s daughter, then colluded with people inside the yamen to have her skin made into the office’s new drumhead. When the farmer came to lodge his complaint, he saw a dark birthmark on the drumhead and recognized the unique mark on his daughter’s body. He had come to beg the yamen to investigate her disappearance, only to find her murdered body rendered into the very drum used for crying injustice. Realizing that the place he had turned to for help was itself part of the crime, he lost the courage to press his case any further, and he took his own life at the yamen gate.
hints: What stopped him was a mark on the grievance drum.
His daughter bore a distinctive dark birthmark, and the same mark showed on the drumhead.
The drumhead was made from the daughter’s skin; the strongman had colluded with people inside the yamen, and the very office he appealed to had taken part in the persecution.

title: The Mermaid’s Blood Letter
story:
The prince took the princess from the sea as his bride, and everyone at court called it a blessing.
On their wedding night, the prince died, and a letter written in blood lay at the bedside.
They read it through, and at once agreed to let the princess return to the sea.
answer: The princess was a mermaid. The court believed that eating a mermaid’s flesh and blood grants eternal life, and many who coveted immortality were already preparing to move against her. To get her out, the prince staged a scene in which he seemed to eat mermaid flesh, then took poison himself, disguising his death as poisoning from the flesh. He had left the blood letter beforehand, stating that he had been poisoned after tasting the mermaid’s flesh and warning that the flesh must never be eaten. Seeing their prince die of that single taste, the courtiers set their greed aside, at least for the moment, and allowed the princess to return to the sea. The legend of immortality they had called a blessing turned, with the prince’s death, into something feared. The princess got away, but the prince never lived to stay at her side.
hints: The princess was a mermaid, and the court coveted the legend that hung on her flesh and blood.
They meant to eat the mermaid for eternal life, but the prince left a blood letter saying her flesh had poisoned him.
The prince faked eating the flesh and took poison himself, planting the idea that mermaid flesh is deadly, and traded his life for the princess’s escape from the court.

title: The Knife That Wouldn’t Come Out
story:
I slipped into the laboratory and drove my knife at the “doctor.”
He did not so much as frown. The point stopped at his chest—no push could drive it deeper, and no pull could draw it back out.
He lowered his head and took hold of my wrist.
answer: The real doctor knew a hit man was after him, so he slipped away in advance and left in the laboratory a defense robot molded in his own likeness. The killer recognized only the doctor’s appearance and never noticed that the body had been swapped. After the point passed through the coat, it struck the robot’s metal chest plate and could not pierce it; at the same instant the robot clamped the blade itself, so the killer could neither drive it in nor pull it free. Then it seized his wrist, overpowered him, and killed him. The knife would not go in because of the metal plate, and would not come out because of the robot’s grip.
hints: The man before him possessed only the doctor’s appearance.
The point struck a metal chest plate while another force clamped down on the blade.
The doctor had put a humanoid defense robot in his place; the killer could not stab through it and was seized and killed by it.

title: Counting the Bills
story:
After I got my hands on that money, she came to me every night. A spiritual master gave me a bamboo tube and told me to put into it the thing she had loved most, and set it before her spirit tablet.
As I always did, I licked my fingertips, counted out a stack of bills, and stuffed them in.
She finally stopped haunting me. By dawn, I was dead at the table.
answer: I had killed my girlfriend and taken her money, and after that her vengeful ghost came after me night after night. The master’s bamboo tube carries offerings to the dead and grants the wish the departed clings to most; and if the offering carries the blood or saliva of the person the departed loves best, the spell will follow those bodily traces, find that person’s soul, and carry it away. I assumed my girlfriend loved money most of all, so, in my old habit of licking my fingers while counting, I slipped saliva-stained bills into the tube. But the one she clung to had always been me. Following the saliva, the spell found my soul and delivered me to her side. She got the person she wanted and her resentment faded, while my body was left dead at the table.
hints: The money came from the girlfriend I killed, and in death she still clung to me.
The bamboo tube can use the blood or saliva left on an offering to summon the soul of the person the departed loves most.
Her deepest attachment was to me; my licked fingers left saliva on the bills, so in offering the money I sent my own soul along with it.

title: The Man in the Gift
story:
He hid himself inside it, meaning to give her a surprise.
After he climbed out, his friend dropped to the floor.
Then he stuffed his friend into the same hiding place and carried it away along with the gift.
answer: He had fallen for his friend’s girlfriend. While the girl was still out, he climbed into the giant plush toy his friend was giving her, planning to step out of the gift and surprise her when she came home. The opening in the toy’s back and its hollow interior were roomy enough to conceal a grown man. The friend got there first, looking for the girl, and saw him climb out of the plush toy; the two fought, and he knocked his friend out. To cover up the assault, he hid the unconscious man inside the same toy and carried the toy off, meaning to get him away before the girl returned. Two different people took turns hiding inside; the hands handling the gift were the same man’s throughout.
hints: The place he stuffed him into was the inside of a gift large enough to hide a grown man.
The gift was a giant plush toy, and the giver’s friend also had feelings for the girl receiving it.
The friend hid in the toy first, planning to reveal himself and confess; when the boyfriend caught him, he knocked him out, then used the toy to hide the man and carry him away.

title: The Three Children
story:
He invited me out to the suburbs to watch a film that circulated only in private.
As I stepped inside, he said, “I’m late—Number Three is running a fever.”
From the screen came a child’s screaming. He only kept on smiling.
“You have children of your own. How can you bear to watch this?”
“Three of them,” he said, raising his teacup. “All at home.”
I stared at his hand and did not dare say another word.
answer: My friend had kidnapped three children and was holding them in a small house in the suburbs, calling them Number One, Number Two, and Number Three in order. He had filmed himself killing Number One, and now he had invited me over to watch. Number Three had come down with a fever and was still locked up; dealing with the sick child was what had delayed him. In the film the killer shows nothing but his hands, the right little finger missing its top joint—and when he poured my tea, I saw that same shortened finger, with blood still caught under the fingernail. Only then did I understand that the three children he kept speaking of were captive victims, and that the killer on the screen was sitting right beside me.
hints: The three children he spoke of were bound up with the film.
The killer in the film and my friend shared the same distinctive hand.
He had kidnapped all three children, and the film recorded him killing one of them.

title: The Portrait on the Third Floor
story:
I died on the first floor of the school building.
Yet every year when school starts, the new students climb to the third floor, stand before me, and say, “Hello, Teacher.”
answer: When the earthquake struck, I was on the first floor of the teaching building shielding three students; the collapsing structure buried me, and I did not survive. After those three students were rescued, the school hung my portrait on the third floor. Every year at enrollment, the teachers bring the new students up to see the portrait and tell them the story of that rescue. The students stand facing the portrait and greet me.
hints: What the students who came after saw was not my body.
The school never forgot what I had done in the earthquake.
I died protecting three students, and the school hung my portrait on the third floor for the students to remember me by.

title: The Sandwich
story:
On my way home from work I bought sandwiches and took her to the park for a picnic.
A boy walked off with my paper bag. I chased him down and insisted he give it back.
In the tussle the bag split, and the sandwiches spilled all over the ground.
He never reached for them; he just kept staring at the other thing inside the bag.
So I had to kill him.
answer: I am a serial killer with a pathological fixation on women’s hands. From each victim I keep one hand, carry it around with me, and treat it as my sweetheart. At the picnic, I had hidden the hand in the paper bag with the sandwiches. A boy picked up the wrong bag, and afraid he would find what was inside, I hurried after him to snatch it back. In the struggle the bag tore, the sandwiches scattered, and the victim’s hand lay exposed. The boy had seen the evidence of my crimes, and I killed him to keep him quiet.
hints: The “she” I brought on the picnic could no longer move on her own.
Something hidden in the paper bag would have exposed my crimes.
I carried one of my victim’s hands with me as my sweetheart, and the boy saw it.

title: The Flashing-Light Trap
story:
The light on the balcony across from mine kept blinking on and off, as if it had been broken for a long time.
Then the former tenant vanished without warning, and a crowd of people searched the place from top to bottom.
A few days later, someone else moved in.
The light was still blinking—but the spacing of the flashes had changed.
answer: The former tenant had been a spy. With the pattern of flashes and the intervals between them, he passed coded messages to accomplices who could see his window. After the police arrested him and searched the house, they worked out this channel of communication. The people who moved in afterward were police as well. They kept the lamp and used the same code to send notice of new meetings, luring the accomplices who had not yet been caught into coming, straight into arrest. The light had never been broken; only the sender and the message had changed.
hints: The flashing followed a pattern, and every interval carried a meaning.
The former tenant’s disappearance was bound up with the search of the house.
The tenant had signaled with the light; once the police took over the home they kept the signals going, using them to trap his accomplices.

title: Going Upstairs
story:
The stairwell light was broken. I stood at the bottom and texted my mom: “Come down and get me. I don’t dare come up.”
Before long, that familiar face appeared at the top of the stairs.
I followed her up.
My phone rang. I read Mom’s reply—and I no longer dared take the next step.
answer: The thing that came to meet me can mimic my mother’s appearance. The stairwell was dark, and I took that familiar face for my mother’s and followed it upstairs. My real mother had been busy at home all along and had only just seen my text; she replied, “I can’t come down right now. Come up on your own.” When I read that reply, the creature impersonating my mother was walking right in front of me. I finally understood that the thing I had followed upstairs had been wearing my mother’s face.
hints: What frightened me was the content of the reply Mom had just sent.
In her text, Mom said she had been at home the whole time.
The monster had copied my mother’s face; my real mother never came down at all.

title: Who Turned Off the Lights
story:
Half asleep, I found the lights too bright, hauled myself up, and switched them off.
Dozens of voices called out my name all at once.
That woke me up for good.
answer: I had dozed off at my desk during evening self-study in the classroom. Half dreaming, I found the lights too bright, and out of habit I got up to switch them off and go on sleeping—I walked to the switch and turned off the lights of the whole classroom. The other students were all quietly doing their homework; when the room went suddenly dark and they saw that I was the one who had done it, they called out my name, and the uproar woke me completely.
hints: The lights I turned off had been shining on a great many people.
The voices belonged to classmates who knew me.
Groggy with sleep during evening self-study, I got up and switched off the lights of the entire classroom.

title: The Foot That Stuck Out
story:
While I was staying at a friend’s house, he warned me: “Don’t let your feet stick out of the blanket while you sleep.”
I laughed at him for scaring me with tales for little children.
Waking in the middle of the night, I finally understood how much in earnest that warning had been.
answer: My friend has an abnormal obsession with other people’s feet; he cannot resist touching them, cradling them, even biting them. He knows his own failing, which is why, while I stayed over, he told me to keep my feet well covered. I took it for a story grown-ups use to frighten children and thought nothing of it. In the middle of the night I was woken by a touch on my foot: my friend was holding the foot I had left outside the blanket and biting it. His warning had been about what he himself would do.
hints: The one warning me knew what a foot left sticking out would draw to it.
The thing that touched me at midnight was inside that very room.
My friend goes for other people’s uncovered feet, hugging them and biting them; his warning came from his own behavior.

title: Late-Night Piano
story:
A little past ten, I was walking by the practice room when I heard some very unsteady piano playing. The same passage went wrong twice, then fell silent for a long while.
The next day, the famous pianist was found dead in that practice room.
When he died, I had not yet reached the practice room door.
answer: A composer who worked behind the scenes for the orchestra had long had his works taken by the pianist and passed off as the pianist’s own. That night he caught the pianist stealing his new score, ready to publish it under his own name. The two fought, and the composer killed him. Just then, my footsteps sounded from outside the door. The composer hid the body under the piano, sat down on the bench, and played, wanting me to believe the man in the practice room was still alive. He could play, but fresh from killing a man and terrified of being caught, his hands kept slipping. Afterwards he left the room. The playing I heard came from the murderer; the pianist was already dead by then.
hints: The death and the playing happened in the same room, but two different people did them.
The playing was meant for whoever was passing outside the door.
The killer hid the body and played the piano himself to cover up the death; his nerves made the playing falter again and again.

title: Three Birthdays
story:
I am almost forty.
Today they wished me a happy twenty-fifth birthday; tomorrow someone will celebrate my twenty-third; the day after, my twenty-fourth.
I already have another name ready for tomorrow, when I go for cake.
answer: I work at a nursing home. Several residents with Alzheimer’s have mistaken me for their own sons and are living in memories of their sons’ younger years. Their families rarely visit, so I sit with them, talk over the old days, and celebrate the birthdays of the sons they remember. Three days in a row, different residents wanted to celebrate their son’s birthday, at ages twenty-five, twenty-three, and twenty-four. I answer to whatever name each resident remembers, and accept their birthday wishes.
hints: Those ages belong to different people; the celebrants have mistaken me for them.
The celebrants are all elderly residents of the same facility.
Nursing home residents take a staff member for their own sons as they were in youth, and he celebrates each of their birthdays with them.

title: Birthday Applause
story:
My friends threw me a birthday party.
I blew out the candles and heard a burst of applause.
Laughing, I said I wanted to hug them one by one.
When the last one’s turn came, my hand found the cake knife.
answer: I was born blind. A year ago we were stranded in the wild and ran out of food. My friends proposed that each of us give up a hand and share the meat, so we could hold out until rescue came. I believed them and lost a hand; everyone else kept both of theirs, simply lying to me that they had done the same. After the rescue, they always touched me with only one hand, and I never suspected a thing. On my birthday night they forgot the lie and clapped without thinking. The sound made me doubt, but applause alone could prove nothing. Under cover of the hugs, I took hold of their wrists and felt both sides of each: every one of them had two sound hands. I finally knew that back then, only I had been sacrificed. Then I picked up the cake knife and turned it on them.
hints: I cannot see them, and I once went through a deadly ordeal together with them.
We all claimed to have paid the same bodily price to stay alive.
I was made to lose a hand while their hands stayed whole; the applause planted my doubt, and the touch during the hugs proved the lie.

title: Go to Sleep
story:
I am so sleepy I can barely keep my eyes open.
That man stays beside me, saying gently, “Go to sleep.”
Yet I fight with everything I have to stay awake. If I go on standing here, I will not last much longer.
answer: I had been kidnapped by a captor who takes pleasure in tormenting people. He left me on a narrow plank suspended in the air, a rope around my neck. I must keep my balance to stay alive: the moment I fall asleep and lose my footing, I will drop and the rope will strangle me. He waits close by, deliberately urging me to sleep, waiting to watch me give out. I am desperately sleepy, but I do not dare let myself lose consciousness.
hints: I cannot sit or lie down; I must keep my balance.
The man keeping me company wants something dangerous to happen once I fall asleep.
I am trapped on a plank suspended in midair with a rope around my neck—doze off, slip, and it will strangle me.

title: Insomnia
story:
After the divorce, I could never fall asleep.
Last night I went to see him, and I slept straight through to dawn.
When I opened my eyes, the sheets were soaked in red.
answer: During the marriage I was used to sleeping with my head on my husband’s arm, and after the divorce I could never adapt to sleeping alone. I went to see my ex-husband, attacked him, cut off the arm I had always used as a pillow, and brought it home. That night I slept on the arm, and when I woke, the sheets had been soaked red with blood. I had my familiar feeling back; my ex-husband was left gravely harmed.
hints: After seeing him again, I brought back something that used to help me sleep.
The red is blood, and it has to do with what I brought back.
I cut off my ex-husband’s arm and took it home to keep using as a pillow.

title: Separated
story:
At a gas station, I keyed a stranger’s car.
The owner grabbed me and insisted on calling the police.
I turned my head and called out, “Daddy.”
He looked at me, turned, and ran.
Later, some strangers took me away—and that was how I finally got to go home.
answer: The man traveling with me was a child trafficker who made me pose as his daughter. I was afraid that if I simply cried for help, he would drag me away again, so at the gas station, while he was inside buying things, I scratched up a car outside the shop so that its owner would seize me and insist on calling the police. At the mention of the police, the trafficker feared they would check our identities; he abandoned me and fled. Calling him “Daddy” kept my cover intact, since he could not very well announce in public that I had nothing to do with him. The strangers who came were police officers. I told them how I had been abducted, and with their help I finally reached my family.
hints: Keying the car was my way of making sure someone held me there and called the police.
The name I called that man came from the role he had ordered me to play.
He was a trafficker who fled rather than let the police find out who he was; the officers taking me away were saving me.

title: Disappointment
story:
“You have disappointed me too deeply. I am never coming back.”
I wrote the sentence over and over, and the wastebasket filled with crumpled paper.
Not one sheet could be shown to anyone.
And she can never correct my handwriting now.
answer: I had killed my wife and wanted to forge a letter in her hand, so that relatives, friends, and the police would believe she had simply given up on the marriage and left of her own accord. Using samples of her old writing, I practiced imitating her handwriting, writing that sentence again and again. Every attempt still showed differences, and I could not get the signature right. I crumpled up the failures and grew more frantic with every sheet. My wife was already dead, so I could never have her write, in her own hand, the letter meant to cover up her death.
hints: The crumpled sheets were practice for a letter meant to be shown to others.
I wanted people to believe that another person had left of her own accord.
I killed my wife and was practicing forging her departure letter, but I could not imitate her handwriting well enough.

title: The Twelve Zodiac Animals Go Abroad
story:
The twelve of us had agreed to travel abroad together.
Beep—cleared. One companion after another passed through security.
When my turn came, the screen first read “camel,” then changed to “deer,” then spilled out a long list of names.
An officer stopped me: “You may take only your own belongings out of the country.”
I looked at my own body and wept.
answer: This is a fairy-tale world where animals can talk, and the twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac were traveling together. I am the Dragon. The security scanner has no complete profile for a dragon, so it judged me section by section against the animals it did know: it took my camel-like head, my deer-like antlers, my snake-like neck, and so on, deciding each part came from a different animal. The system thus reported that I was carrying body parts belonging to other creatures. The other eleven zodiac animals all passed identification, and the officer stopped me on the strength of that false report. I was carrying my own body, and the machine read it as a patchwork of foreign parts.
hints: The twelve companions correspond to a familiar set of animal names.
Several parts of my appearance resemble other animals.
I am the Dragon of the Chinese zodiac, and the scanner mistook my different body parts for parts belonging to other animals.

title: Ten Suns
story:
Last night I told my brother, “Unless there are ten suns in the sky, I will never speak to you again.”
Today I opened my eyes, and there were indeed ten suns outside the window.
And I did not live through that morning.
answer: After our parents died, my brother and I depended on each other. During the quarrel I threw out that angry line and locked my bedroom door. My brother wanted to cheer me up without waking me, so in the night he went around outside my window and painted nine suns on the outer side of the glass. The security grille he was leaning on came loose, and he fell from the building. At daybreak I was startled awake and saw the nine suns on my window—together with the real rising sun, exactly ten. Then I saw my brother’s body on the ground below. Losing my family one after another, I killed myself in grief.
hints: Of the ten suns, nine were put there by human hands.
My brother wanted it finished before I woke, so he went outside my window.
My brother painted nine suns and fell to his death; I saw ten suns, and I saw his body.

title: One More Round
story:
They were playing rock paper scissors in the river.
One of them never came up again.
Afterwards, cries for help were often heard from the river.
And after every cry, a voice would follow: “Rock, paper, scissors.”
answer: Two children were having a breath-holding contest in the water, with a rule: win a round of rock paper scissors and you may surface for one breath; lose, and you keep holding your breath. One child lost round after round and, too stubborn to stop, finally blacked out and could not be saved. After he died he became a water ghost, fixated on the game that never ended. Since then, he drags under anyone who enters the water and forces them to play by the same rule: win to rise for a breath, lose and be pulled back down. Trapped people cry for help while they take their breath, but the ghost only calls for the next round and never lets anyone leave.
hints: Winning or losing the game decided whether you could briefly do the one thing that keeps you alive.
The first to die still takes part in the same game now.
Only a win lets you surface to breathe; the drowned child became a water ghost and keeps forcing others to play.

title: Rock, Paper, Scissors
story:
They backed me into a corner and said they wanted to play rock paper scissors.
“Rock beats paper.”
At last I got my hands on the scissors, and heard them laugh: “This time, paper beats scissors.”
I lost, and I never went back to class.
answer: I was a student being bullied at school. Several of them pinned me in a corner and threw sharp stones at me, smashing through my school uniform, and laughed that rock had beaten paper. I took out a pair of scissors to fight back; they seized my hands, tore the scissors away, and then ripped off strips of cloth and tightened them around my neck. Killing me, the one who had held the scissors, with cloth, they called it paper beating scissors. That is how I died. This so-called game was just the name they gave their violence.
hints: The rock, the paper, and the scissors they named were all real objects.
I got the scissors in order to protect myself.
Stones smashed through my uniform, the scissors were torn from me, and in the end they strangled me with strips of cloth.

title: The Time Slide
story:
Three nights running, coming home from overtime, I saw a child in the park.
He wore a plaid shirt absurdly too big for him, stood by the slide, and stared at me in terror.
On the weekend I passed through the park and, on a whim, took a slide.
When I landed, the cuffs of the sleeves hung over my hands.
Under the streetlight, the me of three days ago was walking this way.
answer: This slide sends whoever rides to the bottom three days back in time, and shrinks their body to childhood size; memory and clothing are kept. When I slid down on the weekend, I became a child, still dressed in my adult plaid shirt, returned to three days earlier. The one walking toward me under the streetlight was myself, just off overtime, who had not yet ridden the slide. Terrified of that reunion, I stayed near the park and watched my past self pass by for three nights in a row. So the child I saw on my way home from overtime was me, after the weekend slide, back in the past.
hints: The child’s clothes were originally meant for a grown man.
The slide changed my body’s age, and also the time I arrived at.
The me who slid down on the weekend became a child, went back three days, and became the very figure I saw three nights running.

title: My Roommate’s Prank
story:
My roommates and I loved scaring Xiaohong. She was bold, and nothing we did ever got much of a reaction out of her.
At dawn, a scream jolted me awake.
A line of writing had appeared on the ceiling.
This time, I could not laugh.
answer: Xiaohong had long been tormented and humiliated by our pranks. We read her silence as boldness and assumed she never minded. That night she left the words “Scared you this time, didn’t I?” on the ceiling, then hanged herself in the room we all shared. Another roommate woke first, found her body, and screamed. I opened my eyes to that line of writing, and to Xiaohong already dead, and finally understood what that question was asking.
hints: We took her endless silence to mean she had never been hurt.
She left that line, and something far more serious happened in the room as well.
She killed herself after leaving “Scared you this time, didn’t I?”, and a roommate woke to find her body.

title: The Radio
story:
He had just finished a big piece of work and was driving back to the city.
He switched on the radio, and the same sentence came through the broadcast again and again.
The phone rang immediately after.
He never made it back to the city—he took his own life.
answer: He was a radio host planning to murder his wife. He had recorded the entire show in advance, to be played during the live slot he was responsible for, then left the station, went home, and did the killing—the voice on the air would serve as proof that he never left his post. On the drive back to the station, he turned on the radio and heard the faulty player looping the same recorded sentence over and over. His colleagues, finding the program malfunctioning and unable to reach the host on duty, had called to summon him back. He knew his secret absence was exposed and the cover he had staked everything on had failed; afraid the murder would come to light, he killed himself.
hints: He wanted the broadcast to prove he had stayed in one place the whole time.
The voice on the radio was his own, but he was out elsewhere at that moment.
The host used a pre-recorded show to cover his absence while he killed his wife; the playback glitch showed his colleagues he was not at the station.

title: The First to Get Out
story:
The time bomb was about to go off, and my teammate was still locked in a struggle with the criminals.
I leapt out the window and hid in the water below.
In the end, that time bomb was left intact.
My teammate walked out alive; I died outside.
answer: We had infiltrated a building standing in the water to stop criminals from detonating a time bomb. I was to defuse it; my teammate kept the criminals occupied. With the timer about to end and the bomb not yet defused, all I could do was jump out the window into the water. The bomb then malfunctioned and never went off. Upstairs, the criminals kept fighting my teammate, and one of them produced a grenade. In the crisis my teammate kicked it out the window to keep the blast away from the room, not knowing I was still hiding just below. The grenade landed near me and killed me. It was the time bomb that stayed intact; what killed me was the grenade kicked out afterwards.
hints: More than one kind of explosive appeared at the scene.
Someone inside the room sent another explosive outside.
My teammate kicked the grenade out the window, and it killed me as I still hid beneath it.

title: The Book Was Borrowed
story: In the middle of class, the teacher suddenly flew into a rage at me. I was not angry at all—if anything, I found it a little funny.
answer: The teacher had forgotten to bring a book to class, so my book was borrowed to teach from. Halfway through the lesson, the teacher forgot the book was borrowed from me, decided instead that I was the one who had come without a book, and flew into a rage at me. I knew the truth, so I was not angry—I found it funny.
hints: The reason for the teacher’s anger had to do with the textbook.
The textbook was off my desk for the moment because I was helping the teacher.
The teacher was teaching from my borrowed textbook, forgot it was borrowed, and took me for the one without a book.

title: Familiar Eyes
story:
My brother has cared for me all these years.
After the earthquake, I lay pinned under the rubble, unable to move and unable to cry out.
A pair of familiar eyes appeared outside the crack in the stones. I blinked with all my might, and she saw me.
Then a tile was laid over the crack.
answer: I was born deaf and mute, and I live with my older brother and his wife. The earthquake pinned me in the rubble; I could not move or call out, only wait for someone to find me. My sister-in-law reached the crack first and saw me signaling to her with my eyes, begging for rescue. She had always seen caring for me as a burden on the family, and she decided to hide the fact that I was alive. She covered the crack with a tile so my brother would not find me, told him this spot had already been searched, and led him away to look elsewhere. My brother never knew what she had done, and I was never rescued.
hints: Those eyes belonged to someone who knew me and knew I could not cry out.
She saw clearly that I was alive, yet covered the very crack through which I could have been found.
My sister-in-law, wanting to be rid of the burden of caring for me, covered the crack, kept my brother in the dark, and led him away from the rubble.

title: Counting the Steps
story:
To prove the school was not haunted, I stayed in the classroom until midnight.
Nothing happened. I packed my bag, and on the way down began counting the steps.
One, two, three…
Only outside the building did it occur to me: leaving this classroom in the daytime never involves going downstairs.
answer: My classroom sits on the ground floor; the corridor at its door is level with the ground outside, and normally I walk straight out of the building along it, with no stairs at all. The rumors of a haunting at night are true. That night, when I left the classroom, a flight of steps that should not exist appeared where the exit is ordinarily flat. Convinced that nothing had happened, I walked and counted my way down, and only outside the building did I notice that the route I had just taken was entirely different from the daytime one.
hints: The classroom’s real floor matters.
I left through the exit I always use, and in the daytime that path has no steps.
The classroom is on the ground floor, yet at night a flight of descending steps appeared out of nowhere.

title: The Waterweed
story:
He had not been back to this river for years.
Sitting on the bank, he asked the old fisherman, “Are the waterweeds down below still as thick as ever?”
The fisherman pointed at the deep pool and said one sentence.
He sat there a long time, and that day he ended his own life here.
answer: Years ago, his girlfriend fell into that deep pool. He jumped in to save her, and in the murky, rushing water he grabbed a handful of something long and thin, took it for waterweed, and let go; his girlfriend was never found. That handful was her hair. Years later he came back and asked about the waterweed. The old fisherman, who had worked and dredged those waters for years, told him, “That pool bottom is nothing but rock. I have cleared it many times — waterweed has never grown there.” Only then did it strike him that what he had released might have been his girlfriend. Unable to bear the remorse of having perhaps held her in his hand and willingly let go, he took his own life.
hints: He once tried to save someone in this water.
While saving her, he grabbed a handful of something long and thin — then let it go.
He had mistaken his girlfriend’s hair for waterweed; once he learned no waterweed ever grew in that pool, he realized he might have let go of her.

title: The Sailor
story:
I used to be a sailor.
After we were rescued, the mere sight of fish made me shake with nausea.
In the hungriest days aboard, we had fish to eat the whole time.
answer: At sea our ship ran into trouble, lost power, and drifted for a long time. Food ran short, and some of the crew did not live through it. To hold on, the survivors used the flesh of dead shipmates as fishing bait and ate the fish they caught, until we were finally rescued. Those fish had fed on our companions, and I had lived on them in turn. From then on, the sight of fish brought it all back — the nausea, the fear — and I could never eat fish again.
hints: I survived a shipwreck and a long wait for rescue.
With no ordinary bait left, we made use of our dead shipmates.
The survivors baited their hooks with their companions’ flesh and ate the fish they caught until rescue came; I have never been able to face fish since.

title: The Illegitimate Son
story:
The man who came to apply for our driver’s job looked far too much like me.
My father was a habitual womanizer. After a moment’s thought, I asked with a smile, “Did your mother used to work at our house?”
He shook his head and said it was his father who had worked at our house.
I stopped smiling.
answer: Years ago, my mother had an affair with the family’s driver and gave birth to me, yet she brought me up all along as the young master of a rich household. The driver, afraid of being found out, resigned and went back to his hometown, where he later married and had another son. That son is the man who has now come to apply for the job — he and I share the same biological father. At first, seeing how much he resembled me, I took him for one of my father’s outside children and meant to probe by asking about his mother. But he said his mother had always stayed in their hometown, that it was his father who had once worked at our house, and he gave the old driver’s name. The resemblance together with this story made me begin to doubt my own parentage. I was afraid the father who raised me would learn of my mother’s betrayal, and afraid the life I had would change because of it.
hints: At first I guessed that my father had another child somewhere outside the family.
The applicant’s mother never came to our house — but his father did, as our old driver.
Both the applicant and I could be the old driver’s sons; the question of birth has landed on me.

title: The Four-Year-Old Mother
story:
The new student told me, “Mom is four years old this year.”
I thought he had gotten it wrong, and went for a home visit that weekend.
The woman who opened the door already had white hair, yet an iron chain was fastened to her ankle.
The student behind her suddenly smiled: “Bro, the new one is here.”
answer: The student is in fact an adult, unusually small in build and boyish in face. By dressing the part and forging identity papers, he slips into kindergartens to lure teachers into home visits, then he and his older brother kidnap whoever comes. Several women are being held captive in the house; one of them has been shut in for four years and is forced to play his mother in front of outsiders. On purpose, he gives the number of years she has been held in the house as her age, acting like a child who got the number wrong, so that I would come and check for myself.
