Bereft of her children, the mother wolf waited until the hunter was away, carried off his two-year-old child in her jaws, and raised the child as her own. That child was me.
After the mother wolf grew old, I began hunting for food, often snatching sheep from the nearby village. The villagers caught me, and finding a creature with a human face living like a wolf, they tied me up to burn me. The hunter in the wolf skin was summoned too.
By the firelight, the hunter made out the crescent-shaped birthmark on my shoulder, recognized his missing child, and at once threw down his torch and set me loose.
All I remembered was Mother’s warning that the man in the wolf skin was dangerous, so the moment I broke free I lunged to attack him. He did not raise his gun to defend himself, and in the end I bit him to death. The photograph that fell from inside his clothes was an old family photo he had carried all along.
hints: The one I called Mother had an old grudge with the man in the wolf skin.
I lived like a wolf, yet the crescent on my shoulder could prove who I was as a human.
The mother wolf raised the hunter’s child; the hunter set him free once he recognized him, and was bitten to death by a child who did not know his own father.

title: See You Again
story: Xiaomei and I took to each other from the moment we met, and decided to spend the rest of our lives together. But when she came to meet my parents before the wedding, she suddenly turned and fled in panic.
answer:
Xiaomei had been abducted and sold as a child, and grew up in the family that bought her. She never forgot the woman who had kept her under guard and beaten her in those days.
Coming to meet my parents before the wedding, Xiaomei recognized that face: my mother was the very person who had trafficked her.
After she fled, Xiaomei told me everything, and it called to mind how, when I was little, a girl had stayed at our house for a time. My mother said she was a relative lodging with us for a while, and the two of us played together every day. That girl was Xiaomei, hidden away in our home by my mother, waiting to be sold on.
When we met again as adults and felt we knew each other, it was because we truly had spent that time together. Xiaomei had believed she had found her love, only to walk back into the very house where she had once been held.
hints: Xiaomei had met my mother long before that visit — and was terrified of her.
I had spent time with Xiaomei when we were little; I just never knew why she was living in our house.
My mother had trafficked Xiaomei; the instant closeness came from the childhood days under one roof, and meeting the parents made Xiaomei recognize the trafficker.

title: Puppy Love
story:
My parents were called in over my puppy love.
The homeroom teacher scolded my dad for not raising his son right; my dad complimented her looks instead.
She actually smiled.
While the two of them talked, I slipped out of the office.
answer:
The homeroom teacher was my own mother; she and my dad had been each other’s early romance back in their day, and later they married.
Mom had called Dad in so the two of them could discipline me together, but the more she said, the angrier she got, and she blamed him for failing to raise his son properly. Dad said the blame couldn’t all fall on him. Mom dug up old scores: “Back then, weren’t you the one who confessed to me first?”
Dad rode the opening and paid her a compliment: “Who could help it, with you that pretty?” Mom laughed in spite of herself, and the two of them drifted into reminiscing, for the moment forgetting me, still standing there waiting to be scolded.
While they talked, I quietly slipped out of the office.
hints: Dad and the homeroom teacher had known each other for many years, and they brought up the romance of their youth.
Besides teaching me at school, the homeroom teacher was also in charge of me at home.
The homeroom teacher was my mother; my parents got to talking about their own puppy love, and I seized the moment to slip away.

title: Never Growing Up
story:
My classmates grew taller one after another, while I could still wear my old clothes.
Mom and Dad fed me “vitamins” every day, and always told me to smile when they took my picture.
They said it would be best if I just stayed this small forever.
It seemed that only if I didn’t grow up would they love me more.
answer:
I was a child model for children’s clothing, and my adorable looks brought the family a fair amount of money. My parents worried that once I grew up the orders would stop coming, so they wanted to keep me looking as young as they could.
They told me the medication I should never have taken for so long was “vitamins,” and gave it to me every day. The long-term improper dosing damaged my body and left me growing far more slowly than children my age.
They kept arranging photo shoots and praising me — what a good child, how pretty I looked. I understood nothing of the money involved; I only saw that my clothes never got much smaller, and that my parents treated me best when photographs were earning money, so I came to believe that as long as I never grew up, I could keep their love forever.
hints: My parents wanted me to stay small because my looks brought in money.
What I was given daily was called vitamins, but it was drugs that damaged my body.
The child model’s parents dosed him improperly to stretch out the earning years, and the child took the praise that came with the money for love.

title: The Number in My Palm
story:
After Father lost his job, he grew thinner and thinner, and came home less and less.
The neighbors told me to keep away from him, and I began to hate him too.
Before he left, he gave me a piece of paper with nothing on it but a string of numbers.
Many years later, I finally received the thing printed with that string of numbers, and clasped it tightly in my palm.
answer:
My father was an undercover officer in drug enforcement. “Losing his job” and “going bad” were cover he had built to get close to the dealers, but I was young and knew nothing of it.
During the mission he came under coercion and was harmed by drugs, and his health went from bad to worse. The people around us saw only a man moving through the world as an addict, and even I was kept at arm’s length. I took my father’s decline for a fall into ruin, and hated him for wrecking our life.
What he left me at parting was his own police badge number, written on a piece of paper. He later died on a mission, and only then did I learn the truth from his colleagues.
I grew up, became a police officer myself, and applied to take up my father’s preserved badge number; the request was approved. The number plate I received bore the same string of digits as the paper. Closing my hand around it, I also took up the profession and the responsibility he had left behind.
hints: The identity Father showed the outside world concealed the work he really did.
The digits on the paper were a professional number, one kept on reserve after Father’s death.
He was an undercover officer who died on duty; I became a police officer and applied to carry his badge number.

title: Finding a Friend
story:
The singing outside the building drew nearer and nearer.
“Searching, searching for a friend…”
Clinging to my gun, I shrank into a cabinet, not daring even to breathe loudly.
Metal feet stopped in front of the cabinet door, and the door was slammed open.
“Found myself a good friend.”
The song ended, and so did I.
answer:
This is a fictional war. I was a soldier trapped inside a building while the enemy hunted for survivors with remote-controlled robot dogs carrying explosives.
The operators had woven a children’s song into the search program: while moving and searching, the machine played “Searching, searching for a friend”; once a target was confirmed, it played “Found myself a good friend,” and then detonated. The song was deliberately used to terrify anyone in hiding.
I hid in the cabinet clutching my gun. A robot dog was steered up to the cabinet door and smashed it open, and the camera showed the operator where I was. The last line of the song sounded, marking me as found. The explosion that came right after killed me.
hints: Clutching my gun in hiding, I was facing a battlefield manhunt.
The metal feet belonged to a remotely piloted machine, and the lyrics changed from one stage to the next.
Once the explosive-carrying robot dog found me, it finished the last line of the nursery rhyme and detonated.

title: Turning Back
story:
I handed her the poison; she thanked me and asked me to close the door behind me when I left.
I made off with the valuables from her home.
I had just left the compound when I suddenly remembered something, and turned straight back.
answer:
I am a burglar who cares a great deal about cleanliness. Breaking in to steal, I thought no one was home; after stowing the loot I even used the owner’s toilet.
The woman in the bathtub was startled awake by the noise. She had been trying to end her life — she had swallowed pills earlier, yet was still alive. When she saw me, she paid no mind to being robbed; she only asked me to hand her the bottle of poison beside the tub.
I did not try to save her; I simply did as she asked. The woman took it as a favor granted, thanked me, and reminded me to close the door well on my way out. I took the valuables and left her to go on with the poison.
It was only as I was leaving the compound that I remembered I had forgotten to flush the toilet. I turned straight back to see to it — what was on my mind was still the mess I had left behind.
hints: She was trying to end her life, and took the handing over of the poison as a favor granted.
I had broken in to steal, and used the toilet along the way.
I turned back only because I had forgotten to flush; my fixation with cleanliness never made me spare a thought for her life.

title: The General Who Came with the Bride
story:
When the prince celebrated his grand wedding, the bride arrived with an attendant in her retinue. Later the prince took the throne, and that attendant rose to be a general.
The neighboring kingdom was invaded, and its royal family was murdered by mountain bandits as they fled. Enraged, the king sent this very general to wipe out the bandits’ stronghold.
The stronghold fell. The princess who had originally come to seal the marriage alliance died inside it as well.
answer:
When the neighboring kingdom’s princess set out to be married, bandits abducted her at the border and kept her at their stronghold. The bandit chief’s younger sister took her place, brought a trusted henchman of her own along as the attendant, and continued the journey to the prince’s kingdom. The two courts had never met face to face, so the prince married the stand-in.
A few years later, the prince became king, the stand-in became queen, and the attendant who had come with her became a general. The real princess stayed a captive in the stronghold the whole time.
The neighboring kingdom was invaded, and its royal family set out to take refuge in the land their daughter had married into. The bandit chief knew they would recognize his sister as a false princess, so he ambushed and slaughtered the fleeing royals beforehand to protect her.
The king, learning that his wife’s family had been killed by bandits, ordered the general to wipe them out. The queen, however, secretly instructed her old henchman to silence the matter for good — to kill everyone in the stronghold who knew the secret of the substitution, without even sparing her own older brother.
The general killed the bandit chief, and he killed the real princess too. The king believed he was avenging his in-laws; in truth he had removed, on the false queen’s behalf, the last people who could ever expose her.
hints: The bride and the princess who died in the stronghold at the end are two different people.
The attendant who came with the bride later became the general; he had been her trusted old henchman from the start.

The bandits swapped the chief’s sister in for the princess and killed the royals to protect her identity; the false queen then used the extermination order to silence her brother and the true princess in one stroke.

title: The Rescue
story:
My wife died in a car crash, and for ten years I ached to save her.
At last, one day, I sat behind the wheel again, and I saw her walk out of that same hotel from back then.
I did not save her.
I lost her all over again — and I have never regretted pressing down on the accelerator.
answer:
I had gotten hold of a time-traveling car that could carry a person and itself back into the past. I drove it to the day of my wife’s fatal crash, meaning to get her away before the accident.
At that same intersection, I saw my wife come out of the hotel with her lover, and the two embraced and kissed. In that instant I understood what she had been hiding from me all her life.
I had meant to pull over and warn her, but in my fury I changed my mind. I pressed the pedal, ran them both down, and then drove the car back to my own time, ten years later.
The hit-and-run from back then, the one no culprit was ever found for, had been caused all along by me, arriving from ten years in the future. The past had always contained this journey; I did not create some new history.
I had suffered ten years over my wife’s death — and in the end, at the very moment I believed I could save her, I caused it with my own hands.
hints: I drove back from ten years in the future and saw her again at the intersection where she died.
What I saw outside the hotel changed my decision to save her.
The driver who killed my wife back then was me, returned through time; the past had always included that act.

title: Only I Woke Up
story:
I woke up.
The corridor was silent; they were all still asleep.
I ran down it, pressing the buttons on one door after another, and no one answered.
At last, I saw clearly the date on the screen.
I broke down.
answer:
I was a passenger on an interstellar liner, scheduled to hibernate alongside everyone else until we reached our destination hundreds of years from now.
My hibernation pod malfunctioned and woke me early — and it could not be used again. There was no spare pod aboard. The other passengers’ pods were governed by the arrival program and could not be woken by hand in mid-voyage; no matter how many times I pressed the call buttons on their doors, they would not wake.
The screen showed that the scheduled waking day still lay hundreds of years ahead. The ship could keep flying and keep me alive automatically, but I could never hibernate again, and I would not live to see that day.
For every year of life I had left, I would remain wide awake aboard a ship full of sleepers. Once I understood that, I broke down.
hints: These people are in long-term hibernation, and the narrator alone has woken early.
Only my own pod is broken; the other pods run on the arrival program, and passengers cannot be woken by hand.
The ship still has hundreds of years to fly; I cannot hibernate again, and I cannot live long enough to see the day they wake.

title: The Treatment
story:
Mother had no money to treat her kidney disease. Her son said he would go and get screened as a donor.
She grabbed hold of him and refused, no matter what.
The son simply assumed she could not bear it for his sake.
answer:
The mother needed a kidney transplant. Her son wanted to donate one of his kidneys to her, and he had not yet gone through the donor evaluation.
She knew her son was already down to one kidney. When he was little, she had struck an illegal deal to raise money for her business and arranged for one of his kidneys to be cut out, then lied to the child that it was just an operation to treat an illness. He never knew.
Now that her son had offered to donate of his own accord, she could not accept it — and she feared the screening would bring the old secret to light — so she stopped him with all her might.
The son later went to the hospital for tests anyway, and only then discovered that he was missing a kidney. Pressed about it, his mother admitted what had happened, and he finally understood why she had tried to stop him.
hints: When the son offered to donate, he had not yet been evaluated and did not know the state of his own body.
The mother knows what that operation in his childhood really took out.
The mother illegally sold one of his kidneys for money when he was little and lied to him ever since; the donation screening would have exposed it.

title: The Fatal Phone Call
story:
A rich man phoned his wife.
The call never got answered.
And yet the wife died because of that call.
answer: The rich man loved his wife dearly. That day a burglar had slipped into the house, and the wife was hiding somewhere inside. When her husband called, her phone was not on silent; the ringtone suddenly rang out and gave away her position, and the burglar killed her.
hints: The ringing phone let someone hear where the wife was.
The wife was hiding in the house, trying to stay clear of an intruder.
Her phone was not silenced; her husband’s incoming call exposed her hiding place, and the intruder found her and killed her.

title: The Fatal Words
story:
His wife fell from the cliff.
Years later, the man brought his daughter to that same place.
The daughter said one sentence to him.
This time, it was he who went over the edge.
answer:
Years earlier, the man had pushed his wife off the cliff and killed her. He later remarried and had a daughter.
In this world, reincarnation exists that carries the memories of a past life — and the daughter was his late wife reborn. She had always remembered being pushed over by him.
Once the daughter grew into her teens, the man took her hiking up that mountain again. At the cliff’s edge, the daughter said: “This time, don’t push me off again.”
The man turned to her in shock. Taking advantage of him standing off guard at the edge, the daughter gave him a shove and sent him over the cliff too. That sentence revealed how she could know about the old days, and it showed that this was no causeless accident.
hints: What the daughter said contained things about the past she had no way of knowing.
In this story, reincarnation exists that keeps the memories of a past life.
The first wife was pushed off by her husband, was reborn as his daughter, and on that same cliff pushed him off in turn.

title: Finally Full
story:
After I was cursed, I stayed hungry no matter how much I ate.
That day, I sneaked into someone’s house, dug out whatever food I could find and stuffed it into my mouth.
The owner came home and, in a fury, threw a question at me.
I answered “Yes” again and again.
That meal, I was finally full.
answer:
I had been a man-eating villain, and I was cursed as follows: only human flesh could ease my hunger, and I could take nothing from a person unless that person asked me whether I wanted something they owned. Once they asked and I accepted, that thing became mine to take — the words took effect literally.
Racked by hunger, I broke into a house and rummaged for food, yet I never felt full. When the owner caught me, he shouted in rage: “You want a piece of me?!”
He meant it as an insult, but the curse took the question as permission to take a piece of him. I answered “Yes” over and over, then set upon the owner, ate his flesh and blood, and my hunger was finally eased.
The owner had no thought of feeding me; one furious turn of phrase met the very condition that bound me.
hints: The owner was not inviting me to a meal; what he threw at me was a stock insult.
The curse reads any question literally, letting me take that very thing from the speaker.
He shouted “You want a piece of me?” — I said yes, and took my piece of him and ate it.

title: The Spider-Silk Town
story:
Dozens of townsfolk vanished one after another, and every house they left behind held traces of spider silk.
A guard post went up at the town gate, and the disappearances stopped for a time.
Before long, the man who lived in the hills behind town vanished too.
This time, the silk stretched from the back hills all the way to the edge of the streets.
answer:
In this invented world there are giant spiders that prey on people, and a man living in the hills behind town had long been raising a brood of them.
The man had once been disfigured by people of the town. He knew that the ones who had maimed him feared spiders, so he decided to use the spiders to create terror. Over and over he abducted townsfolk and fed them to the giant spiders in the hills as food, and he left spider silk in each missing person’s house so the town would suspect the spiders were at work.
After the town tightened its guard, the man could no longer abduct anyone. Deprived of food, the giant spiders turned on the man who had raised them, attacked and ate him, then crawled down out of the hills and into the town to hunt.
The first wave of disappearances was the man’s doing, the silk a threat he planted deliberately; the second wave, with silk strung as far as the edge of the streets, was the giant spiders truly coming down the mountain.
hints: Between the two waves of disappearances, the hand behind them changed.
The man in the hills raised giant man-eating spiders and at first abducted people to feed them.
The guards cut off their food supply; the spiders devoured their keeper and entered the town — the disaster once only staged became real.

title: I Found My Sister
story:
At Grandpa’s funeral, my big sister and I played hide-and-seek.
I searched for a long, long time before I finally saw her.
I ran back, tugged at Mommy’s sleeve, pointed at that blaze of flames and said: “Found her! Sis is dancing in that pretty house!”
When Mommy heard me, she dropped to the ground.
answer:
I was six, and my sister was eight. At the funeral, the grown-ups were getting ready to burn a grand paper effigy house built for Grandpa — the kind of funeral offering made to be burned so the dead can have it. When my sister’s turn to hide came around, she climbed inside it, certain I would never find her there.
When the rite began, none of the grown-ups noticed there was a child inside, and they set the paper house alight. My sister’s clothes caught fire; in her panic, the hem of her dress snagged on the frame inside, and she could not get out in time.
When I found her, all I could see was a figure writhing in the flames. Too little to know it was a struggle of pain, I took it for dancing, and I ran off, thrilled, to tell Mommy.
Only from my words did Mommy understand that my sister was inside the burning paper house, and she fainted from the shock. The others rushed to save her, but my sister was already gravely burned, and in the end she could not be saved.
hints: That house was something meant to be burned at the funeral, and the grown-ups did not know someone was hiding inside.
My sister had hidden inside the grand paper effigy house, and I mistook her thrashing in the fire for dancing.
She was still inside when the paper house was lit; hearing my excited report, Mommy grasped the tragedy at once.

title: I’ll Be It
story:
After years away from my home village, my son started clamoring for hide-and-seek the moment we walked in.
I was It. My wife’s hiding spot was not that good, and yet my son just could not find her.
I remembered the most hidden spot from my own childhood, and walked toward it.
The child inside turned his head: “You finally found me.”
Behind me, my son was calling for Daddy too.
answer:
When I was little, I was about to move far away with my mother. A childhood friend whose family had already moved off snuck back into the village to say goodbye. We played hide-and-seek with the other children; I led him into an abandoned cellar, then pulled the lid shut — it could only be opened from outside — and told him I would come back for him soon.
My mother suddenly hurried me into the car, and I left with her, forgetting my friend still trapped in the cellar. His family did not know he had snuck back to the village, and no one in the village knew where he had hidden. No one ever came for him, and in the end he died in that cellar.
In this story, his ghost stayed on at the spot where he had hidden, still in the shape of a child.
Years later I brought my wife and son back to the village, and while searching for my son I came to that cellar again. The child who turned his head and spoke was my friend’s ghost. My son had actually hidden somewhere else entirely, and had run back on his own, calling for me.
“You finally found me” reminded me of the thing I had left unfinished all those years ago. Later the cellar was opened, and my friend’s remains were found inside.
hints: The child who speaks and the son behind me shouting for Daddy are two different people.
As a child, I once hid another child in that place too — and never went back for him.
My childhood friend died trapped in the abandoned cellar, and his ghost went on waiting; only when I finally returned years later did he say I had found him.

title: The Selfie
story:
A woman he knew only through an online romance asked him to send a selfie.
When she had looked at it, she said: “Don’t get so close to the camera — I want to see where you work.”
He took another one.
The next day, he was dead.
answer:
The man was a commander on the battlefield; the woman was an operative the enemy had sent to get close to him, using the cover of an online romance to fish out intelligence.
The first photo showed mostly his face, so, on the pretext of wanting to see his work environment, she had him take the camp behind him into the frame as well. In the retake, the man sent her the nearby, conspicuous terrain and installations along with everything else.
The enemy already held reconnaissance data on that region, and the photos let them confirm which camp the man was in. The next day, the place was hit by a drone strike, and the man was killed in the blast.
What the woman wanted to see, from beginning to end, was the setting in the photos; the romance was only the cover that made him willing to hand the photos over himself.
hints: The man’s workplace is a wartime camp that must stay secret.
She had him shoot more of the surroundings because she wanted the camp’s position pinned down.
The online lover came from the enemy side; the photos, matched against existing reconnaissance, confirmed the location, and the strike followed.

title: The Broken Bicycle
story:
My bicycle broke, and the repairman at the school gate made a nice little sum off me.
The next day, the teacher’s bicycle and every classmate’s bicycle broke too.
I went and said a few words to the teacher.
Later on, the repairman died.
answer:
My tire was punctured, so I took the bike to the repair stand at the school gate. The repairman went on to deliberately damage parts that had been perfectly fine, forcing me to pay more. I saw him do it, but I was young and did not dare argue with him on the spot.
I held it against him. The next day, I wrecked the teacher’s and the whole class’s bicycles myself, then told the teacher I had seen the repairman sneak into the school and sabotage them.
People watched the bikes fail one after another, and having heard he had a record of padding bills on purpose before, they believed my testimony. Furious parents went to the repair stand to confront him; the quarrel escalated, he was beaten by the crowd, and he died of his injuries.
The extra damage to the first bike really was the repairman’s doing; the second batch was entirely mine. With his past misdeeds and my own lie, I turned the fury of a crowd upon him.
hints: The first bike and the second batch were damaged by different hands.
The so-called eyewitness account I gave the teacher was a lie.
To get back at the repairman, I wrecked the whole class’s bikes, framed him for it, and set off the beating by the parents that killed him.

title: The Right Key
story:
The place downstairs had been under renovation for months; yesterday, it finally fell quiet.
My friend and I came home from drinking. The elevator was out of service, so we had to climb the stairs.
At my door, I opened it with my own key. Every piece of furniture was where it had always been, yet something felt wrong.
My friend told me to lock the door good and tight, then left.
The next day, he could not find me anywhere.
answer:
I had refused a wealthy suitor. He would not give up, and he bought the unit one floor directly below mine, laid out in the same position; the renovation noise came from there.
Whenever I was out, he entered my home, noted down how everything was arranged, and made the downstairs unit into a nearly identical copy of my rooms. He even had a lock fitted that my original key would open.
That night he followed me, saw that both I and the friend walking me home were drunk, and deliberately shut down the elevator and swapped the floor signs on the relevant landing. Believing the signs as we climbed, we came up one floor short and stopped at the door of his unit.
My key opened it, and inside it looked like my own home, so I sensed nothing at first. After my friend left, the suitor, hidden inside, came out and imprisoned me.
The next day my friend went to my real home and, of course, could not find me. I had used my own key correctly — and unlocked my way into a forged copy of my home.
hints: The key was real, but that door’s lock had been made on purpose to open to it.
The long-renovated place was the identically placed unit one floor below, its furniture copied after mine.
The suitor switched the floor signs so that I, drunk, walked into the copied room below, and he then held me captive.

title: The Seventeenth Floor
story:
She lives on the twenty-fifth floor, and heading out she always rides the elevator straight down to the first.
Coming home, though, she rides only as far as the seventeenth and climbs the rest of the way herself.
On the day it rained, she could ride straight up to the twenty-fifth.
When someone shared the elevator with her, she could too.
answer:
She is very short. In this building the elevator buttons are stacked from the lowest floor to the highest, and the seventeenth floor is the highest button she can reach; the button for the twenty-fifth floor sits beyond her grasp.
Heading down in the morning, she can press the first-floor button at the very bottom. Coming home on a normal day, she can only ride to the seventeenth and take the stairs from there, because nothing she carries day to day can be used to press the higher buttons.
When it rains, she has her umbrella with her, and its tip can reach the twenty-fifth-floor button. A fellow passenger can also press it for her — so in those two cases, she can ride all the way to the floor she lives on.
hints: Going down and going up, the buttons she needs to press sit at different heights.
A rainy day gives her one extra object long enough to reach up with.
She cannot reach the twenty-fifth-floor button; an umbrella tip, or a fellow passenger, can press it for her.

title: My Favorite
story:
Mommy always feeds me vegetables and fruit; my little brother loves to feed me ice cream.
I love Daddy best of all. Now my belly is full of his flesh.
Ever since then, I have not seen Mommy or my brother again.
Only Daddy has stayed with me, the whole time.
answer:
The “I” telling this is the family’s refrigerator: the narration calls food being put into it “eating,” and calls the family members Mommy, little brother, and Daddy.
Mommy often put the vegetables and fruit she bought into the fridge, and the child put the ice cream in. Daddy, again and again, beat his wife and children after drinking.
After one such beating, Mommy killed Daddy while he slept, cut his body apart and placed it in the fridge, then fled the house with the children.
So the flesh came from Daddy, and the one who put it there was Mommy. I never saw Mommy or my brother again because they left; Daddy stayed inside, becoming the one thing that was never taken back out.
hints: “Eating” can also mean something being stored into a container; the narrator is not a child of this family.
The vegetables and fruit, the ice cream, and at the last the flesh all went into the same refrigerator.
Mommy killed her abusive husband, hid his body in the fridge, and left with the children; the flesh that stayed behind is Daddy.

title: Tears on the Wooden Ladder
story: Late at night, a man collapsed dead drunk in the open wilds, an old, battered wooden ladder pinned under his body. When someone shook him awake, he stared at the ladder before him and suddenly broke down.
answer: He drank out of despair, planning to end his life by lying down on the railway tracks. Stumbling, half-blind with drink, into the wasteland, he took a wooden ladder lying flat on the ground for the rails, and lay down on it. Waking up, he realized he had failed even at killing himself; grief welled up over him, and he sobbed aloud.
hints: The drink made him mistake the wooden ladder for something else with a similar shape.
He had been trying to end his own life.
He mistook the ladder for railway tracks; waking to find himself still alive, the despair came over him all over again.
